The Legislature of Illinois having propesed to pass a bit. -requiring hotel keepers to furnisa every room above the second story with a rope ladder, as a fire escape, the land- lords bit back by-saying that it is a mere device on the part of the legislatort to enable them to slip away from ,their hotel rooms without paying their bills! A witty nobleman once asked a clerical gentleman, at the bottom of the table, why the goose, when there was one, -was always Placed next to the parson. "Really my Lord," zaaid the clergyman, "your question is somewhat difficult to ,answer, and so remarkably odd that I row I shall never see as goose aga:n withoutlee:ng reminded of your Lordship." A CONSERVATIVE FA.RADISE.—There is an old riddle which is us follows, "Why is a bald head like heaven ?" • The answer to which is, "Because it is all clear and shining, and therre is no part-irg there." This conundrum was pro- pounded to the late Lord Derby when leader of the Tory -party. Re replied-en the instant, "The answer is.palpable : because there are no Whigs there." Acre-legged Welshman named Jones was pretty success- ful in bantering-sea Irishman, when the latter asked him, How did you come to lose your leg?" "Well," said Jones, "on examining my pedigree an looking up my descent I found there was some Irish blood in me, and be- oming convinced that it had settled in that left leg, I had =it cut off at once." "Be the powers," said Pat, "it would 'lave been a better thing if it had settled in your head." Each of us ought to strive for excellence in one thing; ',but we also need "a little knowledge" in many others. We -cannot all be lawyers; but we all need some acquaintance with the laws of the land we live in. We cannot all under- stand medical science; but we all need some general insight into the laws of health. We cannot all be politicians; but we all want some cognisanee of our own public affairs. We cannot all be mechanics; yet we shall all at times want to know how to use tools. TUE STRENGTU AND MODESTY OF Glesters.—Leech was singularly modest, both as a man and an artist. This came by nature, and was indicative of the harmony and sweetness of its essence; but doubtless the perpetual going to nature, and drawing out of her fulneSs, kept him humble, as well as made him rich, made him what every man Of sense and 'power must be—conscious of his own strength; but before the great mother he was simple and loving, attentive to her lessons, as a child, for ever learning and doing.—John Leech, by Dr. John Brown. A Cussous COINCIDENCE.—When George 111. went to .Plymouth in 1787 to lay the foundation-stone of the great North Dock, he noticed that the architect had exceeded the ,dimensions which had been given to him by the Navy Board, and requested an explanation. Mr. Parlby, the builder, said it was so altered because the French were then constructing at Toulon a ship called the Commerce de Marseilles, which was so large that none of Majesty's docks but this would be large enough for its accommodation. Curiously enough, when war broke out, and Toulon was given up with its ship- ping and arsenal, this very vessel was brought into this dock, and was the first it received.—London Society. • UNITY AND VARIETY.—The hoof of the horse, the horn of the ox and rhinoceros, the nail of the finger, the rich plumes of the peacock's train or the dazzling brilliance of the humming bird's breast, the soft tresses of a young girl, the scale of the serpent or fish, the tusk of the elephant, and the claw of the tiger, are only modifications of one and the same structure. There is now before me a series of specimens in which this modification is so perfectly illus- trated, that however different a tooth, a claw, a feather, and a hair may seem to be, it is impossible to draw a line which will separate either of these' structures from the other.— Good Words. ABUSING TIIE MOTHER-TONGITE.—What with the gram- mar makers and the grammar unmakers, the good mother- tongue has been sadly troubled in our time. The rule now is to speak incorrectly and as verbosely as possible. The mere dregs of euphuism—euphuisnewithout euphony; with no thought of grace and with no desire for grammar—are now left us. We say, "A certain person informed me that such was the ease," WIWI them was no ease, when the per- son was not certain, when he may or may not have been a person, and when he neither did nor could inform. The old way of speaking would have been, "Somebody told me so." This is sense and grammar; there are four words instead of ten to speak, sixteen letters instead of forty-two to write; and, written or said, there is precision against gibberish.— Gocd Words for June. A BIRD'S APPETITE.—The appetite of the bird is won- derful. A thrush will eat at a meal the largest snail that England produces. °lf a man could eat as much in propor- tion, he would consume a whole round of beef for his dinner. The redbreast, again, is a most voracious bird. It has been calculated that to keep a redbreast up to his normal weight an amount of animal food is required daily equal to an earthworm fourteen feet in length. Taking a man of aver- age weight, and measuring bulk for bulk with the red- breast, I tried to calculate how much food he would con- sume in twenty-four hours if he ate as much in proportion as the bird. Assuming a sausage nine inches in circumfer- ence to be a fair equivalent of the earthworm, I find that the man -would have to eat sixty-seven feet of such sausage in every twenty-four hours. I mention this in order to illustrate the amount of work which is done by insect-eating birds.—Good Words. NEGRO Astusnatzarrs.—Fating, smoking, sleeping, fight- ing, dancing, gambling a little, and wrestling, may be said to form in outline the list of a Central African's amuse- ments. Even the exer+ ion necessary to amuse themselves is too much energy for the Negro character. Accordingly they take little pleasure in the active out-door amusements which, we have already seen, some savages even lower in the scale of civilisation than they delight in. Wrestling is about the only manly amusement they care for, for hunting and fishing are their daily occupations, and therefore cannot be looked upon as amusements. Wrestling, however, is only practised among the more civilised races, such as the Bergharni, who, though possessed of a certain degree of polish, are very negro-like, their skin being black. They are, however, noted athletes. So keenly do they contest in wrestling, that it is not an unfrequent occurrence for one of the contestants to be left dead on the ground. Great men among this people will keep in their pay,- or as slaves, powerful wrestlers, on whose prowess they highly pride themselves. A wrestler once beaten is looked upon as good as done for altogether, and, if a slave, would be sold for a mere fraction of the price he was valued at before meeting with this reverse of fortune. In addition, all the Berghami, but particularly the women, are good dancers, being active and yet graceful in all their movements. Their dancing is a sort of acting in &nib show, and all the while they keep up a low plaintive song, which adds wondrously to the pleasant impression the scene makes on the onlooker. Music and dancing are passions throughout Africa.—The Peoples of the World. WEALTH, ANT) How TO ATTAIN IT.—There is one im- portant practical truth that can never be told too often, as upon it depends the comfort of the mass of our people. It is this order to be wealthy—that is to have such a competence as secures independence and comfort—men must save. Would that it might be written a hundred times on this page, and each one of the hundred read a hundred times. To save is the practical point of the subject, and the one that should ever be insisted on. It matters not what may be the system of practical economists as to wealth and the means of production, unless it be one which can be prac- tised by the mass of the labouring people; the products of the labour of wealth are constantly in use, and must be con- stantly renewed; therefore man may as well accept, Without a murmur, the fact that he must lead a life of labour, and not ot play. It is unwise, and in the main useless, for the majority of the active men of to-day to seek large fortunes —that is, to become millionaires—simply because it is im- possible. But, on the other hand, there is no reason why our induetrious labourers of all sorts should mil become pos- eessed of sufficient wealth for comfort. The great trouble lies in the fact that young men do not begin to save when they are young. But something in the savings bank at the age of twenty, and continue to do so each week until fifty, and there will be a snug little fortune for a man and wife ; fail to do this, and there will be nothing. Begin by small savings rather than not begin at all, for the finest showers often begin with a few gentle drops. One gee cause of the poverty of the present day is the failure of our common people to appreciate small things. They feel that if they cannot save large sums they will not save anything. They do not realise how a daily addition, be it ever so small, will soon make a large pile. If the young men and young women of to-day will only begin, and begin now, to save a little from their earnings, and plant it in the soil of some good savings bank, and weekly or monthly add their mite, they will wear a smile of competence and independence when they reach middle life. Not only the pile itself will in. crease, but the desire and ability to increase it will also grow. Let clerk or tradesman, labourer or artisan, make now and at once a beginning; store up some of your youth- ful vigour for- future contingency. Let parents teach their children early to save. Begin at the fountain head to con- trol the stream of extravagance, and the work will be easy. Choose between poverty and Haws. Let your youth go on in habits of extravagance for fifty years to come as they have for fifty years past, and we shall see a nation of beg- gars, with a moneyed Aristocracy. Let a generation such as save in small sums be reared, and we shall be free from all want. Do not be ambitious for extravagant fortunes, but seek that which it is the duty of everyone to obtain— independence and a comfortable home.

Detaille, the well-known painter of battle-scenes, is show- ing his friends and acquaintances at Paris a magnificent little sketch bearing the signature of Meissonnier. It ap- pears that the latter called at the house of his colleague in the Avenue de Villiers, and, finding hira_out, went into the billiard-room to have some practice. In making a difficult stroke he cut a hole in the cloth. Not knowing how to re- pair the damage, he took a piece of paper and made a sketch of a man and then pasted it over the hole in the cloth, as some recompense for the injury. An amateur has etered £4O for the sketch, b M. Detaille prefers to keep it as a souveniel ARTIFICIAL LIZATTIEE FROM LEATIIER, WASTE.--An arti- ficial leather, consisting of leather waste mixed with from 5 to 10 per cent. of sinew, and pressed in sheets lEte ordinary card-board, has recently been made in Germany. Both materials are prepared separately; the leather pieces are washed, cut, boiled in alkaline lye, torn, neutralised with hydro-chloric acid, and finally carefully washed once more to remove all traces of acid ; the sinews are treated simi- larly, but steamed in an acid bath until they begin to assume the consistence of glue. The materials are then mixed, pressed into sheets, moistened on both sides with a concen- trated solution of alum, and the upper surface is'finally treated Ivith a thin coat of ' a solution of 'caoutchouc in carbon bisulphide to increase its resemblance to leather.— _ Engineering. At a recent regional show at Faix, some novel and in- teretting experiments were tried, with the view of protect- ing Tines from the spring frosts. M. Lestelle, sub-inspector -of posts and telegraphs at Mont de Marsan, is the inventor of the system, which consists in firing 'combustible mate- rials by means of electricity, and so producing artificial clouds of smoke, to prevent the radiation of heat from the ground. Two platinum wires are passed into the mercury of a thermometer, and fixed with screws to two copper wires communicating with a cell battery. From the battery copper wires are carried over the surface of the vineyard, and divided at as many points as are required for centres of combustion. . At these centres resinous and other combus- tible matters are heaped. The descent of the temperature produces contact, and causes the instantaneous kindling of all the combustible centres. THE TRANSMISSION OF Sounns ale Gascs.—M. Neyre- neuf has communicated to the French Academy of Sciences the results of experiments made by him on the intensity of sonorous vibrations transmitted through different gases. He placed a sound source on one side of the gaseous cham- ber, and 'a sensitive flame on the other, and observed the action of the flame. The gases tested thus far are air, car- bonic oxide' lighting gas, and carbonic acid. Air and car- bonic acid have a transmission power about equal. Air and lighting gas give very unequal results, probably_ because of the. hydrogen in the. latter. The msults:vary with the chemical constitution of the coal gas employed. The trans- missive power through carbonic acid is much greater than through air. The results show that Hauksbee's law is not correct, and the author is continuing his researches with a view of throwing further light on the dynamical theory of

gases ..—Engineering. THE RADIATION OF SILVER IN SOLIDIVICINO.—At the international congress of electricians in 1881, M. J. Violle proposed, and M. Dumas, the famous chemist, seconded, the use of an absolute unit of light consisting of the radiation emitted by a square centimetre of platinum in melting. At the instance of M. Coehery, the French Minister of Posts and Telegraphs, an investigation •of the subject has been begun by M. Violle, and his first experiments have led him to some observations on the radiation of silver in solidify- ing. A bath of -pure melted silver was placed under a thermo-electric pile connected with a mirror galvanometer. The radiation from the bath fell normally on the battery through an aperature in a double-walled screen kept cool by circulating water. As the bath cooled, the pile showed that the radiation slowly decreased until the instant just before solidifying, when there was a slight increase, pre- ceding the -final 'decrease after solidification.—Engineering. NATURAL Snown.u.r..s.—lt may not be generally known that the wind now and then takes it into its head to make snowballs, and that it can make very good ones too. Quite recently many square miles of country in the United States were covered with snowballs of all shapes and sizes, which the wind had rolled up in a single night. On the previous evening a light but damp snow fell on the frozen ground, and the wind, changing to the south, began to set in mo- tion small pellets of snow, and to roll them all along until they became too large to be moved farther. Some of the snowballs were no less than three feet in diameter, while others were very much smaller. In many cases the path of the ball could be traced for a distance of twenty-five, thirty, and even sixty feet, and in certain instances the tracts showed that the snowballs had actually been blown up hill. This curious phenomenon, although very rare, has been no- ticed before in several countries.—Little Folks' Magazine, for June. Numismenc TREASURES.—A sovereign of Edward VI., presumed to be the second best known, was knocked down on Monday by Messrs. Sotheby for £lOO. This famous coin, which bears the likeness of the King seated in his chair of State, has held place of honour in the Grey, Mead, Whet, Durrant, Brown, and Addington cabinets. Its late owner is a leading member of the Numismatic Society, who is disposing of his duplicate collection. Many other coins were sold for high prices. A sovereign of Henry VII., with the King seated under an ornamental canopy, realised £3l; another of Henry VIII., once in the Murchison cabinet, £2l; a thirty-shilling piece of James 1., fine and rare, £ll 17s. 6d.; and a noble or "spur royal," bearing a design of his Majesty standing in a ship, £l3 10s. Another specimen of the latter coin sold for £9 2s. 6d. only, being cracked. A half-sovereign of "Good Queen Bess" brought £6 2s. 6d.; a milled crown of the same reign, described as "a little gem," £18; a rose rial of James 1., £9; an angel of Richard 111., a 178. 6d.; and a crown of James I. (silver), £4 4s. A cracked silver Anglo-Saxon penny was snapped up at £1 138. •, another in perfect condition, of the time of Athelstan, was briskly competed for up to £7 55.; and a London silver penny of Edward IV. realised £3. -

THE TEACHING OF THE DEAF.—The annual meeting of the Society for Training Teachers of the Deaf and the Dif- fusion of the "German" System in the United Kingdom was held on Wednesday afternoon, at the Training College, Elmhurst, Castle Bar Hill, Ealing, General Cotton presid- ing. The report, an abstract of which was laid before the meeting by the Secretary, Dr. Buxton, congratulated the friends of the society that the pure oral teaching of the deaf, established in Germany by Samuel Heinicke about 130 years ago, has since the establishment of the society in 1877 met with remarkable success in this country, the preoccu- pation of the ground by other systems being the great ob- stacle to more rapid progress, though these were, it was remarked, rapidly losing their position. The schools in which the teaching of speech by means of speech is the adopted method of instruction were now more than 60 per cent. of the whole number in operation throughout the world, the proportion having risen to that point from 52i per cent. in 1882, while the number of pupils rose during the same period from 10,506 to 13,246. The work of pre- paring students in the society's Training College and of in- structing deaf children in the school went on successfully. Sevpnteen students ha(l passed the examinations since the college was opened. The demand for teachers continued, es- pecially for the instruction of children in classes formed or contemplated under School Boards; and it was much to be wished that the school authorities of every large town would address themselves to local needs and es- tablish classes for their own deaf children. The committee of the Manchester Schools for the Deaf and Dumb had warmly taken up the pure oral system, the most serious drawback which they found being the want of trained teachers, a want which that society was established to sup- ply. At the Mansion House meeting and others held during the last year strong appeals were made for substantial addi- tions to the society's funds; but, £lO,OOO being needed, only £l,OOO had been received. Two years ago the college was removed to more extensive grounds, in order that increased accommodation might be built; but the work of enlarge- ment could not be commenced until the property had be- come the freehold of the society, and it was under the obli- gation to buy that the new premises were taken. The balance sheet showed that the expenditure of the year ex- ceeded the ordinary income by £B4o.—After the business meeting there was a conversazione, and an opportunity was afforded to visitors of witnessing the oral method of instruc- tion in actual operation, and observing the progress of the pupils. It appears that numerous applications for teachers on that system thus illustrated beyond what the society can meet are constantly being received from the United Kingdom, the colonies, and other countries.

How extravagantly unjust party spirit makes men.— Macaulay. ABOUT amis.—There is a quaint story to be told of the origin of many crests. The origin of the motto may be worth noting; for instance, the motto of the Leslies, Grip Fast, is historical. When Queen Margaret of Scotland was , shipwrecked and drowning near the shore, a Leslie threw his belt to her, shouting, "Grip fast !" and saved her life. , Again, the Dukes of Hamilton have but one word, Through —because an ancestor of theirs eseaped from pursuit in a forest by changing clothes with a wood-cutter; and when his pursuers reached the spot, he bade the woodmen work- ing with him not to stop in sawing a tree trunk, telling them to saw it " thtough, by which presence of mind he remained unsuspected. The incident furnishes the crest of the fatally—an oak tree with a saw half through it. The Stanleys, the Earls of Derby, have a very curious crest—an infant closely swathed in a cradle, with an eagle standing over it. It is an erliblem of the rescue of a little child of the family, who was carried up into a high tree by an eagle. The Dukes of Leinster have a monkey for their crest, in memory of another rescue, when, long ago, the child who was the heir of the family was stolen and hidden by a mis- chievous monkey. Under the crest is the representation of a twisted wreath. It was once the wreath worn on the helmet, and twisted of gold or silver lace and silk, of the principal colour and the principal metal in the arms upon the shield. This wreath was made by the knight's "faire ladye" before he rode to tournament or battle. Instead of it, there is sometimes a coronet or crown. A ducal coronet is marked by standing strawberry leaves round its rim ; they were once oak leaves, the symbol of victory. A "mural crown" shows the battlements of a tower, and is placed under the crest of soldiers who have been the first to enter a besieged town, while the "naval crown" is given for naval victories; and thus it was that our brave Nelson—Who, with only one arm and one eye left, did such great wonders on the sea—had under his crest the honour of the naval crown, with little square sails' and sterns of ships standing up all -round its edge.—" Little Folks". for Tune.

Over .100. farms in Orange County, New York, are adver- tised .or sale by a New York firm of agents. The reason assirgted is that the land is worked out, and the farmers are de'siroue to try the West. A big, sew, weighing no less than 39i stones was killed this week on the farm of Cardryne, Kirkmaiden.- This huge animal was bred by Mr_. Milvain, and purchased by Mr. MWilliani, Stranraer. Prtiessor Birner says that the loss of nitrogen in manure on long keeping is considerable, hut-almost disappears if the manure is protected against moisture. On the addition of 1 per cent. of kainit and 1 per cent. of magnesium sulphate, the nitrogen is increased by absOrptiOn from the atmosphere. An extraordinary case or cattle poisoning has occurred on the estate of Major Roberts, at Holborough, near Chatham. About fifty head of cattle were grazing on some marsh land, When they came across some red lead which had been incau- tiously left there, and all the animals partook of it, with the result that they were all poisoned. Fourteen have already died, and it is expected the majority of them will sucicumh. . M. Mine presided at the annual dinner of the Horticul- tural Society. In the course -of his toast to the Minister, M. Lavalles, president, remarked that market gardening, confined of old to the neighbourhood of great towns, is gradually extending into the most retired portions of the provinces, and forms a serious rival to agriculture. The view of this progress and activity has caused thedetermina- tion of the society to open an international exhibition in 1885. BONE MEAL.—Experiments at the American College of Agriculture with bone meal have-led to the following con- alusions : That it is • admirably -adapted for renewing some of our soils which have been impoverished by injudicious cropping. We may even go farther, and say that some soils at present giving good crops could he 4.ressed with the bone meal with a very decided increase in the net profits derived from their cultivation. Very striking illustrations of this have been given in our garden of economic plants at the trniversity, which has a black gravelly clay loam, quite different in character from the clay soil of the ridge on which the above experiments were made. There, not only cereals, but beets, turnips, onions, Jerusalem artichokes, &c., respond most satisfactorily to this fertiliser. FARMYARD MANI:MRS.—In a covered yard less straw is wanted to keep the cattle in a comfortable and healthy con- dition than in an open yard, for the simple reason that the straw and manure is not deluged with rain. If it takes a certain amount of the straw to absorb the liquid manure, it stands to reason that it must take more to absorb not only the liquid manure but the whole rainfall, will& is necessary in the case of the open yard. Continued rain is apt to re- duce the whole in an open yard to a nauseous mass, from which the most valuable part of the manure escapes into the drains, and the cattle are rendered disagreeably uncom- fortable. Undoubtedly the best manure is made in the Covered' yard; because the virtue remains in it, and at the Same time the cattle are kept dry and warm as opposed to the damp and cold of the exposed farmyard. The manure may be made to ferment or rot rapidly, but this is not de- sirable, by so arranging it that the air may pass pretty freely through it. The action of the oxygen on the air is absolutely necessary to this process. Consequently, if it is desired to retard the rotting,.it can be done by pressing it down lightly, or by watering it. The water, by filling up the passages by which air would have penetrated, causes it to rot slowly. This slow rotting is a considerable advan- tage, for in the chemical changes which accompany it the nitrogen is more likely to be retained. Thus it is that the best farmyard manure is that obtained from covered yards, which has afterwards been treated with liquid manure from the tank. The heap should not be permitted to get too hot or too dry. Liquid manure thrown on should regulate this. A FLOCKMASTER'S EXPERIENCES.—A flockmaster has given us an account of his experiences during the past season in sundry particulars and although it was not written for publication, we take the liberty of quoting it, as it must be of interest and value to our readers. The ewes have lambed fairly well, the number of doubles being rather less than the average but the single ones have done well. The ewes have not 11.4. d a single turnip during the winter, and they were never more healthy, only three ewes having been lost from inflammation in a flock of upwards of twenty scores. They got half a pound of decorticated cotton cake, increased latterly to about three-quarters of a pound daily. This experience we would commend specially to the atten- tion of all who maintain that a large allowance of watery bulbs are almost indispensable for lambing ewes. Probably they would have been all the better for a limited quantity of turnips had they been available, but in that case the al- lowance of cake would have been reduced. Our corres- pondent has been treatinghis sheep according to homcepathic principles. Two ewes were attacked at different times by severe inflammation previous to lambing, the symptoms being heaving sides, quick pulse, inability to rise, and re- fusal to eat There were administered to each five drops of tincture of aconite in a dessert spoonful of water every hour, and the effect was marvellous; both animals re- covered, though another which was treated on more drastic principles succumbed. The symptoms were precisely simi- lar in all three cases' and the shepherd had given up all hope of recovery. No cases of inflammation after birth have occurred in the flock, carbolic oil having been used in severe cases with complete success. Two or three lambs have been lost from inflammation caused by the formation of curd in the stomach; the dam had too much ;ilia (not- withstanding, be it observed, the want of turnip), and as .the lamb did not draw sufficient from the udder, conse- quently the milk soured and injured the lamb. The remedy in such a case is the natural one—starvation for the while. —Dumfries Courier. AN EXTRAORDINARY Tornx CASE.—A somewhat novel action to recover arrears of extraordinary tithe came before -the Under-Sheriff for Kent at the Maidstone Town Hall, last week. The former vicar of Orpington (Rev. E. F. Dyke, now vicar of Maidstone) has a claim against Mr. Jno. Wood for two years' extraordinary tithe at 7s. per acre, in respect to the fruit plantation at Orpington of 16 acres 38 perches. Mr. Wood had paid the charge from 1876 till 1880, but latterly he has taken a prominent part in the Anti-Extraordinary Tithe Agitation in West Kent, and has ceased his annual payments. There are three remedies against defaulters under the Tithe Commutation Act of 1836. The first is to distrain, as has been not unfrequently done of late, but in this case there was nothing on the land to distrain. The second is to get the landlord to pay the charge, and recoup himself by increasing the rent, but Sir W. Hart-Dyke, Bart., M.P., the landlord in this case, de- clined to move in the matter. The third, and consequently only course open to tlie Rev. E. F. Dyke was to apply to a judge of the High Court of Justice for a writ to ascertain by means of a jury the amount of tithe in arrear, then to take possession of the land and farm it until he has re- couped himself. Mr. M. Smith, barrister, now attended to prove before a jury the amount of arrears and the service of the necessary notices. The sum due was shown to be £ll 19s. 10d. At this inquiry the defaulting tithepayer had no locus standi, and the only objection raised by Mr. Eve who attended for the tenant, was to a service of notice, which, however, was found to have been legally done. The juryat once found that the amount:due was Ell 19s. 10d., and a verdict was entered accordingly. Mr. Dyke will now be enabled to take possession of the fruit plantation, and recover the arrears by farming it himself. This is only the second case of the sort tried in Kent, and it attracted a great deal of interest among payers of extraordinary tithe. STACK COOLING.—Mr. Neilson, originator of the system of stack cooling which goes by his name, has, in response to an inquiry from the Editor of the Field, sent to that journal a letter, which shows that last summer he amended one de- tail in the modus operandi very materially. The assertion, up to a recent period, had been made that Mr. Neilson finds drawing up a sack stuffed with straw amply sufficient to form a chimney in the centre of his stack, but it appears by the letter referred to that at times he has found this to get choked through the uneven settlement of the stack after being formed, and that the method he now deems best is that of braiding what he terms "an open frame of brick- work" surrounding the valve, by which he, no doubt, means bricks set with regular apertures between them, so that there should be a substantial frame, but allowing almost as much suetion ' to operate through and beyond it as if nothing of the kind was there. But Mr. Neilson makes it four feet square, and builds it four feet high, so that it occupies no inconsiderable space, and the question may well be asked whether a framework of less size would not answer the ob- ject in N iew equally well, which is to prevent too close a settlement at the base of the rick ere fetmentation is at its height to render satisfactory suction possible. Two stout pieces of wood are fixed across each other en this frame- work at the ter, and on them, where they meet in the centre, is placed the stuffed sack of straw to carry the chimney about four feet higher. Mr. Neilson's letter is de- fective in one respect He does not say how many stacks he has built on this plan, and what has been his actual ex- perience in respect to this new departure in detail. When the non-success of the Neilson system at Reading was so strongly and unfairly chronicled in the Royal Agricultural Society's Journal last year, I pointed out that not a single one of the competitors professing to display Mr. Neilson's system in full operation had actually done so, and that con- , sequently that system ought not to Is condemned in onse- ' quence of their failures. One short sentence in the letter referred to- above proves this to be true, and he therein states it to be a fundamental principle that the exhaust should be applied "immediately on the temperature begin- ning to rise." Was there one of the Reading competitors that did this? On the contrary, did they not, one and all, maintain that it was all essential that a very high tempera- ture should be attained ere the fan was brought into play?

bIIUNKENNESS AT CARDIFF.—Mr. CALLAN suggested, in a question, that the increase of drunkenness at Cardiff since the Sunday Closing Act came into operation was in a great measure caused by illicit drinking and the remarkable in- crease in the number of clubs.—lt was the opinion of Mr. Censure that the close proximity of Monmonthshire, where the Act was not in operation, had a great deal to do with the results mentioned.—The HONE SECRETARY could not give any opinion upon this point, but he thought the ques- tion of clubs was well deserving of consideration. ' • THE EGYPTIAN EXILES.—Mr. ASHLEY informed Mr. La- bouchere that the Governor of Ceylon had expressed his opinion_ that the allowance made to the Egyptian exiles was insufficient, and the Egyptian Government had in- creased the allowance by £5OO a year, in addition to the al- lowance originally made. • THE ALAEAMA (Amts.—Mr. C. KENNARD - asked for in- formation respecting the new departure of the Court of Comniissioners of the Alabama claims at Washington, and was told by Lord E. Fltzmaurice that it was not the inten- tion of the Government to -interfere farther in any way whatever. - IRE DUKE OF ALBANY AND THE GOVERNOR-GENERAL- SHIP OF CANADA.—The delicate.question put by Baron H. , De Worms as to the Duke of Albany and the Governor Generalship of Canada was not ianswered by the Prime . Minister, as it was upon a question which unless for very grave and Public reasons it was not desirable to bring into discussion in the House of Commons, but the right hon. gentleman was ready to admit that the Government were aware that the Duke of Albany was willing to render ser- vice to the Crown and country, and such desire they con- ceived did him the highest credit. BASUTOLAND.—Mr. BOURKE desired to know what were the intentions of the Government with respect to the future of Basutolaud.—Mr. GLADSTONE replied that on the side of the Basutes and on the side of the Cape Government, there existed a state of things and a prospect pointing to an im- mediate change. The Basutos had declined to attend a conference summoned by the agent of the Cape Govern- ment, and the interpretation put upon this by the Cape Go- vernment was that the Easutos desired to have no farther communications with the colony. The Colonial Govern- ment had appealed to the Imperial Government to take the matter into their serious consideration without delay. The Government would make known to the House at the earliest practicable moment what particular steps they intended to take. Till CORRUPT PRACTICES BILL.—On .the motion for the second reading of the Parliamentary Elections (Corrupt and Illegal) Practices Bill, Mr. WARTON moved that it be read a second time that day three montbs.—The amendment was seconded by Mr. C. LEWIS on the ground that it would press harshly on "honest and sensitive men," lightly on the "un- scrupulous and reckless," that it was "grossly unjust, enormously severe, and ridiculously unequal."—Mr. George Russell characterised this statement as " cilumnious and in- solent." In a very thin House the discussion was continued by Mr. Shell, who would not oppose the second reading; Mr. Stuart Wortley, who gave the Bill general support; Mr. Carbutt, who hoped to see introduced a clause closing pub- lic-houses upon electiop day; Mr. Cowen, who thought that the only way to deal with political corruption was to throw legitimate expenses upon the constituency and to permit of Ino other; Baron de Ferrieres, who thought the Bill , should be deferred till after the franchise had , been extended and, seats redistributed ; Mr. H. Fowler, who, whilst supporting the Bill, criti- cised the provision by Which rich men were allowed to lend their carriages for the bringing up of voters at elections; Mr. Gregory, who thought that it was a fair attempt to re- medy an undoubted evil; Mr. Grantham, who would sup- port the second reading; Mr. Whitley, who was very much obliged to the Attorney-general for introducing the Bill; Colonel Kingscote, who thought the measure would be a little stringent in counties; Mr. Raikes, who regarded the Bill as a great improvement on that of last year; Mr. Edwd. Clarke who would cordially vote for the second reading; ' Mr. I,Vaddy, who mentioned incidentally that in the borough represented by_Mr.-Charles Lewis, votes cost 8s 2d each; and Sir R. Cross, who, so far as the principle of the Bill was concerned, promised it the hearty support of himself and his colleagues on the Front Bench. After a few words from the Attorney-General, the Bill was read a second time. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY.

The Bishop of CARLISLE moved the second reading of the Cathedral Statutes Bill, whicb, he said, was framed on the recommendations of the Royal Commission appointed by that House, and was substantially the same as that intro- duced last year.—The Bishop of PETERBOROUGH spoke in opposition, but, after some remarks in its favour by the Archbishops of Canterbury and York and the Bishop of London, the second reading was agreed to. HOUSE, OF COMMONS.—TIIESDAY.

THE DUBLIN MAIL CONTRACT.—Tho POSTMASTER GENERAL stated that as soon as possible after the tenders had been received an opportunity would be given for dis- missing the Dublin mail contract.—With reference to the assumption that possibly facilities might not be afforded for the conveyance of passengers to Holyhead by the London and North-Western Railway Company. Mr. FewcETT said there would be no objection to insert in the contract pro- visions which would secure that passengers should be carried by the mail train and that there should be facilities for booking through to Dublin. AGRICULTURAL HOLDINGS (SCOTLAND) BILL. The second reading of the Agricultural Holdings (Scatland) Bill Was moved by the LORD ADVOCATE.—Sir H. MAXWELL, while offering some criticisms on various provisions of the recognised in it an honest attempt to deal with a com- plicated question, and gave it his cordial support.—Mr. JAMES BARCLAY said this was not such a bill as the tenants of Scotland had a right to expect, after the declarations of the Premier and other members of the Government.—After a short debate, the LORD ADVOCATE thanked the House for the way in which it had received the bill, and the motion for the second reading was agreed to, the Committee being fixed for Monday next. BALLOT ACT CONTINUANCE BILL.-011 the order for going into Committee on the Ballot Act Continuance and Amendment Bill, Mr. BERESFORD HOPE appealed to the Government not to hurry on this measure in the last quarter of an hour of the sitting, and he was speaking when the time arrived for the adjournment of the debate. The sitting was shortly afterwards suspended.—There was a count-out im- mediately on the reassembling at nine o'clock. HOUSE OF CO MM ON S.—WEDNESDAY.

THE AMENDMENT OF RAILWAY BILLS.—Sir A. OTWAY moved a long amendment on the Standing OrAers in refer- ence to the payment of interest on railway shares during the constructioz of a railway.—Sir J. W. PEASE opposed the alteration—After some debate, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said the Government were not interested in the question as a Govern- ment, but several members of it were in favour of the motion, including the Prime Minister. Do what they please, they could not protect the unwary investors, and, therefore, he could not see that the argument about the standing order being a safeguard for small investors had any force. He thought the proposed alteration a very moderate one, and hoped the House would adopt it. Mr. MOLLOY complained that this Motion bad been discussed all day in preference to an important Irish Measure. As a protest against tbis waste of the time of the House be moved the adjournment of the debate.—Mr. O'CONNOR POWER supported the motion for the adjournment. —Sir WM. HARCOURT stated that the Government had nothing to do with the setting down of this motion for to-day.--It was entirely in independent hands. He urged the withdrawal of the motion for the adjournment.—The motion for the ad- journment was withdrawn, and the House divided on the amendment of the Standing Orders, when there voted for the motion 131, against 123. NEW WRITS.—New writs were issued for North Leicester- shire in the room of Major-General Burnaby (deceased), and for Derby in the room of Mr. M. Bass (resigned).—The House adjourned at 5-53. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THURSDAY.

The Poor-Law Conferences Bill was read a third time and passed, and the Irish Constabulary and Police (Pay and Pensions) Bill was read a second time.—On a request for papers by Earl de la Warr, the Earl of DERBY stated that the total cost of the removal to Malta and the relief there of refugees from Egypt was £33,000, of which £15,000 was for transport, which was entirely provided by the Imperial Government. Of the £lB,OOO expended in relief, £6,400 was provided by public subscription in London and £6,000 by a grant from local resources, and Malta was only called upon to pay one-fifth or one-sixth of the whole outlay, though nearly all the refugees were connected with Malta, and the finances of the island had gained very much by the Egyptian war. lIOUSE OF COMMONS.—THIIESDAY.

SCOTCH BUIINESS.—The HOME SECRETARY was ques-, tioned respecting the resignation of the Earl of Rosebery, and he said he gladly availed himself of the opportunity to announce publicly—and he was desired to say it on the part of his Lordship—that there was not a word of founda- tion for the assertion that something he (Sir H. Harcourt) had said or done had conduced to the resignation of the noble Earl. Sir William further explained that the ap- pointment of Lord Rosebery was understood to be only a I temporary expedient, and that his Lordship had always de- sired that there should be a different and permanent arrange- ment for the control of Scotch business; and he added that he hoped to be able to state on an early day the plan which had been devised for the conduct of Scotch affairs in Parliament. THE CORRUPT PRACTICES BILL—On the order for going into committee on the Parliamentary Elections Corrupt and Illegal Practices Bill, Mr. BROADHURST moved that it be an instruction to the committee that they have the power to in- sert a new clause charging the returning officers' expenses at Parliamentary elections upon the rates in boroughs and counties.—Mr. GLADSTONE said the Government were friendly to the principle of this instruction, but it involved a large extension of the scope of the bill, which had made a progress at this moment which it would not have Made had it contained such a controversial proposal. While he (the Premier) would have voted for the alteration if the question had been rai :ed in a separate bill, he could not accept such vital change in the present bill, which was admitted on both sides of the House to be of gnat benefit to the

To this circumstance, as I stated at the -time, the-utier spoliation of the whole of the hay stacked with water in it ought to be attributed. Does it not stand to reason that whenever a farmer is unfortunately compelled to stack in bad condition the sooner the steam is drawn off after being generated the better it will be for the hay? But the fan- owners at Reading allowed their stacks to remain sweltering in the steam generated for days and even weeks together, and the inevitable result was an enormous development of mould.—Notts Guardian.
An English book called "People I have met" is having quite a run. Its American counterpart will be entitled "People I have dodged; or those whom I saw before being seen."

Sandy Merton was a half-witted fellow who lived in. a small town in the west of Scotland. One day Sandy en- tered the doctor's shop, carrying under his arm a rusty old gun. "Well, Alexander," said the doctor, "who gave you the gun ?" " Maister Tamson, the publican, gied me it, an' he said the only kind o' poother it wud shoot wi' was Seid- litz poother ; sae gie tuppence worth."

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

LIMETez.—If some otthe most forward of these are tied I loosely they will bleach sooner and consequently be more I tender. Tying sho_uld not be done when they are very wet, nor when the sun is very hot on them, as it hastens decay in both cases. We usually select the early part of the day if dry, or a dull, dry day. Another sowing may now be 'made of the Alexandra cos and All the year: rbund" cab- bage lettuce. At this season of the year we draw drills an inch deep, and We drop a few seeds es-try eight inches, They May also be evenly distributed over the drill; in either .case the*. should he ultimately thinned out to one plant at every eight inches. The advantage of this method is that they do not require transplanting, neither are they so liable to run to seed, which lettuce transplanted in dry weather are disposed to do. PEAS may still be sown. If the ground is not in good heart, a trench 18th. or 21t. deep, and similar width, may be made; place four inches of decayed manure into it, then add more soil and more manure on that; the remaining space may be filled with soil. If there is no decayed manure for the purpose, throw out the trench and put it back again; this will loosen the soil and make it easier for the roots to travel. Information as to sorts is given below, in reply to a correspondent.. • PARSNIPS.—We are now taking the smallest out, leaving them about four inches apart; they will be finally thinned to eight inches. Advantage should be takento_hand weed these and similar crops immediately after rain, as the weeds come up so ranch easier than when the ground is dry and hard.

BROAD BEaxs.--Of these we have made our last sowing, seleCting the green Windsor for the purpose. They will do dribbled between the Potato rows, if there is no other space that can be devoted to them. _ _ _ _

GENERAL WORK consists of hoeing, hand-weeding, fork- ing up. vacant ground, as well as forking amongst potatoes and. other crops. -.Preparing ground for pricking out winter greens, also the beds for the late vegetable marrow plants. This plant delights in having a heap of half-decayed vege- table matter for its roots, partly because of the freedom it presenti,for them to travel into it and the slight bottom heat it affords, the result of fermentation. THE Fncwr GauDEN.--7Attention should be directed to this now, so that every vacant space should be filled by something that will assist to embellish it daring the sum- mer. Suppose the garden to consist chiefly of a centre bed, which if large enough should have a dahlia; sort and colour we leave to the purchaser. From the road this plant would , look as well if placed on the side of the .bed nearest the building, and as our cottage friends have no objections to us gazing at their flowers they will oblige us by arranging' the others in front of it. By so doing our view will not be obstructed. Geraniums may form the first border round the dahlia, allowing space for the taller China asters, marigolds, or larkspurs, unless there are a few herbaceous plants to form a break already. ' Presuming that annuals are already sown, a few verbenas, dwarf asters, and blue lobelia, or blue viola, will create a charming sight for a cottage front. The rose maggot has made its appearance, and must be diligently sought after and destroyed. Some- times the leaf will be seen somewhat curled, but in many instances two leaves will be adhering together. The maggot is the cause of both, and without taking the trouble to search we press such suspicious parts between the finger and thumb. THE WINDOW.—As many of its tenants will or should be
outside, there are but fei subjects to claim attention. Spirea japonica is a plant we have observed in more than one instance recently. ...As it may not be recognised by its _ _ _ . . _ .

botanical name we will give a plain description' of it. It is usually furnished with ample green spreading foliage, ex- tending far beyond the sides of the pot. The flowers are produced in panicles, which in the early stage look like so many small white granules clustered together; these ex- pand, and, when fully developed, our panicle looks more like a snowy white pyramidal plume which is most attrac- tive, and is much used for hand and button-hole bouquets. The plant is perfectly hardy, and after doing duty in the window it should be planted in the open ground, where it will flower the following season, and the year after it may be taken up again and potted for the window. It requires an unlimited supply of water if grown in pots, and when well clothed with foliage the pots may stand in earthenware saucers containing water.
THE HUYTON QUARRY STABBING CASE.

At Prescot on Monday, William Knox was charged on re- mand before Mr. W. L. Evans, with unlawfully and mali- ciously wounding Samuel Knox, willi a certain instrument, to wit a penknife.—Superintendent Barker conducted the prosecution, and Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the prisoner. —Samuel Knox, the prosecutor, deposed that he was a collier and son of the prisoner. About midnight on Satur- day the 19th of May, prisoner came home and appeared as if he had had drink. lie (prosecutor) met him in the back yard, and asked him ha was going to give anything towards his keep. He asked the question because his father had only given a few shillings to his mother. Prisoner did not reply but gave him a shove ann went into the house. A man named Robert Williams got between him and his father He followed the prisoner, who looked angry, into the House. Shortly afterwards prisoner went out by the back door and broke a window with his fist. Prosecutor followed him. He found him bending down near the coal heap and struck him, because he thought he was picking up something to .strike him with. Re pushed the prisoner out of the yard, and prisoner said he.wouldgo for a policeman. He returned into the house, and while standing at the front door his mother told him someone was,breaking the back window. He therefore sent again to the back door, and saw his father and a crowd round the door. He ran out and struck his father, and then they had a struggle, during which he felt blood running down his legs. Having called to his brother to separate them he shouted "I am done," and on moving kis shirt be found be had been stabbed. He had neither coat nor waistcoat on. • His brother parted them, and he was assisted into the house by his brother and others. Dr. Gorst attended him a quarter of an hour or 20 minutes afterwards. He was stabbed under the left nipple, and suffered a great deal of pain on the following day. He felt lble to work now. He had' had two bottles of porter on the day of the occurrence.—By Mr. Swift: When his father came to the back door he told him he should not come intodthe house unless he turned up some money, and stood between him and the door to prevent him getting in. His father shoved him on one side, and be struck him. When prisoner ran out of the house he struck him again, and they had a hand-to-hand fight. He held his father down by the hair of the head, hitting him on the face, while his father was hitting him on the ribs. He held him down as much as he could and knocked him about as much as he could.—By Supt. Barker: There had been a bother several times about his father drinking.-He had been on the spree about a fortnight, and everyone at home was getting tired of it.—Dr. Gorst, Huytoi, stated that between twelve and one o'clock on Sunday morning, the 20th May, he was sent for to prosecu- tor's house, and found prosecutor in bed. He had a punc- tured wound on the left side, an inch and a half to the left of the breast bone, and just two inches below the nipple. He passed a probe into the wound, and it came in contact with the ribs. He stitched the wound and dressed it. He hardly thought from the position of the wound that the prosecutor had lost much blood. The wound might have been , caused by the penknife produced. Three days after be first saw • prosecutor he found him suffering from acute pleurisy. He was not fit for work yet. Robert Williams having given evidence in support of prosecutor's statement, P.C. Hall* stated that about midnight on the 19th ult. he heard shouting and Screaming in Elm-place, where prisoner resided: He went into the house, and saw prosecutor lying on a sofa in the kitchen. Prosecutor showed him his left breast, and from what he stated he took the prisoner into custody. He searched him, and found a small penknife in his pocket. He also reached the back yard and found another penknife which had red marks upon it, and which prisoner said he used for cutting tobacco. He took the prisoner to Prescot, and charged him with stabbing his son. Prisoner made no reply.—This was all the evidence, and prisoner was com- mitted for trial at the sessions, but admitted to bail—him- self in £5O, and two sureti,s of £5O each.

A contemporary mention‘ a case beyond the ordinary oculiit. It is that of a young lady, who, instead of a pupil, has a professor in her eve. If you think nobody cares for you in this cold world, just try to learn to play the trombone in a populous neigh- bourhood.

A little boy went into the country on a visit. About the first thing he had was a bowl of bread and milk. He tasted it, and then hesitated a moment, when his mother asked him if he did not like it; to which he replied, "Yes, ma; I was only wishing our milkman kept a cow." REAL WORK AND MERE Terx.—You know that clever talk touching joinery will not make a chair; and I know that it is of about as much value in the physical sciences. Mother Nature is serenely obdurate to honeyed words; only those who understand the ways of things, and can silently and effectually handle them, get any good out of her.— Professor Huxley on Technical Education. DR. MOFFA.T AND TIIE BOER.—In October, 1816, Robert Moffat was ordained, in Surrey Chapel, London, a mis- sionary under the auspices of the London Missionary So- ciety, and was appointed to South Africa. (John Williams, "the martyr of Erromanga," was ordained at the same time.) On the last day of that month he sailed for the Cape of Good Hope, being then just about twenty-one. At first he was engaged in the colonial territory, where he learned Dutch and preached to the Boers. A story of this period illustrates the spirit and ready wit of the man, quali- ties which stood him in good stead then, and more so in later life. At the house of a rough Boer, where he had begged a night's lodging, the good frau asked him to preach. Moffat, knowing that over a hundred Hottentots were em- ployed in the service of the Boer, was disappointed to find only his host and hostess and five children as his congrega- tion. "May not your servants come in ?" he asked the Boer, modestly. "Eh !" roared the Boer. "Hottentots! • Are you come to preach to Hottentots? Go to the moun- tains and preach to the baboons; or, if you like, I'll fetch my dogs, and you may preach to them !" Moffat calmly proceeded to give out his text, " Truth, Lord; yet the dogs eat of the crumbs which fall from their master's table." It made no apparent impression, so he repeated it. "Hold on !" cried the Boer, rising hastily from his seat. "I'll have no more of that. I'll bring you all the Hottentots in the place." And so he did; the barn was full ; the people heard the Word gladly, and at the conclusion of his sermon the Boer, now mollified, asked the young preacher, "Who had hardened his hammer to deal such a blow on the head as that ?" and declared that he would never again object to the preaching of the Gospel to Hottentots.—" Heroes of Britain in Peace and War."

div.head: TIIE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: TIIE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

On the inquiry resuming on Monday, Mr. E. Leader Williams, the engineer to the scheme, was first called, and examined by Mr. Pember, Q.C. Ho said the total length of the proposed canal from Runcorn to Manchester was 21 miles 5 furlongs. Rather less than one-fourth of the canal would be entirely tidal, and three-fourths would be lock navigation, of which the lower part would be increased 2ft. 6in. in depth at spring tides. At the Manchester end of the candl, where ships might be delayed, there would in his scheme be ample room for three ships abreast ; in the middle portion, where it was merely a question of traffic, there would be room for two; and at the Runcorn end, where there might be ships waiting for the tide, there would be ample room for four ships abreast. The depth of the ship canal from Manchester to Irlam would be 26 feet, from Irlam to Walton 24 feet, and from Walton to Runcorn 24 feet, which would be increased to 241 t. 6in. at , spring tides. The object of the greater depth at the upper end was to allow water to be drawn off for using the locks without destroying the navigation. The total fall of the ship canal would be 59 feet, and he had no doubt that the supply of water would be sufficient. The supply of water in the Mersey was considerably in ex- cess of any probable requirements. Supposing there were an exceptionally dry season, and there were a chance of fal- ling short, the deficiency could be supplied by pumping power. Water could also be stored in the upper part of the river, where there was a great depth of bank. The docks at Manchester would occupy the site of the racecourse. The total amount of quay space there amounted to two miles seven furlongs, while there would also be a quay along the canal from Barton to the termination of two miles six fur- longs. In regard to the quality of the water in the canal, the sluices would be better than the existing weirs, as they would not cause the same odour, the temperature of the water would be lower because of the greater depth, and whatever nuisance there was would be smaller than that which existed. The dye-water would have no bad effect on ships' bottoms, as the iron of the lock-gates on the Mersey and Irwell seemed to be preserved by the action of the water. The head of the ship canal would be in connec- tion with a vast network of canals going to various parts of the country, all of which were in fair working order. At Warrington a small dock of 114- acres was proposed, which would connect the canal with the Mersey, and he looked forward to a large trade in lighterage at that point. There were only four roads of any importance that crossed the route of the canal, two being near Warrington and the others at Warbur- ton and Barton. At these places swing bridges would be placed, worked by hydraulic machinery, and clauses had been arranged with the justices, who were the authorities in the case of three bridges, while in the other no opposition was offered. At Barton the ship canal would go under the aqueduct of the Bridgewater Canal, which crossed the Irwell at that point, and this it was proposed to convert into a movable aqueduct or trough, working on a swivel to allow ships to pass underneath. This principle had always been carried out at Anderton, where barges were lifted in a trough by hydraulic power from the river Weaver to the Trent and Mersey Navigation, a height of 50 feet. The aqueduct in question was not on the main line of the Bridgewater Canal, but on a portion belonging to the Bridgewater Trustees, who did not oppose, but with whom negotiations were going on. The effect of the ship canal upon floods must be, if not entirely to do away with them, to minimise them to a very great extent. All the landowners, with the exception of Sir Humphrey de Trafford, were at one with the promoters, as their land would be improved without any cost or rates charged under the Floods Prevention Bill. Witness pro- ceeded to deal with the deviatiens of railways under the bill. The first was the main line of the London and North- Western Railway Company between Moore and Warrington, and the second the joint-line of the London and North- Western and Great-Western Railway Companies near the same point. These would be carried over the canal by viaducts. Deviation No. 3 was the Warrington and Stockport Railway, which it was proposed to take under the Mersey at the former place into Arpley Station. Deviations Nos. 4 and 5 were of the Glazebrook and Stockport Railway and the M. and L. Railway, 'both of which belonged to the Cheshire Lines Committee. The gradient in the case of the viaducts would be increased to lone in 114, which was the same as that leading to Runcorn Bridge on the Lancashire side of the Mersey. The height of Runcorn Bridge was 75 feet above high water, and the headway under Walton Viaduct would be 66 feet at a spring tide and 75 feet at a neap tide. The difference would be accounted for by the time it would take for a ship going from Runcorn Bridge. At the other viaducts there would be a headway of 77 feet 6 inches. He had gone closely into the details of the estimates, and had fixed the prices care- fully based on his own experience. One advantage of the scheme was that work might be carried on simul- taneously at different points. The total cost of the canalised works was estimated at £4,087,127 16s 7d. Rock excavations, at 2s 6d per yard, would cost £1,271,723 17s 6d ; and the removal of soft soil, at Is Id per yard, £1,374,563 13s 4d ; or a total of £2,646,287 103 101. His estimate of stone facing to the slopes of the canal was £116,494, and he put down the following items: --Weir in Runcorn and Latchford Canal, £2,000 ; locks and sluices at Walton, £147,852 9s ; sluices at Walton, £15,000 ; sluices, dzc, at Woolaeton, £3,000; locks and sluices at Ir- lam, £147,138 7s 6d; locks and sluices at Barton, £140,215 12s; and lock and weir at Throstle Nest, £B,OOO ; Irlam Basin, £9,000; Barton basin, £9,000; caul for Barton basin to entrance of Manchester Docks, £25,000 ; entrance of Manchester docks te termination of ship canal, £25,800; bridges at Moore, £19,550; at Wilderspool causeway, £17,550 ; at Latchford-road, £19,000 ;at Warburton, £l7, 550; at Barton, £20,100; Barton aqueduct, £20,300; con- duit at Irlam, £2 945 1034 d ; accommodation works £60,000; contingencies at 10 per cent, £347,178 63 lid ;and land buildings (714 acres) and compensation, £268,166, making up the total mentioned above. The cost of the railway deviations would be £60,508.

The Committee were on Tuesday occupied in hearing the further evidence and cross-examination of Mr. Leader Williams, the engineeP. He said the canal would not seri- ously interfere with the water mains of the Liverpool Cor- poration, which in their course from Vyrnwy crossed the river three miles above Runcorn. The canal works, he thought, would take four or five years to complete, but he could give no definite information as to the payment of in- terest on subscriptions during the construction. They pro- posed to close the navigation above Warrington whilst the works were in progress, and he was confident that the periodical floods could be safely dealt with. He appre- hended no difficulty in regard to the swing aqueduct at Barton, through which an ocean steamer could get in five minutes.

The Committee had before them on Wednesday Mr. Aber- nethy, consulting engineer to the scheme, who considered the canal would prove a great benefit to the trades and in- dustries of the district, in addition to exercising a beneficial influence in the mitigation and prevention of floods. So far as regarded the actual construction, there was no serious engineering difficulties. It would, he estimated, take two years to complete the training works in the Mersey estuary, and three years to construct the canal between Walton and Manchester, but if the Committee insisted upon the low- water channel being dredged to its full depth bf twelve feet before a commencement was made with the upper portion, three years more—or eight in all—would be requited. He did not apprehend the slightest injury to the estuary from the training works, and if such injury resulted, the walls could be removed. Mr. J. F. Bateman, engineer to the Man- chester Corpor;ltion, also gave unqualified support to the scheme, which presented very simple engineering problems. The deviations of railways which would be rendered neces- sary were easy of accomplishment, and he did not anticipate injury to the different companies. Further evidence on the subject of railway gradients and, their bearing upon the deviations was offered by Mr. Price Williams, C.E., and the Committee again adjourned. Further evidence on the engineering merits of the canal scheme was offered on Thursday. Mr. Fowler, referring to the proposed deviation of railways, said the different companies might reasonably be asked to acquiesce in the alterations. They had themselves frequently interfered, by bridges, with navigable waters, and in each case bad refused compensation, on the ground that they were act- ing in the public good. He considered thit the same argument now held good, the positions b2ing reversed. The other witnesses included Mr. J. Brundlees, president of the, Institute of Civil Engineers, Mr. A. Giles, M.P., and Mr. F. E. Duckham, engineer to the Millwall Docks, who were unanimously in favour of the scheme as an engineering possibility and a commercial benefit.

div.head: MISCELLANWAJS.
div.p: MISCELLANWAJS.

Miss Pearson, daughter of a Manchester merchant, has l_c!et her life by falling from the cliffs into the sea at Puffing Role, near Kil tee, county Clare. The police made a descent on a gambling house in White- chapel, on Saturday night, and arrested 25 persons who were found playing with cards or dice. !all:ports from all parts of Yorkshire agree that the fruit c!op of the present year is almost unprecedented, espe- tV of apples and pears, which are largely cultivated in ine county. Mr. Justice Hawkins, who presided at the Central Crimi- 'lal Court on Saturday, said, in replying to an observation nin a juryman, that" at least 75 per cent of the crime of this country was due to drink." _ The three women charged with causing the death of tsridget Gallagher, on the 2Gth ultimo, were, on Monday, might up on remand before the Liverpool stipendiary _magistrate, and were discharged. The coroner's jury had eturned an open verdict in the case. GARIBALDL—At Stafford House, on Saturday, in the pre- sence of Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, Earl Shaftesbury, and the American Minister, the Duchess of Sutherland unveiled a Marble medallion portrait of General Garibaldi. Mr. Glad- atone afterwards delivered an address, in which .he referred to the Italian patriot's career and character, and said that besides his splendid integrity, his wide universal sympathies, and besides the seductive simplicity of manner which never departed from him, he would almost select from every other luality which was in apparent contrast but in real harmony int,Gari.baldi, the union of the most profound and tender t lanity with his fiery manner. .URDAY OBSERVANCE IN SCOTLAND.--AbOßt midnight Saturday two steamers, conveying a large quantity of fresh and kippered herrings, arrived at the western terminus of the Highland Railway. The fish was consigned to the London markets, and it was intended to have it at once "voYed to its destination. About one o'clock on Sunday tn orning, however, the residents of Strome assembled in large numbers and protested against the sanctity of the "oabbath being thus invaded. They took possession of the Pier and railway property, resisted the efforts of the police to dislodge them, and refused to permit the removal of the alb during canonical hours. e SINGULAR CHARGE OF FRAUD.—At Sheffield, on Tues- day, "Professor " Howdin, described as a manager, of ✓arlington, was charged with obtaining money by false pre- tences. He has been going round soliciting advertisements e *or the Graphic, Illustrated J.Yetos, and other papers. It is alleged that he obtained £3 15s from Mr. Walker, Royal note', Sheffield, for an advertisement to be inserted in the '3Portin9 and Dramatic News, but, as the advertisement didnot appear, the " Professor " was arrested at Darlington. It he stated that Howdin has a large advertising business at Darlington, and he altogether denies that he has committed any fraud. On his business card, which is richly engraved, IA the following :—" Graphic, Illustrated London .2Vews, aPorting and Dramatic Leaflet Company. W. J. Howdin, taanager." He was remanded for a week. A. cynic might observe on reading the proceedings of our courts that one half the judges were always occupied in sett- ing the other half right on points of law. In the Lords Justices Court, on S;iturday, in a contract cise, it appeared that Mr. Justice Day had given judgment—say for A. Ate ,appeal was taken by B to a divisional court, and Justices "emnan and North decided that Justice Day was wrong. The appeal being of course carried further, the Master of the Rolle and two of the Lords Justices decided on Satur- uaY that Justice Day was right and, ergo, Justices North an„d Denman wrong. If the appeal should be carried to the Rouse of Lords, it is possible that in the course of a year or an that august tribunal may find that the Master of the 11418 and his colleagues were wrong, and that the divisional Court was, after all, in the right. And all this on the inter- Pretation of a clause in a written contract. APPREHENSION OF A SUPPOSED FENIAN IN BIRMINGHAM. :.The Birmingham police on Monday arrested a man '4l. need George Smythe, who has lately come over from Litrnerica, at a public-house situate in the centre of the job- bing gun-finishing shops, where he had declared his deter- mined intention of "making mischief" at the forthcoming 'aright celebration next week. Smythe carried a revolver, and at the moment ef the arrival of the police, who had, in ennaequence of the character of the threats, been communi- cated with, startled the neighhourhood'by discharging two °et the chambers of the weapon. A severe struggled ensued before be would allow himself to be handcuffed. Smythe was on Tuesday convicted of drunkenness, and ordered to Pay 20s and costs. It was stated by a police official that the clan had been drinking heavily for some time, so that the In_agistrates were, no doubt, perfectly justified in treating nue offence with the leniency they have shown. RESIGNATION OF LORD ROSEBERY.—Following the news of Lord Rosebery's resignation of the Under-Secretaryship at the Home Office comes the further announcement that the t'esignation has been accepted with regret, and that Mr. Hib- l?ert will probably be appointed to the recent office. A Lon- can Tory journal has attributed Lord Rosebery's resignation ,to anger at a remark by Sir W. Harcourt to the effect that the arrangement as to the Under-Secretaryship was not in- nded to be permanent, but had been made simply to " pro- Pitiate the Scotch members." The truth is that the whole tone of the debate on the subject was calculated to touch the Susceptibilities of Lord Rosebery, and especially the strong declaration in favour of the Under-Secretary being a com- moner. His lordship has discharged the duties during his brief tenure of office with marked ability, and is highly Popular with the Scotch members. It was, therefore, hoped that though be would naturally feel some chagrin at the language used in the House of Commons, he might be pre- vailed upon to withdraw his resignation. This he has not done, but his severance from the Government will, it is to be hoped, be only temporary, and on the rearrangement of offices which has for some time been looked forward to, and to which Sir W. Harcourt's observations pointed, it is not improbable that Lord Rosebery may be provided with a seat ja the Cabinet. This recognition of his ability would be re- garded with much satisfaction in Scotland.

CLAIMANT TO THE ENGLISH THRONE.—The Army and I 4)" ally Gazette says his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales Was somewhat inconvenienced some weeks back by a gentle- of German-Jewish descent, who imagines himself to be the real heir to the English thrones This person, who is Well known through his long black curly locks and general Intidy appearance, has been in the habit of promenading rall Mall, in front of Marlborough House, during several L ours of the night. Being foiled in his attempts to gain an interview there, he recently made a flying visit to Ans- i*. outh, where he continually haunted Prince Edward of laaxe Weimar, calling several times a day to request to be Proclaimed Prince of Wales, until the Governor's boatmen, stationed at the gates of Government House for the purpose, denied him admission. He then escaped from his medical at- Who had followed him to Portsmouth, and betook !itself to Cowes, intent on obtaining an audience of the Cttjleen, to press his claim to being the rightful heir to the 'asne• The detectives and household police at Osborne effectually checkmated this design. Since then the good P,?°Ple of Cowes have been somewhat amused, but not a ttle frightened, by his various antics, notwithstanding that :s is watched by three robust attendants. But, unfortu- s"atelY, at present the law is on his side owing to the tender- neartedness of his patents, to say nothing of their dread of notoriety. The baron and baroness whose son is thus men- tally afflicted are well known in society. se SHOCKING DISCOVERY AT GLOUCESTER.—A man named .4ees and his wife were on Monday brought before the magma- at Gloucester, charged with unlawfully disposing of several dead bodies of children.
