A fire broke outs on Monday, in the fine aft gallery of Mr. W. W. Winter, Derby, destroying several valuable paintings. An excursionist from York, named Nash, was drowned whilst bathing southward of the Scarborough Spa, on Mon- day afternoon. The Mayor of Derby has fixed the nomination for Monday, and the polling for Thursday following. It is believed that Alderman Ross is not likely to be opposed. The Cock Tavern, in Fleet-street, London, has been re-sold by Mr. F. Statham Hobson to Messrs. Spiers and
Pond. The Irish in Canada are opposing the Marquis of Lans- downe's appointment as Viceroy, because of his anti-Irish views. Their organ, the Montreal Post, leads the opposi-

tion. Mr. George Russell has been appointed Parliamentary Secretary to the Local Government Board in succession to Mr. J. T. Hibbert, the new Under-Secretary at the Home Office. • Two children, aged eight and 10 years respectively, were drowned on Wednesday evening in the Regent Canal, Lon- don. Some hours elapsed before the bodies were recovered. The parents of the deceased lived near the spot. Sir George Bowyer, who sat in the last Parliament for Wexford County, died on Thursday morning at his chambers in the temple, aged 72. The hon. baronet had been ailing some time, but his immediate decease had not been

antiCipated. The Home Secretary has appointed Sheriff Guthrie Smith t 3 adjudicate upon the claims of the parties who gave in- formation enabling the authorities to :trace the authors of the Dun Echt outrage. The reward is £6OO, and there are

three claimants. There is not much encouragement to be gathered from the Board of Trade returns for May. The exports of home produce show a falling off, as compared with May last year, of fully half a million sterling; but the imports have risen in value £320. Two colliers were suffocated, and several others placed in great peril, by a sudden outburst of gas in a shaft they were sinking on Wednesday at Whitfield, near Tunstall. The re- mains of 23 men are entombed in the same mine where an explosion occurred some time ago. Lord Lytton, who was present on Wednesday night at a banquet of the Middlesex Conservative Association, said the present Ministry might have to render an account of their stewardship, for it was well known that the robust Liberals of the provinces ware beginning to require explanations about matters peculiarly to provoke criticism. Mr. Plunkett and Lord George Hamilton also spoke. About seven o'clock on Thursday morning a fire boke out in a lodging-house at St. John's-square, Silsden, near •Keify.hley. One of the lodgers raised an alarm, and in the confusion which ensued a woman, named Margaret Taylor, of Oldham, was burnt to death. A man was severely injured in jumping from the window of his bed- room on to the ground below. A daring burglary was perpetrated in Liverpool on Wed- nesday night or early on Thursday morning. When the shop of Mr. Isaac Jones, pawnbroker and jeweller, was opened it was discovered that the premises had been entered through the roof and thoroughly ransacked, jewellery and other valuables to the amount of £5OO having been stolen. The thieves left behind them some property which had been stolen from a neighbouring public-house. No clue to the perpetrators has yet been obtained. QUESTIONS IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.—The Times says: "In consequence of the grave and unwarrantable im- putations introduced into certain questions 'put in the House of Commons on Irish affairs, it is in contemplation to call the attention of the Prime Minister to the necessity of modifying the rules which relate to questions. Mr. Trevelyan has more than once recently protested against this danger- ous practice; and as this class of questions has increased considerably of late, it is intended to press the reform on the leader of the House. Loss OF THE HILDEGARDE.—Mr. Rothery, Q.C., Wreck Commissioner, gave judgment on Thursday, at Liverpool, as to the ship liildegarde, lost with all hands on a voyage from San Francisco with wheat. In the opinion of the Court there could be no doubt whatever that the vessel was grievously overladen, and it seemed abundantly clear that the blame for this rested with the instructions given by the owners. Mr. Rothery did not say the owners wilfully sent the vessel to sea with the object of drowning the crew, but they did not take reasonable precautions. HOSTILITY BETWEEN ENGLISH AND IRISH.—The English v. Irish disturbances at Turton, near Darwen have assumed a serious phase, and a collision between the parties seem inevitable. On Thursday night the English assembled in a bogy, and notice was given to the Irish that they must quit the town, or they will be driven out. It is only a week ago since a whole gang of labourers were driven out, and ever since the ill-feeling has increased. The Irish have had several meetings, at which hostile threats were made and knives brandished. The disturbances arose out of the recent Dublin trials.

A CRUEL AND FURIOUS WOMAN.—A shocking case of inhumanity by a widow named Connor was revealed at an inquest at Newport, Mon., on Thursday. Catherine Regan, living apart from her husband, lodged at Connor's house. The latter beat, kicked, an dragged her about by the hair for, as the neighbours asserted, an hour and a half on the night of Thursday last. A policeman broke into the house and found Regan lying almost nude in a pool of water thrown over her by the landlady. Neither of the women were under the influence of liquor. The landlady wanted to get rid of Regan as a lodger. A surgeon said the body was covered with bruises. A verdict of manslaughter was re- turned.

RECENT Wits.—The following have been proved :—Of the Right Hon. Lady Charlotte Wentworth Fitzwilliam, late of Warmswerth Hall, Doncaster, the personal estate exceed- ing £23000; of Mr. Francis Morley, late of Breadsall Priory, Derbyshire, over £71,000; of Alderman Sir Thomas White, late of No. 61, Mark-lane, of Great West Hatch, Chigwell, Essex, and of No. 144, Sloane-street, over £68,000; of General Sir Charles Hastings Doyle, K.C.M.G., late of No. 18, Bolton-street, Piccadilly, upwards of £55,000; of Mr. Charles John Eyston, J. F'., late of East Hendred, Berks, ex- ceeding £20,000; of Mr. Charles Edward Barlow, late of The Lawn, Camden Park, Tunbridge. Wells, over £28,000. —lllustrated London News. Mr. W. E. Forster, M.P., presided on Wednesday at a meeting held in the Bradford Town Hall in furtherance of the objects of the Royal Albert Asylum at Lancaster. The right hon gentleman spoke of the good work which is being done in alleviating the sorrowful condition of children afflicted with idiotcy, and commended the institution to the practical sympathy of the public. There were, he said, many signs at the present day that were encouraging, one of which was that society was more and more acknowledg- ing its duty to those who were helpless amongst its mem- bers. Lord Wintnarleigh, Sir Andrew Fairbairn, M. P., Mr. J. P. C. Starkie, Mr. W. Forster, and other gentlemen also spoke in support of the claims of the Asylum to a generous support of all classes of the community. CONVERTING A LIVERPOOL BOY INTO A ZULU.—A piti- ful tale was told in the City Police Court, Liverpool, on Thursday, by Superintendent Williams, about the conver- sion of a Liverpool boy into a young Zulu. His story was that a man, named John Davey, called upon a Mrs. Jones and told her that he wanted to engage a boy for a Liverpool waxwork exhibition, promising her that if she would let him have her boy she shou'd have ss. a week and permis- sion to see the child every night. The woman accepted the offer, and the boy went to be exhibited as a Zulu. But the mother became anxious, and upon inquiry discovered that her child had been taken to Selkirk, and that he was being exhibited there. Davey was accordingly prosecuted for feloniously and fradulently taking the boy away. His ex- planation, supported by the evidence of Robert Cantrell, of Lotv-hill, placed the matter in a very different light, and showed that he was agent for a showman going about the country exhibiting curiosities. He called upon Mrs. Jones in what appears to have been his regular way of business, gave her his address, told her that her boy was to go to Carlisle next day, and then to Scotland, and paid her two weeks in advance. Mr. Raffles was quite satisfied with this explanation, and Davey was at once discharged. THE LABOUR MAREET.—The Labour Market, although good, is somewhat unsettled, owing to demands for increased wages in several places. The continued fine weather favours building operations and railway and public works construc- tion, which are being carried on vigorously, and the demand for workpeople is very keen, hands being wanted in all quarters. Farm labourers are also much in request, and the approaching hay harvest is visible by the inquiry for hay- makers. At the ironstone mines, work is plentiful-; but the ironworks are standing idle, for want of coal, owing to the North Staffordshire colliers' strike, which promises to con- tinue, as the colliers at work all over the country are liberally subscribing to the strike funds, and the mine- owners have drawn their horses from the pits, and resolved to adhere to their terms. On the 4th, the workmen of the Bridport railway extension works struck for 2s a week in- crease. In North Wales, coal-mining is active through the Staffordshire strike. Shipbuilders and marine engineers are very busy, especially in the North. The Eston strike continues, the proposed arbitration having been futile. At Middlesborough, new steel-rail works have been opened this week, and many hands are employed. At Birmingham, all branches of industry, except jewellery, are very busy. The Sheffield armour-plate and edge-tool makers are very busy, other branches of cutlery manufacture some- what quiet, aed the dispute in the file trade continues. At Wolverhampton, galvanised-iron makers are very busy. At the Newcastle-on-Tyne chemical works, the output is bell= reduced. In the textile trades, there is little change. At Halifax and Bradford,worsted coating manufacturers are well employed, and Botany spinners very busy. At Leeds, fancy suitings and cloth makers are busy. At Kiddermirester, the Brussels carpet looms are very active. At Manchester, manufacturers somewhat quiet. At Leicester, some !nanu- racturcrs are very busy, and others their machinery is par- tially standing idle. The Nottingham machinery is not very busy. At Huddersfield, weavers are working regular time. Work in the Kentish hop and fruit gardens is brisk. At the leading shoe centres, work is in fair supply. Emigration • seems increasing.—The Labour News. PRIZE FIGHT IN Levsnrome—At the Liverpool Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. Raines, stipendiary magis- trate, John Dodd and John Stewart, two young men, were charged with fighting indeKensington Fields; and William Langliam and William Edwards wefe charged with aiding and abetting them. The police stated that between four and five o'clock on Tuesday morning their attention was called to a fight in Kensington fields. Steward and Dodd were fighting, and the other two prisoners were acting as seconds. They were taken into custody, and on the way to the bride- well Dodd told one of the constables that the fight was for £lO a-side. He also said they could get a fight up in Man- chester, but they could not in Liverpool. Stewart and Dodd admitted that they were fighting, the former stating that there was a little animosity between them, and they took that way of settling the dispute. Dodd and Stewart were each fined 20s. and costs, or in default 14 days' imprison- ment, and Langham and Edwards 40s. and costs each, or one month's imprisonment. THE DYNAMITE CONSPIRACY.—The trial of the six prisoners committed to the Central Criminal Court upon charges of treason-felony in connection with the dynamite conspiracy will be commenced at the Old Bally on Monday next. The seventh prisoner, William Joseph Lynch, other- wise Norman, will be called as a witness on behalf of the prosecutian. A special court, consisting of Lord Chief Jus- tice Coleridge, Lord Justice Brett, and Mr. Justice Greve, will be formed for the trial of these prisoners. The judges will sit in the Old Court. The Attorney-General (Sir Henry James, Q.C. M.P.), the Solicitor-General (Sir Farrer Herschell, Q.C., M.P.), Mr. Poland, and Mr. R. S. Wright will prosecute on behalf of the Crown; Mr. Edward Clarke, Q.C., M.P., Mr. J. J. Sims, and Mr. H. J. Broun will defend Dr. Thomas Gallagher; Mr. M. W. Mattinson will defend Bernard Gallagher; Mr. Bowen Rowlands, Q.C., and Mr. Keith Frith will be counsel for John Curtin; Mr. R. W. Burnie will appear for William Ansburgh ; and Mr. G. Geoghegan will defend Thomas Wilson. The prisoner Albert George Whitehead, being without funds, is at present un- represented by counsel; hut we understand that his solicitor, Mr. W. F. Morris, has advised him to write to the Treasury, requesting either a grant of money for his defence, or that counsel may be instructed on his behalf. About 64 witnesses have been subpoenaed by the Treasury for the prosecution, and the trials will, it is expected, last about a week.

RESULT OF A LOVER'S Quannm—The Liverpool coroner on Wednesday held an inquest upon the body of a young woman named Mary Jane Wood, 19, who committed suicide on Monday evening by taking carbolic acid. It appeared from the evidence that the deceased, who was a saleswoman in a boot shop, had for the past two years been keeping company with a glazier named John Abrahams, and on Sunday night last she was told by him that he did not wish to see her any more. She was consequently much distressed in mind, and on Monday afternoon she purchased some car- bolic acid and poisoned herself. Three letters were found upon tho deceased, one of them addressed to Abrahams, in which the writer said that before Abrahams received it she , , should be dead, as she could not endure the thoughts of life without him. She told him on Sunday night that she should put an end to her life, and she hoped that she had done so. She was doing a very wicked thing, but she could not help it, as the blow he bad given her on Sunday night when be told her that he did not love her had been too much for her. The other two letters, addressed to friends of the deceased, were to the same effect. Abrahams himself gave evidence, and said that be had no particular fault to find with the deceased, and the reason be told her he did not want to see her any more was because be was tired of her— that was all. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased committed suicide whilst in a state of tem- porary insanity, and at their request the Coroner censured Abrahams for his heartless anl cruel conduct towards the deceased.

SURVEYOR'S REPORT.
OPENING OF WARRINGTON CRICKET AND BOWLING CLUB'S PAVILION.

The handsome pavilion erected on the ground of the Warrington Cricket and Bowling Club was opened on Saturday afternoon last, but in censequence of the event not being widely known there was a small attendance at the ceremony. Tne Mayor (Mr. John Crosflekl) had consented to open the pavilion, and at a quarter to two o'clock his Worship, accompanied by Mr. Walter Milner (a vice-presi- dent), and Mr. Wm. Owen, entered the ground. On arrival at the pavilion Mr. Owen, at the request of the committee, presented the key to the Mayor, remarking that he was very proud to do so, and could only say that it required no key to unlock the generosity of his Worship's heart, which was patent to all. The committee were proud that as the Mayor of Warrington he had consented to open the pavilion to the members for ever, or rather as long as it stood.—The MAYOR, having accepted the key, said it afforded him a consider- able amount of pleasure to open the building. He was, be believed, the only member now living of the old club, which was started about the year 1847. The club was cer- tainly not then in a flourishing condition, but he and Mr. Peers determined that cricket should not die in Warrington, and that they would do what they could to help it on. He was proud to see that the club had grown, and that by the fortunate removal to Arpley Fields it had become still more successful and was now in a thoroughly flourishing condi- tion. He thought the pavilion was not only a credit to the architect (Mr. Owen) but to the builder (Mr. Beckett, of Hartford). Cricket—and they must have a good cricket field—was a necessity in a large town, and was a means of wholesome recreation; and it afforded him much pleasure to open the pavilion for the use of the members of the War- rington Cricket and Bowling Club.—The Mayor then, amid applause, unlocked the door of the pavilion, over which he was conducted by Mr. H. Fairclough (captain of the club) and Mr. Owen. Tbe committee then assembled in the re- freshment room, where several toasts were drunk.— Mr. Leos. JOLLEY, president of the Bowling Club, proposed the health of the Mayor. They were pleased to see him amongst them, and he (the Mayor) was no doubt proud to be president of the club consisting of 250 members, and whose names were known, respected, and honoured. He thought theirarchitect, Mr. Owen, deserved great praise, as he had given his services without money and without price. (Applause.) There was another gentleman whose services should not be overlooked, namely, Mr. Wm. Robinson, who had been their treasurer for many years, and who had long worked diligently for the club. He also deserved their confidence and respect. (Ap- plause.) The MAYOR briefly returned thanks. Mr. JOHN WHITE, in proposing the health of Mr. Sydney Crosfield, said he hoped the committee would allow him to suggest that having now such an excellent pavilion and a ground second to none in the county, the next step would be to get up some first-rate cricket matches. The love of cricket seemed to be increasing in the town and neighbour- hood, and he thought it was very desirable that they should give the rising generation an opportunity of seeing some , first-class cricket. He wan, glad that there was one bearing the Mayor's name following in the same steps as himself and rendering such assistance to cricket. In years gone by ' he (the speaker) had the pleasure of playing in many Imatches with his. Worship, who had done excellent service, both in making good scores and alsa with that particularly destructive bowling for which he was then famous, the like of which was prcbably never seen before, and had never been I seen since. (Laughter.) He begged to propose Mr. Sydney Crosfield's very goad health, to congratulate him upon the , excellent scores he had made at Oxford, and to congratulate Ithe club that it had a member who reflects so much credit I upon it.—The toast was heartily drunk, and the party hav- ing been photographed by Mr. Birtles, of Sankey-street, the proceedings terminated.

The SURVEYOR called the attention of the Board to the bad state of the surface bearding on the iron bridge across the canal, at the end of Brookfield-road. On some portions of the bridge the boarding was completely worn through, and required to be renewed for the safety of the traffic as well as to preserve the under timbers of the bridge.— Tenders had been invited for the repair of the bridge, and Mr. Newburn's, for £l7 103., was accepted. CLAIM FOR COMPENSATION.

The CLERK reminded the Board of the matter of Mr. Jackson's claim of £4O as compensation for the sewer pas- sing through his land, the consideration of which had been left over from a previous meeting for consideration that evening.—Mr. ROGERS stated that since then hp had had an interview with Mr. Jackson, and that gentleman had con- sented to accept £lO in settlement of his claim. Mr. Jackson had also told him that he thought the costs would not amount to more than 10s.—Mr. APPLETON said that Mr. Jackson told him that morning that there had been a mistake in the matter by the solicitor.—The CHAIRMAN said that when the claim was made it appeared there was some mistake about it.—Mr. ROGERS then proposed that Mr. Jackson be offered £lO in settlement of his claim, and that the costs be paid—The CLERK pointed out that it would be better to limit the amount to be paid for costs ; and Mr. ROGERS then amended his motion to the effect that a sum not exceeding one guinea be paid for legal and ether ex- penses, and the motion having been seconded by Mr. Dewhurst, was carried. THE GAS QUESTION.

Mr. J. Paterson's report on the state of the gasworks and mains was read and accepted. It stated that he had to report favourably on the cmdition of the works compared with that of his previous visit some years ago. The works he found to be in good condition and or-der, and to reflect credit on the industrious and painstaking manager. The producing and storage power of the works were ample and adequate for a greatly-increased supply; their weakness lay in the inadequacy of the distributing plant, a condition by no means unusual in the case of gas industries. He found the capacity of the trunk mains from the works to the town greatly too small. The distance might be taken at 730 yards from the governor at the works to the point of the juncture at Eagle Brow, where the discharging power under the pres- sure of 1-inch on the governor was equal to 8,200 cubic feet per hour, a volume which was quite inadequate for a satisfactory supply, being greatly diminished by its sub - divisions into a number of small mains , where the rubbing surface was considerable. He recommended that a 9-inch main be substituted, the dis- charging power of which, at the point named, under similar pressure, would be 30,000 cubic feet per hour. He stated in detail his observations and opinion respecting several other deficiencies, and the cheapest and most satisfactory method of correcting them. The total cost of the altera- tions and additions which he suggested were estimated by him at £770 is 6d, including the item of £355 the cost of laying complete the 9-inch main from the works to Eagle Brow.—lt was decided that the report be printed, and a copy presented to each gas consumer.—Mr ROGERS moved that a 9-inch main be laid from the gasworks to Eagle Brow in place of the 6-inch main, as suggested by Mr Paterson. He did this on behalf, and with the acquiescence of the Gas Committee.—Mr. DEWHURST seconded, and it was carried unanimously.—A number of tenders for the supplying of the 9-inch main pipes were then considered, and it was ultimately decided to accept the one of the Staveley Coal and Iron Co., Limited, for the supply of 763 yards of 9-inch coated mains, at £4 10s. per ton, de- livered at Lymm station.—Mr. ROGERS moved, Mr. DEW- 111111ST seconded, and it was passed, that £350 be borrowed on the gas account for the purpose of carrying out the pro- posed improvements.—Tenders for the supply of coal and cannell were considered, and that of Messrs. Fletcher, Bur- rows, and Co. for the supply of 600 tons of coal, at 103. per ton, and of the Bridgewater Trustees for the supply of 300 of eannell at 14s. per ton were ultimately accepted. The Board shortly afterwards separaten.
EXTRAORDINARY CASE AT RUNCORN. MR WIGG AND THE CAPTAIN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr Wil- liam Bankes and Mr James Reynolds, William Williams, captain of the schooner Barbara, surrendered to his bail to answer a charge of having, on the 31st May, feloniously stolen a piece of paper, to wit, an authority or agreement in writing of the value of id, the property of Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company. Mr Lake appeared for the defendant, and pleaded not guilty.—From the statement of Mr Wigg, general manager of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company, it seemed that the Barbara arrived in Runcorn Docks on the 28th ult, with a cargo of nitro cake for the Alkali Company. Mr. Wigg refused to receive the cargo until charges amount- ing to is per ton, due to the Bridgewater Navigation Com- pany, were paid. The defendant promised to pay these charges, and signed a letter containing au agreement to that effect. On Thursday morning the defendant visited Mr. Wigg's office, and asked that Mr. Millington, a ship- broker's clerk, by whom he was accompanied. might look at the letter. Mr. Wigg read the letter, and Millington ex- pressed himself satiefied, but the defendant pressed the latter to take the letter in his own hands. Mr. Wigg then j showed Millington the letter, when the defendant rushed forward, snatched the letter from his hands, and tore it to pieces. By Mr Lake: The defendant voluntarily agreed to pay the charges. On Wednesday the defendant applied for an advance on account of the freight, but his re- quest was refused, and in consequence the firm received a notice on Wednesday night to stop delivery.—Mr. Lake: You asked them not to stop delivery? Mr. Wigg: I don't remember that —and when he declined, didn't you call him an impudent fellow? No; I did not.—Quite sure? Certain. I did afterwards.—Didn't you get to heated words then about this advance and order the Captain out? No, not about that. It was when he commdnced to speak in a dis- respectful way that I ordered him from the office.—The , Capt&n was not satisfied with hearing the letter read No; he premeditated. snatching the letter from my hand.—Mr. Lake: But we cannot go into that.—Mr. Wigg: But I think it ought to be gone into.—Mr. Lake: That is a ques- tion for their worships. Didn't you tell the Captain to stand back? I did not speak to him.---Never called him a scamp? No.—Nor an impudent fellow? I have answered that before.—l think you got enraged at him when he snatched the letter? No doubt I did.—You called him a thief? Yes, I dare say I did.—And scamp and sundry other expressions. Did the Captain express sorrow after he had torn up the paper? No; he was most insolent.— Then, as ea matter of fact, is it not more a question of insolence than the value of the paper? No; it is a question of a commercial transaction.---if it had not been for the insolence should you have prosecuted? Most certainly. He came into the office and deliberately stole the paper.—Come, now, Mr. Wigg, you have had some experi- ence of commercial transactions; do you mean to tell us that this piece of paper was a contract? It is, most certainly, a contract —Then lam afraid Your definition of a contract does not tally with most.—Mr. John Poole, clerk in the employ of the Alkali Company, deposed to the drawing.up of the [he captain did not make any objection to the charges.—Mr. Thomas Tomlinson, cashier to the firm, deposed to seeing the defendant snatch the letter from Mr. Wig's grasp, crumple it in his hand, and then place it in his pocket.—By Mr. Lake: Mr. Lake called the defendant an impudent fellow, and ordered him from the office before he tore up the letter.—?.S. McMichael said Mr. Wigg gave the defendant into his custody on a charge of stealing a letter. The letter was tern to pieces, which was lying on the floor. When charged the defendant said. " Who piat my name there? If I had done I would not have pulled it out of his hands."—The Bench intimated that they intended to com- mit the defendant for trial, and Mr. Lake reserved his de- fence. He, however, called Mr. William John Millington, clerk to Mr. Owen Thomas, ship broker, who was acting for the prisoner. He deNsed to accompanying the defendant , to Mr. Wig's office to ask for an advance on account of freight. When the captain would not agree to Mr. Wigg's terms the latter got angry, and called tle cap- tain an impudent fellow. When Mr. Wigg was showing the letter to witness the captain snatched it from him and crumpled it in his hand, but did net place it in his pocket. Mr. Wigg got into a passion, and called defendant a thief, and sent for. a policeman. Afterwards the captain said he J was sorry his temper had got the be,ter of him, and hoped Mr. Wigg would excuse him. Mr. Wigg appeared to take no notice of his words.—The defendant was then- formally committed for trial.—. Mr. Lake applied for bail. Both magistrates said the case was a serious one, but admitted the defendant to bail, himself in 450, and two sureties 0.1 £'2s each.

THE STALE OF THE CROPS.
state of the crops in this Below we give repolts of ti,c district, for which we are indebted to agricultural correa. nondentB in the several localities named.

IluyToN.—Wheat is looking well, the weather for the last few weeks having been most favonraMe. Oats have a good appearance, but are beginning to suffer from the drought. Clover grass is generally below an average ; second years' lays and meadows will be a complete fail cre. Potatoes are looking well; but turnips and mangolds are suffering from drought, and unless we have some early rain will be a fail ure.

LIALTON.—egin is in a promising growing condition, but rain is much needed. Grass i 5 not so plentiful this year as in previons years, and light crops are expected Root crops will be light. The season has been a good one for seeds, and if we have a good growing time, there is every appearance of a good harveat. ASTON.—Clover, ivhict was allowed, to cover before dry weather came, is an average crop, but is seeding too early to get heavy. The quality is good. Upland meadows arc very ligha, but berbv ; Jowlands- are average, and quality good. Oats are abcalt an average where sawn in. due rime; late scwn will be 7ery short in- straw, and ear- lies have suffered from the "'out" worm, and are too thin in plant. Autumn sown wheat is about average in plant, but the acreage is lets than other years, though it looks like a good quaility. Though spring sown, is-over the average in acres, and rather thin in 'tint, it is. improving rapidly, and looks like a good crop,. if a favourable July comes, with plenty of sun. Ear :y potatoes are ender average both in acres and crop, the land being shor: of moisture. Winter potatoes are very late, but are coming up healthy, and the seasoa will suit the Magnum Bonum whir,h is almost universally planted. It can stand dry weather better than other kinds, being less given to run at the root in a dry time. Swede turnips show good plant where sownr early, but late sown are doubtful as the seed cannot yet germinate, and will almost certainly be destroyed more or less with the fly. Mangolds are over average in plant, and the quality is very good; a dry season enita mangolda. Barley, which is not sown extensively in this district, looks well and quite up to average. Beans show average crone, and are doing well where planted early, which is the case hereabouts. Pasture is bare, but stock are doing fairly well. Sheep are feeding well, and lambs are growing and feedirz well.

WOOLSTON.—Wheat is fairly good but very late. Oats are good, except in some few instances where " bots " have made great havoc. Seed grass and clover arc light from want of moisture during earlier stages of growth, but meadows being later may still be good if rain falls soon. Early potatoes are looking tolerably well, but are uneven in the rows in consequence of severe frosts directly after planting. It is too soon to report upon late sorts. Afengalds are in a state of stagnation for want of rain ; and swede 3 are suffring from the same cause, with the addition ot a somewhat severe attack of "fir." GREAT BUDWORTII.—There is not so much wheat sown as usual, owing to the very werautumo and early winter, but what has been sown is looking well, and likely to prove an average crop, especially if this dry, warm weather in which the wheat plant delights, continues. Oats, of which there is a larger breadth sown than usual, are looking very promising, especially on broken ground. The grub, known by the name of the " bot," made its appearance in several fields of ley oats, and did considerable d image, in some cases neces- sitating a second sowing. Of barley, very little is grown let this district. Potatoes, with which there is a goc,d breadth planted, are not very promising for a heavy crop—l mean the early ones—a great breadth having suffered by the spring frost, which greatly weakens their vitality. The , later sorts are just getting throngh the r-round. Turnips (swedes) are nearly all sown. In many cases they arc above ground, but if rain does not come shortly Ike:hers are likely to have to sow again, the turnip fly havin T got to wort:. WINWICK.—The crops in this locality may be taken as more than ordinarily promising. Rain is now wanted, but nothing is suffering for lack of moistures, unless there is a deficiency in either manurial agency, or fi • quency and depth of tillage operations. Cabbages are s rail in the heads where planted in beds and properly worked amongst, and not in drills as is too much the practice in this locality. The same may be said of potatoes and all other green crops. Corn looks very promising, as does also clover and first year's grass seeds where in good heart. The probability is that the season will be such that good husbandry will manifest it- self in a striking manner, as already I can point out fields, equal in every respect as to natural capacity, where there is now fully three times the difference in the productive realisation. This is not a good district for grass farming in fact it is very materially neglected. The only good ex- ample is a field belonging to, and in the occupation of, the rector of Winwick. This will have this year fully three times the amount of produce of neighbouring lands 40( equal natural status ; though it appears to be a little flagging compared with what the rector displayed in his earlier years of possession. ANTROBUS.—The state of crops in the district of Antrobus and Sevenoaks is much better than for the last three years. Wheat, oats, grass, and potatoes are in a very satisfactory condition, and are looking well. Potatoes will be ready for the market in about ten days. THELIVALL.—Wheat, not looking well, thin and very late; oats, fair but want rain; rye-grass and clover, very thin crops, about half the quantity of last year; meadows. -rot good, very short ; potatoes, looking very well, if rain come* will be heavy crops; mangolds, very fair; turnips, want rain, plagued with fly.

TIMRSDAY.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge A LYMu DOCTOR SUED FOR LAW COSTS.—In this case, Mr. Thomas Addenbrook (for whom Mr.G. Moore appeared) was plaintiff, and Mr. Rawson Senior, defendant.—Mr. Moore said the plaintiff was a solicitor, practising in War- rington and Lymm, and sought to recover from the defend- ant £49 19s lid for professional services rendered, for mouey paid, and for work done.—lt appeared that at the Spring Assiz.?s, at Chester, last year, the defendant retained Mr. Addenbrook to conduct a case for him. Defendant, who is a medical man, residing at Lymm, purchased for agentle- man named Cartwright, also a medical man, his business there. Defendant gave certain promissory notes to the plaintiff of that action which were not met, and therefore plaintiff sued Mr. benior at unener Asstz.s for a cenaln amount. The verdict went against the defendant, but be did not know whether he had paid the costs of that action.— Defendant: No, I have not.—Mr. Mo ire said the costs of Mr. Addenbrook in the action amounted to considerably over the sum which plaintiff claimed. Mr Senior was not in a posi- tion to pay, and he had to file his petition. There were also , the costs of the petition in liquidation. Those proceedings ' fell throne-1iI but an amount was run up in costs. Applica- tion was made in due course to the defendant for 'payment of the costs, which amounted to £3B 5s 4,1, but in order to put the case in court the plaintiff had abandoned I£3B 6s 4d, which left a balance of £49 19s, for which he ' now sued. An assigned bill was sent in on the 3rd May last year, and an account was rendered. Defendant had always made excuses. He had never repudiated his liability —to the larger portion of the bill at any rate; and he had never made any attempt to get the bill taxed. Plaintiff had been very lenient and kind to defendant, who had had no less than four applications from his (Mr. Moore's) office, but he always put him off by saying he could not afford to pay, and one thing and another, and plaintiff was compelled to ask his Honour, if he saw his way, to sive him a verdict.— Defendant said it was simply impossible for him to pay. At the tithe of his composition he offered 5s in the X. His Honour : You don't dispute the bill ? Defendant said, certainly not, but he was , totally unable to pay. Five shillings in the X was offered to Mr. Addenbrook, and he would not accept it.—His Honour: Tfiis is a matter for von and your creditOr to settle. All I can do is to give judgment against you.— Defendant said the bills under £2O, for which the creditors had accepted 5s in the X, he had paid already.—His lion- our: I don't know anything about that. The question is whether you owe this debt to the solicitor for services reudered.—Defendant : I ewe it, but I cannot possibly pay a penny. There is no chance of any improvement. We have another doctor, and Mr. Addenbrook sent for him to see his wife.—His Honour: This is a matter I cannot attend to. If you admit that you owe this debt then judgment must be entered against you.—Defendant asked how it was the debt had been reduced from £88•to £49. That was a most extraordinary thing. £8 had been paid, and that £8 was procured in a very extraordinary way —such a way as his Honour would be very sorry to hear.— His Honour : What do you mean P—Defendant said Mr. Addenbrook promised to throw the matter up if he paid £B, and he raised it on his silver.—Mr. Moore said that was for counsel's fees, and they gave credit for the amount.—His Honour said he must give judgment against the defendant. As regarded payment, he must make the best terms he could with the plaintiff, because be had no power in proceedings under this statute except to give judgment,in the ordinary way—that was judgment forthwith.—Defendant said he could no more pay than fly.—His Honour: You must make he best terms you c
A RUNCORN PUBLICAN'S LICENCE ENDORSED.

Selina Ogden. landlady of the Swan inn beerhouse, Shaw-street, was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, on a charge of keeping her house open after closing hours. About half-past two, on the morning of the 19th May, Sergeant McMichael and Constable Finney were in Shaw-street, when they observed that the backyard and kitchen doors of the defendant's house were open. They entered. Sitting on a sofa in the kitchen was the defendant, who was under the influence of drink, and by her side was seated a young man. Two other young men and the de- fendant's mother occupied seats in different parts of .the house. On a table was a glass of- beer and several empty glasses. The landlady alleged that the men were lodgers, and to give colouring to her words, two of them walked up- stairs, but the third kept his seat by her• side. Shortly, afterwards P.S. McMichael also went into the bedroorris' and his search revealed the two young men lying beneath the sheets, but fully attired. After obtaining the names of the delinquents, the officers left the premises, but P.C. Finney concealed himself to watch, and presently saw three men emerge from the house, and walk towards the docks. Mrs. Marsh, keeper of the Ellesmere Hotel, regent•street, deposed that one of the young men, named William Bond, had until the night in question lodged with her. On that occasion she waited until one o'clock for him. He had not returned.—The de- fence to the charge was that the young men were lodgers, but the bench considering the previous bad character of the house, thought otherwise, and fined the defendant 20s. and costs. Her license was also endorsed.

SERMONS AT WARGRAVE CRIIRCII.—The annual sermons in aid of the funds of the Sunday schools connected with Emmanuel Church, Wargrave, were preached by the Rev. G. Carson of Liverpool on Sunday last. There was a large congregation both morning and evening, and in the after- noon the teachers and scholars listened to an excellent ad- dress from Mr. Carson. The services realized the sam of , z 22 14s H.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

Mr. Justice Barry is made a Lord Justice of Appeal, and the vacancy he leaves in the Queen's Bench is to be filled by the elevation of Mr. Murphy, Q.C. Mr. M'Coan has withdrawn from the Trish Parliamentary party, giving as his reason that "with veiled Communism and rebellion he can no longer maintain even nominal relations." The Lord-Lieutenant for Ireland has replied to the memo- rial forwarded to him on behalf of Tim Kelly, sentenced to death for the murder of Mr. Burke, stating that his Excellency sees no reason why the course of the law should be interfered with. Kelly will be hanged to-morrow morning. It is stated that James Carey, the informer, pesters the authorities daily about his release. He insists on it as a right; and his latest threat is to have the attention of Par- liament called to his case. Carey complains that the Government have broken faith with him, and he will not leave Ireland unless fo-ce is used.

A woman named Curley has given evidence at Parsons 7 town, King's County, to the effect that, while listening out- side a house at which a number of men in custody used to assemble, she heard the arrangements discussed for the mur- der of Constable Brown, committed some months ago. Several of the prisoners are specifically incriminated by the woman's statements. RELEASE OF MESSRS. DAVITT, HEALY, AND QUINN.— Messrs. Davitt, Healy, M.P., and Quinn were released from gaol on Monday. They have undergone about two-thirds of the term of six months' imprisonment imposed upon them in default of their giving surety for their good behaviour. The prosecution was for seditious speaking at a land meeting. It is proposed to raise funds for the purpose of making a suitable presentation to Mr. Field, the juryman whose assassination was attempted by the Dublin "Invincibles." His business is boycotted, his employes threatened with death, and suspicious parcels from England, labelled "not explosive," are delivered at his premises. It is believed that he will have to leave Dublin. THE MURDER CONSPIRACY IN THE WEST OF IRELAND.— The magisterial inquiry concerning the murders- of Head- constable Kavanagh and two men named Ltydon, at Letter- frack, over two years ago, .closed on Monday. John and Martin Faharty, Edward Donnell, and Thomas connolly were committed for trial for wilful murder, six others were committed for treason-felony and conspiracy to murder, and two, named Michael M'Donnell and Peter Nee, were allowed out on their own recognisances to appear when called on. THE PHCENIX PARE MURDERS: EXECUTION OF CaYrnEY. —Thomas Caffrey, the fourth of the six men condemned to death for the murder of Mr. Burke in the Phoenix Park, was executed on Saturday morning in Kilmainham gaol. Very few persons assembled outside the gaol. Before leaving the chapel Caffrey paused, and said with great deliberation," I hope my fate will be a warning to all young men not to join secret societies." He left a letter addressed to his mother, in which communication he con- fessed his crime .and stated his preparedness for death. ALLEGED POISONING BY THE INVINCIBLES. - Strong suspicion is felt that, in addition to using the knife, the Dublin Invincibles have resorted to poison: Fourteen days after the Phenix Park murders' Mr. H. J. Jury, a Dublin hotel-keeper, suddenly died, and some suspicion arose at the time as to the cause of the death. Now it is reported that Mr. Jury inadvertently opened a letter that was intended for "Number 1," who was at that time staying at his hotel, and on this becoming known it was decided to poiso,i him. This story is now being investigated, and it is stated that other suspicious deaths are also being inquired into.

ARCHBISHOP CROKE AT TlPPERARY.—Tipperary was illuminated on Saturday evening in honour of Dr. Croke, who administered confirmation in the town on Sunday. Bands, with processions, marched through the town, the scene being a lively one. After the confirmation an address was presented to the archbishop, which said it was tolerably well known that he and the people of Tipperary were united in heart and sentiment, and that it sh9wed whoever strovo faithfully to advance the cause of social comfort and con- stitutional freedom in Ireland Would find ample reward for his exertions in the prayers of the people. His Grace briefly replied.

THE ACTION AGAINST A PRESTON
BROOK BOAT OWNER.

On Saturday, in the Queen's Bench Division of the High Court of Justice, before Mr. Justice Watkin Williams, Mr. Justice Cave, and Mr. Justice A. L. Smith, the case of Clare a. Mousley came on for judgment on the rule nisi obtained by the defendant calling on the plaintiff to show cause why there should not be a new trial on the ground of misdirec- tion and verdict against the weight of evidence at the trial on a former occasion. The rule was argued before Justices Williams and Matthew, and judgment reserved. Mr. Justice Watkin Williams, in delivering the judgment of the court, said the action was one brought by the plaintiff, au owner of flats on the Mersey, against iefendant, canal boat owner, of West Bromwich and Preston Brk, for damages sustained by a flat belonging to the plaintiff while a canal boat of the defendant's was entering a dock at Widnes. "t appeared that the defendant, in the ordinary course of busi- ness, hired steerers to do the journey with his canal boats from West Bromwich to Preston Brook. and on the boat which did the. damage was a Mail named Forster. Defendant gave the right to these steerers to get cargoes on their own account back to West BromiCk but instructed them not Co take the boats Int) tidal waters. On the day in question Forster was proceeding across the Mersey to enter the dock at Widnes for the purpOse of get- ting a cargo on his own account. For the plaintiff it was contended that, notwithstanding this fact Forster was in defendant's ',employ, but an opposite contention was set up that he was not. He and Mr. Justice Matthew thought there was evidence upon which the jury :might find that; the steerer was in the service of the defendant for the pur- poie of navigating the boat on the canal ; bat the boat was taken off the canal, and they thought there was no evidence upon which the jury ought to have been asked to reject the positive statement of the defendant and his witnesses, that there was no evidence of Forster acting in defend3nt'hein- ploy, therefore the verdict was wrone., and the rule would tm absolute for new trial.

FIRE AT..MR. HOLBROOK GASKELL'S RESIDENCE.-At about half-past one o'clock on Tuesday afternoon informa- tion was received at the Central Fire Station, Hatton-gar- den, that a fire had broken out at Mr. Holbrook Gaskell's residence, in Hillfoot-road, Woolton. The fire brigade, with a manual engine, in charge of Deputy-Superintendent Nis- bett, promptly turned out and fireman Long- bottom, with the Salvar4e Corps and trap, immediately afterwards followed suit. Upon arriving at Ilillfoot-road it was found that the fire was confined to a barn in the farmyard stored with straw and to a four-ton stack of bay. About thirty men were set to work at the pumps, and every precaution was taken to keep the flames from spreading. In about three hours from the time of the outbreak the flames were got under, but not before the barn with its contents and the hay bad been destroyed.

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 13, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (June 7th)

Whilst the minor markets have exhibited no great activity and no decided all round movement, business in rails and other prominent securities has been good, and course of prices against buyers. The continuance of brilliant weather and other influences have caused a pretty general advance in value, but fears as to the future of money has exerted an adverse influ- ence, induc'ng some decline from best figures attained. Foreign Funds do not show much change, the alterations being pretty fairly balanced The c indition of affairs between France and China regarding Tongain precludes much spring in those stocks, the values of which are mainly influenced from Paris; still the situation has not yet exerted much adverse influence. Quotations for miscellaneous investments are not revised to any great extent, nor do the revisions indicate decided leaning in either direction.

CURIOUS CIRCUMSTANCE A7t RUNCORN.—During the pre- sent week Messrs. S. and F. Yarwood, veterinary surgeons, made a post-mortem exsAnination of a pony belonging to Mr. Griffiths. Ir the stomach, inflammation of which had caused the animal's death, they found three stones of boulder shap'a, each weighing over a pound. FIRE AT A WIDNES CHEMICAL WORIES.—About half- past eleven on Friday night, one of the sheds belonging to the Atlas Chemical -Company, Limited, was discovered to be on fire, and an alarm was at once given. A crowd of persons and a posse of police quickly assembled, but the measures taken for the extinction of the flame were so suc- cessful that damage to the amount of £2O was only sustained. It is supposed that the fire originated through a spark from one of the chimneys falling on the roof of the building, which was of wood. PRESENTATION TO A RUNCORN GOOD TEMPLAR.—At the usual meeting of the Hope of Runcorn Lodge of Good Templars on Friday evening last week, Sister Mcßride, who is about to leave for Australia, was presented with a beauti- fully illuminated address and the regalia of the Grand Lodge. There was a numerous company present, including the members of the Juvenile Temple, and representatives of the various lodges in Widnes. Bro. Thomas Faulkner, G.L.E. deputy, made the presentation in a few appropriate .remarks. Bro. George Riley acknowledged the gift on be- half of the recipient. Toe address was the work of Mr. J. B. Imison, of Widnes. RUNCORN SHIPPERS HEAVILY FlNED.—Before Mr. W. Bankes, and Mr. James Reynolds, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Messrs. John Simpson and Co. were summoned to answer a charge of keeping a canal boat named King Orrey on the Bridgewater canal without having it duly registered, the registration mark being defaced. Mr. W. H. Linaker appeared to prosecute. The defendants were not represented. Mr. Thomas Booth, inspector of canal boats proved the dise, which the Bench characterised as one of gross neglect, and fined the defendants 20s. and costs. Mr. Linaker applied that his fee of £1 is. should be paid by the defendants. They were a wealthy firm, and had taken no notice of the Court's summons.—Mr. Banks : Very well, we allow a guinea. • THE WIDNES LOCAL BOARD AND HUTCHINSON'S TRUS- TEES —The arbitration concerning the claim for way-leave, made by the Hutchinson's trustees against the sewerage scheme, was resumed at the Lion Hags], Warrington, On Saturday. Mr. H. Linaker, of Frodsharn' was the arbitrator for the Local Board, and dr. Dan'ng for Hutchinsot.'s trus- tees, while Mr. E. Railford, C.E , of Manchester, acts as the umpire. The Board were represented by Mr. Segar, bar- rister, and Mr. Robert Davies, solicitor. Mr. Walton, bar- rister, and Mr. Woodcock, solicitor, represented the trustees. The proceedings, which were of a private character, were concluded, but the arbitrator's award is not expected to be made for several months.

-- RUNCORN OPEN-AIR CONCERTS.—On Thursday evening the Volunteer band, under the leadership of Mr. Wood, ren- dered a programme of classical music in unimpeachable style in connection with these concerts. Their performance was listened to with marked attention by a very large num- ber of people. Next Thursday evening, at half-past seven, the Parish Church band will go through the following pro- gramme on the market ground :—Fantasia, " Elmire," Mul- lott ; quadrille, "Inspiration," Smith ; romanza, " The wanderer," Round; seranade "Evening star," Round; waltz, " Light and shade." Lund ; grand slow march, " Apollo," Linter; cornet solo, polka 4 Spick and span," Round; galop, ",Climax," Linter ; "God nave the Queen." DROWNING FATALITIES AT RUNCORN.—Mr. WOlSley, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Barleymow Hotel, on Monday, touching the death of George Walker, five yeats of age, son of a boatman living in Vine-yard. After tea on Sunday the boy told his father that he was going to play by the canal side. As he had not returned at nine o'clock a search was made for him, and his dead body was found in the canal at Toplocks by a boatman named Joseph Twigg. A verdict of found drowned was returned.—Mr. Worsley also held an inquiry into the circumstances of the death of Thomas Robert Pickstock, who was drowned in the Weston canal on Friday evening. The facts have previously ap- peared in The Examiner. A verdict of "Accidentally drowned "was returned.

SWINE FEVER AT WESTOE.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, John McCloud, living at Weston, was charged that he having a pig suffering from fever, did neglect t 3 re- port the outbreak of the contagions disease to the police. On the 16th inst, Inspector Hollingsworth, who is the In- spector under the Contagious Diseases Animals Act, found en the defendant's premises a pig which had all the appear- ance of suffering acutely from swine fever.—Defendant ad- mitted that the pig had been ill for a week, but added that he was unaware that he ought to have reported the fact.-The Inspector AnnsEquentiv mllPci in a veterinary surgeon, who declared that the pig in question :1.`,1 another in the sty were suffering from fever, and they were slaughtered by order of the local authority.—Superintendent Williamson remarked that notices had been frequently posted with re- gard to swine fever. The chief constable bad no wish to be severe in this matter, which he left in the hands of their worships.—The bench ordered the defendant to pay the cost of the summons, and now that he knew the law, be careful to observe it in the future. ALLEGED BURGLARY BY BOYS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, John Howard and James McCormick, boys, were charged with breaking into the shop of David Halton, shoemaker, Dock-street, Widnes, on Sun- day last.—Mrs. Halton stated that at nine o'clock he saw her sweets and cakes all safe in the window. he went to bed after locking Elp her house. About four o'clock in the morning she was awakened by a noise, and going down found that a woman was there wanting a pennyworth of matches. She sold her some, and when she had gone she went and lay down dressed in the bed. When the went on- stairs everything was safe. About half an hour afterwards she heard a noise at the front window' and going down- stairs found that someone had brol3en the window, and had abstracted some of the sweets. She opened the door, and saw the prioner John Howard standing near eating dates. There were three e.r four other boys in the street, Her hus- band subsequently gave information te. the police—P.C. Thompson deposed to apprehending sht prisoners.—The Bench committed prisoners for Wel at the next Quarter Session.

EXCITING SaNg AT RUNCORN RAILWAY STATION.—Thb danger to which passengers are exposed at too many rail- way stations through being compelled to walk across the lines in order to pass from one platform to another is obvious, and many are the accidents that have occurred in consequence. At Runcorn station this objectionable mode of crossing.is in vogue, and on Saturday night a woman had a narrow escape from a frightful death. Several young men belonging, to the Birkenhead Ringers Cricket Club had passed from one platform to the other to await the arrival of the Liverpool train. Observing a train rapidly approach- ing, they shouted to a companion, who had stayed behind, to cross the line immediately. He did so, and a woman, carrying a child in her arms, follow,d his example. Her motions, however, were not so rapid as the man's, and to the persons on the platform it seemed that she would be knocked down by the express as it rushed through the station. Excited directions to "come back" and "go on" were shouted to the poor woman, who becoming bewildered, stood irresolute in the path of the approaching train. In another instant she would inevitably have been killed, but for the young man alluded to, who, reaching forward seized her, and succeeded in dragging her to the platform just as the train whirled past. The woman heartily thanked her rescuer, who afterwards received the congratulations of his companions on his courage and presence of mind.

THE ALKALI Acr.—The Manchester Guardian, in an article on Dr. Angus Smith's latest report as Inspector under the Alkali Act, says :—" The chief want in the salt districts of Cheshire is efficient smoke burning. The chimneys which send out great quantities of black smoke may be counted by hundreds, although the proprietors are all liable tJ fines for not preventing such exe,ssive discharges. The salt district can nev. r be considered as sufficiently protected until smoke. burning is made absolute. It will be necessary to deal with the salt and muriatic acid from such works all the same, but a bc_‘ginning should be made with the smoke, which itself carries up salt only partly decomposed. The call used in the salt district should be first turned into coke, and with this object Dr. Smith would have works for distilling coal established in the salt districts, the ammonia and tar to be sold, the sulphur converted into sulphuric acid, and the gas and coke used as fuel. Dr. Smith attacks the waste heaps near alkali works, the rain and other streams from which poison books and rivers, and work incalculable mischief in other ways. The new Act gives power to deal with them, and the Inspector means business. Steps have already been taken at Widnes, an 4 railway companies, amongst others, havja been warned that their embankments made of waste are henceforth to cease to be the sources of streams giving off sulphuretted hydrogen. ji beginning has been made at Widnes, but St. Helens and other places are duly warned by the report before us that they also will bare to bestir them- selves in the matter."

BREACH OF THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACT AT Wanmas.—On Wednesday, at the Widnes Petty Ses- sions, before Messrs. F. H. Gossage (chairman) and H. S. Hall, Andrew Quinn, heerseller, Moss Bank, Widnes, was charged with committing a breach of the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, by selling six pigs which had not been 14 days upon his premises.—Superintendent Barker characterised the case as a most important one. The infor- mation was hr,mg,ht tinder an order in Council made on the 22nd March last, in which it was stated that no cattle could be sold in a district infected with foot-and-mouth disease which had not been on the owners premises 14 days at least. Now, he should prove that the defendant sold the pigs in the street, to say nothing of the fact that they had not been on his premise; 14 days. He might state that, in conse- quence of people going about selling pigs, swine !ever had spread in at:alarming manner through that division of the county. No lest, than £3O was paid by the county to Widnes alone from August, 1882, to March, 1883, as compensation. —P.S. Strickland deposed to seeing the prisonv with pigs in Tanhouse-lane. He saw him deliver them to several houses there. Witness spoke to him, and he said he had sold them to a Mrs Bulger, and added that he had brought them straight from Ireland.—Thomas Potter, provision dealer, 43, Ann-street, said that otrthe preceding Thursday he bought four pigs from the defendant. The bargain was struck in Sutton'-lane, where he met the defendant with them. He paid him £5 15s. for them.—lnspector Barnett said he was the appointed cattle inspector for Widnes, and on Sunday last a man named Hessman reported to him a case of swine fever. Mr. Weisby, veterinary inspector, came on Monday to see the case. Hessrnan stated that he had bought the pig from the defardant.—John Higginbotham, cattle inspector in the West Derby Division, said there were two infected places in the division, and the order was now in force.—The Chairman said the defendant would be fined 10s. for each pig, and coats; altogether £4.

HOLY TRINITY YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION, RUNCORN.—Tne members of this association concluded their winter's session on Wednesday by a picnic to Eaton Hall, the residence of the Duke of Westminster. Starting from Runcorn railway station at a quarter-past eight the party, numbering about 36 ladies and gentlemen, arrived in Chester about nine o'clock. After traversing the quaint streets and viewing the many interesting relics of the ancient city, the party had a pleasant journey down the Dee to their destination. Clothed in its summer garb the park presented a beautiful aspect, and the party spent a delightful day roaming about the grounds. In the evening they returned to Chester where they had tea, and then departed for home, where they they arrived safely about nine o'clock. The arrangements of the day were successfully carried out by Mr. William Cunningham, the secretary of the society. RUNCORN UNION PROSECUTIONS.—On Monday, at Run- ' corn Petty Sessions, Charles Platt avaa summoned by the Guardians of the Runcorn Union for £3 7s. 6d , money ad- vanced on loan. Mr. Houghton said the defendant acknow- ledged the debt, and had made an offer of 23. per week. The Bench made an order for the payment of 23. 61. per week.— Samuel Mercer was summoned for £lO 75., amount due by him to the Guardians under an order of the justices made on the Ist August, 1881. Mr. Banks inquired why Mr. Houghton did not take action in these cases earlier. Mr. Houghton said tpe case had been adjourned several times to give the defendant an opportunity to pay. An order was made for payment forthwith ; in default, a distress warrant to be issued.—Wm. Stanley, of 76, Chohnondeley-street, Widnes, appeared on a similar summons, the amount due being £8 93. In this case Mr. Houghton had held a distress warrant, but on the defendant promising to pay the money he had not acted upon it. The defendant then removed, and for 18 months Mr. Houghton had been unable to trace him. The Bench granted a distress warrant. —Wm. Wright was ordered to pay to the Guardians the sum of £l2 Lk, at the rate of is. 61. per week. He was only in receipt of 16s. per week, and had three children to maintain. "WHEN DOGS BEGIN TO BARK,&C.:" A WIDNES CASE. —At Widnes Petty Sess'ons, on Wednesday, George Hold- ing, dog breaker to Mr. Baring, of Liverpool, !vas charged with assaulting Patrick Murray, chemical labourer, on the 22nd May; and there was a cross-summons. Mr. Husband • appeared for Mr. Holding.—Murray stated that on the day in question while on his way to Sullivan's chemical works he met the defendant, who was on horseback. Complainant had a lurcher dog with him, and the defendant was accom- panied by nine or ten young dogs. His dog and the defen- dant's dogs began to fight, and he took up a handful of cinders and threw at them. The defendant thereupon raised his whip and struck him on the head with it repeatedly, and tried to ride his horse over him. The defendant pre- I sently junarsd off his Imrse, and hand-to-hand fight ensued. The defendant seizA him by the throat.—Cross- examined by Mr. Husband: Complainant had previously been fined for poaching. He was not looking for game on the day that he met the defendant. He called the defen- dant a coward.—William Duffey said h 3 saw the defendant raise his whip and strike Murray across the shoulders and on the face. He lashed him repeatedly.—Robert Hjgginson Gray gave confirmatory evidence. During the hand-to- hand fight that took place Murray seemed to be acting entirely on the defensive.—The cross-summons was then heard.—George Holding stated that he was out with nine dogs on tke day in question. They were attached by the lurcher belonging to Murray, and one of them was so badly injured that it was now on the point of death. Murray called him a coward and challenged him to come off his horse. He did so, and blows were exchanged.—The Bench dismissed the case against Murray, but Holding was fined 10s. and costs.

The annual meeting of this society was held on Wed- nesday evening, in the committee room of the Lacey-s.reet echools, under the presidency of Mr. J. W. Coxon. There were also present Messrs. S. Robinson, Lord, 'Tingley, Lamb, J. Betney, J. H. Lee, J. Farrant, Ben., J. W. Davies, H. Lea, J. Farrant, jun.' W. Ch idwicle, J. Treacy, Priest- nall, R. Fogg, Jones, J. Davies, Reay, Hague, T. S. Swale, E. Seddon, and F. Lawrinson.—Mr. W. TREACY, jun. (secre- tary), read the second annual report of the Board of Man- agement, which -stated that the society was making progress, having added 49 members during the year. Since the last annual meeting there had been six appropriations, making eight since the formation of the society, appropriating £1,900, of which £1,400 had already been taken up. The directors regretted that the society had not yet its full com- pliment of members, and begged to call the attention of the members to the fact that the sooner the society was in that condition, the sooner the working expenses would be lessened and the appropriations be more frequent. Any member haying less than four shares might on any subscription eight increase them to that number. The statement of accounts showed that the principal items in the receipts were :—To balance £304 03 91, members' sulsscriptions less amount refunded to widow of deceased member—James Makin-I-1897 7s, small items £4O 12s 3d, and repayments of appropriation £4B is, total £1,290 Is. The payments were :—By appropriations advanced £1,020 183 6.1, Milner Safe Company (Limited) for new safe .Cl 5 Os, working expenses during the year, including rent of office, £l3; auditors' fees £2, directors' £l9 Gs, secretary's £45 Os 6,1, altogether £93 3 241: balance in secretary's and in Parr's Bank £lO4 163 '4l; total £1,296 is. The capital account included the following items of interest to mem- bers :—Subscription last year, less subscriptions forfeited, £760 Gs•' members' subscriptions present year, with deduc- tions, £892 15s; total £1,653 is, less two I years' working expenses en 774 shares at is 31 per share—£l,ss6 Gs, plus profit and loss account £1,564 I.ls Gid. By balance of appropriation, £1 323 4s 8d; formation expenses per last year's account, £53 us ; cost of safe, less depreciation, £l2 ss; balance in bank, £164 4s GI The advance account was as follows :—Amount advanced. £1,379 Os ; amount repaid, £56 is 4d; amountdue, £1,323 438d.—The CHAIRMAN moved, and Mr. J. H. LEI seconded, a motion for the adoption of the accounts.—A discussion arose on the propriety of advertising, but no decision wee arrived at.—The SECRETARY pointed out that it was to the advantage of the members to canvass themselves.—Mr. CHADWICK said he noticed that the working expenses bore a proportion of ten per cent. on the income of the society, which was a very large proportion considering the business they had. He did not consider this satisfactory. If any public society spent so much on working expenses the share- holders would have something to say about it.—Mr. S. ROBINSON said if the members were to increase their sub- seriptions would be more, and their expenses proportionately less. It was not in the power of the directors to decrease the expenses, but it was in the power GI the members to increase their numbers.— Mr. Cetanwecee said if the society had only two-thirds of the fail complement of members, the officials were only doing two-thirds of the work. That being the case, they might reasonably ask them to take two-thirds of the pay Mr ROBINSON pointed out that when the society got into full working order the directors would not have to give so mucn time to it, but they had to attend numerous meetings, some of which occupied a long time, which were for the benefit of the society, and if Mr Chadwick thought 2s too much, he did not agree with him.—The SECRETARY, in answer to questions, said the sum of £45 9s 6d, secretary's salary, was for five quarters; and, therefore, £lO Os Gd ought to be. deducted from the year's working expenses. There were several items which wonld he lessened in future, and some that would not occur again.—Mr. Fono, while thinking Mr Chadwick's remarks were to the point, observed that be had looked carefully over the accounts, and he could net put his finger on a single item which he could say might be reasonably reduced. Ihe expenses at the commencement of a society were necessarily large, but during the next five years the expenses would decrease, and they hoped the income in- crease. The fact was they had not sufficient members. If they could add to the list, the income would increase and the expenses decrease. The report was adopted —The elec- tion of directors then took place, the following gentlemen being nominated and voted for as follows: Messrs. J. W. Coxon 29, S. Robinson 27. T. Hingley 19, J. Betney 17, J. Farrant 14, W. Chadwick 14, F. Lawrinson 8, W. Hague 7, and J. W. Davies G. The first four, who are the retiring directors were declared elected. Messrs. Farrant and Povah, the retiring auditors, were re-appointed, their votes beim.? respectively 21 and 19. Messrs. W. Chadwick and J. W. Davies. the other candidates, received 18 and 14 votes re- spectivelv.--The CHAIRMAN pointed out that the secretary's salary was fixed by rule, and there would he no change.— Mr. FOGG naid a tribute to Mr. Treacv's ability, and spoke highly of the efficient manner in which he had fulfilled the secretaryship.—The meeting then separated.—The next appropriation of the society takes place on the 14th inst.

The first business was the question of • removal of the ' Board's offices to Waterloo House.—Mr. SIMPSON said Father Fennelley and himself were the only members of the Board who met the com- mittee of the Commissioners at Waterloo House. They both, he thought, agreed that the rooms would do very well.—The CHAIRMAN laid it seemed to him that there were two points to be considered. First the ques- tion of rent, whether they should be the losers by removing; and secondly whether the the rooms would enable the Board to carry out the intentions of the Education Department. Mr. SIMPSON said there was little difference ef opinion on the matter at the meeting to which he had referred, as to whether it would be so con- venient for the people who wished to see the Inspector, and to visit the Beard. But there was a more important point, perhaps. He understood that the Board could not get free from the lease of these premises until the time had expired. They had, too, incurred considerable expense in the present office, and he thought they would have to incur consider- able expense if they removed, so that he did not know whether they should get clear under s6ene £5O or £6O at least. The present Board dissolved at Christina, and he was rather of opinion that it would scarcely be wise for them to decide the matter, as they had so short an existence before them. He was inclined to think it would be better to leave the matter to the next Board.—Father FENNELLEY said the committee of the Commissioners received Mr. Simpson and himself at Waterloo with great kindness, and promised to do everything in their power to accommodate and make them comfortable. He thought the rooms were better than the present offices, and far more suitable for the business of the Board. It was, in fact, like , going from a cottage into a palace. The Board could have three • or four rooms if they required them, and the attendance officer's room would be attached to the Board room, which would be a great convenience. It was also sufficiently large to accom- modate the people who would visit the Board. • The clerk's office would be far superior to his present one. He could not understand how an expenditure of more than a few pounds could be incurred. He asked Mr. Shaw about the question of rent, and he said the Board would not have to pay any rent at all until their present lease expired. Indeed, it appeared to him (Father Fennelley) that by removing to Waterloo House the Board would save the ratepayers about £25 or £26 per year.—The CHAIRMAN: At the end of four years.—Father FENNELLEY : Na, each year. Here the money goes into Mr. Rigby's pocket; there it will go into the ratepayers' pockets.—The CLERK: But you would have' to pay it whether or no.—The CHAIRMAN : And you would have to pay the rent of these offices. How do you save £26 a year. Father FENNELLEY : We don't say for these faur years. We have nothing to pay for the offices in Waterloo House for four years and a half, and we have the chance of finding a tenant for these.—The CHAIRMAN I doubt whether we are able to let these.premises according to the lease.—Pather FE/iNEL- LEY : If We don't we lose nothing.—Mr. NORMAN, referring to the question of expense, observed that the Commissioners while they were at work might as well make the improve- ments and alterations for all the offices.—The Cleanness : Oh, certainly. But how is this Board to know that the Commissioners at the end of the 4f years won't charge us with £5O a year rent ?—Father FENNELLEY: They won't' do that. —Mr. NORMAN: They will charge the same rent we pay here.—lt was suggested that people would have a difficulty its finding the Board's offices at Waterloo House, and the Chairman observed that perhaps the Commis- sioners would keep a porter in blue to direct inquirers.—Nlr. SIMPSON said there was no doubt that if the Board re- moved to Waterloo House it would be a saving to the town.— The CLERK pointed out that the Board had expended in fixtures, which could not be removed from their present offices, the sum of about £6O. Waterloo House was nothing but bate walls, and the BoArd wanted cupboards, archives, and various other conveniences which they now had.—Mr. NORMAN 'said he should certainly suggest, if he had anything to do with it, that the Commissioners fit up the rooms. He thought all fixtures ought to be provided by the owner of the property, and he was astonished to hear that the Board had spent £6O or £7O for fixtures in those offices. He thought it was wrong.—The CLERK: These offices were taken from Mr. Garrett, who was the lessee. The whole arrangement was made with him. Mr. SIMPSON: If the landlord had put up the things we should have had to pay extra rent. It is as bread as long.— The CLERK said the Board paid Mr. Garrett £l5 a year. Mr. Garrett made the agree- ment, with the Board and then he trans- ferred the lease. Ha (the Clerk) wished it to be distinctly understood that the whole agreement was between i the late Mr. Garrett and the Board, and that the fact of his ' having anything to do with the offices was simply as a suc- cessor, and not as having had part or parcel in the matter in any particular way, either as regarded the expenditure in fixtures, respecting which it had been mentioned as being a monstrous sum, or as regarded the taking of the offices. Everything was done through the Law Clerk of the Board. FT-9.1.1/!;;g was urnereci through the Board, and in the in- terests of the public and the ralepayers, and with a full , sense of the propriety and responsibility.—Father FENNEL- LET: That is not the question.—Mr. NORMAN: Mr. Chair- man, I don't think the Clerk has any right to make any allusions of this sort. No one has said anything about it.-- The CLERK: I think you said it was an outrageous expen- diture.—Mr. NORMAN: SO I did say, and say again distinctly, that it would have been better not to spend so much money on the rooms.— Mr. SIMPSON said in discussing this matter those members who were not members of the Board at the time should be acquainted with the circumstances before they expressed a very decided opinion as to whether it was right or wrong to expend the money-. He thought that would be the beat course to take, supposing it was necessary to 'express any , opinion at all.—The CLERK said his object in making that statement was simply this, that if he was an outsider and a ratepayer—by the way, he was a ratepayer—he should look upon the thing in this light, independent of haviog any direct interest in the office. He should wish it to go before i-the public, whether right or wrong, that. it was owing to cir- cumstances that he held the offices. He had nothing in the world to do with the agreement.—Father FENNELLEY : It ie well known that you hid nothing to do with it. You were i expected to come into the property.—The CLERK was pro- ceeding to give particulars of the cest of the fixtures, one item being £l2 18s 6d for oilcloth, which, being glued to the floor, could not be removed, when the CHAIRMAN interposed, and mid it was not necessary to go into this. The matter resolved itself into this (motion : What was for the benefit of the ratepavere, and how could they best carry out the principals of the Education Act.—Father FENNELLY said be understood Mr. Shaw to say that the Commissioners wiluld accommodate the Board in every way by providing fixtures and not , chareing any rent until the lease expired.—The Chairman consulted the lease, and the CLERK remarked that from two paragraphs it appeared that the Board were de- barred from letting the offices, or using them for Rey other purpose except that of School Board, and that they were obliged to maintain them as regarded external arrange- ments as if they were inhabited. If the offices by reason of being shut up for four years and a half sustained any damage they would have to be put in exactly the same re- pair as they were on the day the Board took them. The Clerk wenr on to say that at present much had to be done with parents by moral suasion, and it was a question whether the people would attend the offices At Waterloo House, which was in a more conspicuous position than the present offices.—Father FENNELLEY said it was ridiculous to suppose that the Board could not carry on their business quite as well at Waterloo House.— the CLERK, referring again to his position, said he had no desire to land the ratepayers in any direction u hich should be disadvantageous to them.—lt was ultimately decided that the Board meet the Waterloo House Committee at any time as may suit the latter.
