Mr. BOWYER presented the following report:—Returns from the Public Elementary Schools for May, 1883: -Certi- fied Government accommodation, 2,716; total number on the rolls, 2,927; number on the rolls corresponding period of last year, 2,818; increase in the number on the rolls, 109 ; total average atttendance, 2.166 5, average attendance corresponding period of last year, 1,931 8; increase in average attendance, 234.7 ; per crntage of attendances, 74. ; average attendance for the year 1874, 1.252; increase in average attendance, as compared with 1874, the year preceding the formation of the Board, 914 5 ; accommedation in excess of average attendance. 549 5; number on the rolls in excess of accommodation, 211; num- ber in attendance at private adventure schools under nine- pence per week, 61. The returns for the past month, ending May 25th, shows an improvement in the attendance at the various schools. Hooping cough is very prevalent, and several cases of measles have been reported during the past month. Since the last meeting of the Board, I have taken proceedings against the list of 22 parents reported for con- travention of the Education Acts, 21 have been proceeded against under the bye-laws, convictions have been granted in the whole of the cases, and the usual fine of ss. imposed. One attendance order has been granted. This was all the business.

IMPROVED RAILWAY FACILITIES AT NVIDNE. For a considerable period prior to 1882 it was acknow- ledged that the railway facilities between Garston and St. Helens were inadequate for the steadily increasing goods traffic between those places, and early in that year the Lon- don and North-Western Railvvay Company decided to lay down an extra double line of rails from Speke Junction to a point near Widnes goods yard. By these lines it was justly considered that the heavily laden luggage trains would be able to travel with greater speed towards their destination, besides to some extent giving greater freedom of passage to passenger trains by leaving the other lines clear. Plans for carrying out the scheme were immediately prepared and Mr. T. D. Lewin was entrusted with the sole manage-, meat of the work, Mr. James Evans, of Birmingham, being the contractor, aal Mr. A. A. Macgregor, C. E., the resident engineer, with Mr. W. Johnson, as inspector. The extension, which is five miles 45 chains in length, has presented several features of great difficulty, especially that of carrying the line under the embankment of the railway below Runcorn Bridge, but it is satisfactory to find that so lar engineering skill has overcome them. The course taken by the line has rendered it necessary to erect a large number of bridges. In every instance they have been constructed with iron girders, the material being supplied by Messrs. J. O. and C. E. Brettell, engineers, of Worcester. The most difficult in construction, and the one expected to be most important in its results, is the bridge under the main line of rails, on which run the passenger trains from Runcorn. Four Sundays, when traffic was stopped, were occupied in placing the girders and most of the ironwork in position, everything having been previously prepared, and the struc- ture is rapidly approaching completion. The bridge will be of colossal proportions, the iron used in its construction weighing at least 150 tons, and it is justly regarded as a triumph of engineering skill. The success which has so far attended its construction reflects great credit upon Mr. Win. Watson, under whose superintendence the work has been carried out. At Ditton station it is intended to replace the old arch 'next to the Hale side by a fine girder bridge, while Brook Bridge, in the vicinity will be widened, asavill another bridge nearer Widnes. There have also been ereeted between Ditton and Speke several new girder bridges, and a fortnight ago at the latter place the quaint old bridge, the keystone of which was put in in January, 1852, was destroyed by dynamite. Considerable numbers of people were attracted to the spot by the unusual proceedings, and a scene of excitement followed the terrific explosion. No mishap, however, occurred. An important alteration is that which is to be made to Hale Bank station. During the summer months Hale Bank is besieged by plea- sure seekers en route for the picturesque village of Hale, and the present inadequate station is to be enlarged and otherwise improved. The extension is expected to be ready for traffic before the lapse of many months, and although at present Widnes is well situated for railway communication, it will then occupy a much improved awl more convenient position, while the traders of St. Helens, it is hoped, will re- ceive their goods with a despatch that will give no cause for complaint. THE RESTORATION OF SANKEY' CHURCH. THE RESULT OF THE SALE OF WORK.

The sale of work held at Sankey Bridges, in aid of the fund for the Restoration of Sankey Church, closed on Saturday, when the weather was all that could be desired, and was a pleasing contrast to that which prevailed the previous day. The rain OR -Friday considerably militated against the attendance, as it must have affected the receipts, and on Saturday the number of visitors was not so large as might have been expected considering the bright sunshine— yet the result on the whole is most satisfactory to the promoters who are to be congratulated on the success of their efforts no less than on the excellence of their arrangements. The marquee in which the sale took place was commodious, tastefully decorated, and posseessed many attractions; while the out-door amusements were such as to sitisfy the vayled tastes of the rieitore. Too much praise cannot be given to the gipsy girls who danced round the I may pole at intervals, their graceful movements] giving pleasure to all who witnessed them ; asd the bands of the Union Industrial and Blue Coat Schools are also deserving of a word of commendation for their excellent performaucem. The gross receipts, we may men- tion, amounted to £270 78 lid, £228 9s 4d b4ng received at the six stalls of fancy work, £lB lOs 31 from the, re- freshment still, £l6 4s 10d from admissions to the sale, Ll 5s from the games, and £4 183 GI from donations. IThe payments (which comprise £l7 73 4d for the hire of the maqpiee, and £ll 10s 63 for printing, posting, and advertising) amount to £3B is 103, leaving £232 65 Id of nett proceeds which has been paid to Parr's Banking Company. Perhaps it is not too much to hope that this amount will be increased ere long to £250 nett. A very handsome sum has now been obtained towards the estimated coat of the restoration of the sacred edifice and the purchase of a new orgarn and no doubt the balance will be forthcoming in due time. In addition to those mentioned last Saturday, the following ladies presided at the stalls : Mrs. S. Jones, Miss Atherton, Miss Wheeler, Miss Harding, and the Misses Kerfoot. We understand that during the week a contract has been entered into for fixing in the church new windows in cut stone, and cathedral rolled glass in place of the old ores, which were found to be thoroughly rotten; and a further contract has also been let for the replastering of the structure, owing to the pre- sent plaster being so very much diskturcd.

S. HELENS BAND or HnEE UNICVS.—Tt is the intention we understand, of the committee of management of this union to send a choir of about 70 persons, male and female, to sing at the great National Temperance Fete, to be held at the Crystal Palace, London, on the 10111 July. The choir has'been practicing for the past few weeks under the conductorship of Mr.Skaife,and promises well to be in a high state of efficiency by the time mentioned. There will pro- babl!. be fully fifteen thousand singers at the thystal Palace who will be divided into three monster choirs; and judging by the attendance on previous years the nutnber of visitors present at the fete will doubtless not be less than sixty or seventy thousand. A FAITHLESS SWAIN.—On Monday, a buxom young woman named Mary Eden apillied at the St. Helens Police Court fur an order to be made out against a John Segar, who was said to be an auctioneer at Ormskirk, to contribute to- wards the maintenance of her illegitimate child, of which she said he was the father. She stated that this was the second child she had had by the defendant, the former, however, towards which defendant had contributed ss. per week, being now dead. It was also stated that defendant had promised to marry her, but was now married to some- body else; and although he was an auctioneer, he was not yet set up in business for himself.—An order was made against the defendant, who did not appear, to pay ss. per week.

No change has taken place in the condition of Loid J.)tm Manners since Thursday. Sir William Gull will this after- noon again visit the noble lord. The Central News learns that Mr. LaboucLere intends to persevere with his motion respecting Lord Wolseley's pen- sion, notwithstanding the result of to-day's debate. There is no doubt the 'authorities have exhumed the body of Mr. Jury, the hotel proprietor of Dublin whose death was rumoured to have resulted from poisoning by "Number One."

The Duke of Edinburgh, who is unavoidably prevented from being present at the debate in the Lords on the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill, has agreed to pair with the Earl of Hosslyn. The Duke of Westminster has intimated to the Council of the National Smoke Abatement Institution that he pro- poses to contribute £5OO to the Smoke Abatement Fund recently opened.
A fisherman named Connors died on Thursday night in the hospital at Limerick from the effects, it is alleged, of a fight with another fisherman named Clandey, who has been remanded without bail.

A dangerous revolt has taken place among the convicts in the galleys of Piombino, in Italy. It was put down with some difficulty only by the troops using firearms. Eight convicts were wounded, four badly. We understand that Dr. Cory, director of the animal vaccine department, is the official who, in the interest cf scientific investigation as to the possible effects of inocula- tion from impure lymph, has seriously suffered by his experiments. The preparations for the Bright celebration are rapidly approaching completion. Triumphal arches are being erected at Birmingham, and the appearance of the streets on Monday will be extremely brilliant. It is estimated that the procession will be two miles long, and will be the grandest ever seen in Birmingham. The men engaged in the various branches of the building trade at Holywell have (riven notice to the masters of their intention to strike work to-morrow unless the employers consent immediately to the men dropping their tools at one o'clock instead of at three on Saturdays, and also to allow walking time after the first mile at the rate of a quarter of an hour for each mile.

Mr Broadhurst's motion respecting the expenses of te- turning officers was supported by Messrs. Arnold and Thomasson. Among the majority were Messrs. Agnew, Claeetham, Coddington, and Ecroyd, Sir R. A. Cross, the Hen. Algernon Egerton, Mr. Fielding, the Marquis of liar- tington, Messrs M`Minnies, Tomlinson, and Warburton, and the Hon de Tatton Egerton. At ten o'clock on Thursday night, Charles Barratt, 35, formerly of Walsden, weaver, committed suicide by drown- ing himself in the mill pond belonging to Kay's mills. The deceased was seen smoking on the lodge bank, and after- wards he jumped into the water. He refused to lay bold of a lump of wood held out to hint for his rescue. The deceased had been despondent some time. The body has been recovered.

As a boat containing two men was going up the Ribble with the tide from Freckleton, near Lytham, one of the men dropped the anchor to recover another boat which had broken away. The result of. the sudden stoppage was that the boat capsized. One man swam ashore with difficulty, and the other was drowned. When the body was found later there were wounds on the face from which blood was flowing. Deceased is William Billing- ton, of Preston. ACCIDENT TO H.M.S. LIVELY.

Upon inquiry at the Admiralty, yesterday, a correspon- dent learns that a telegram had been received announcing the stranding of the Lively, and stating that no lives had been lost; but no further details had, up to noon, been re- ceived. Three ships—the Seahorse; Jackal, and Forrester— bare been sent to the Lively's assistance; but nothing is known at the Admiralty as to the extent of the damage done; or the probability of the vessel being got off. Another correspondent says that the ship lies in an exceed- ingly dangerous position. Her false keel has been carried away, and she is so damaged that there is little likelihood of her floating, if got off.
IRISH gURDER PLOTS.
"INVINCIBLE" AND " VIGILANT " PRISONERS,

Yeaterday, at the Dublin Commission Court, Joseph Poole, who was charged with having been connected with the murder of Constable Cox in Abbey-street, in November last, was put forward, and at the application of the Crown a nolle prosequi was entered against him. The accused was glen discharged; but on leaving the court he was arrested on a charge of having murdered a man named Kenny. He will be charged at the police court. At a subuquent period Sylvester Kingston and Thomas Gibney, against whom true bills have been found in connection with a conspiracy to murder Poole, were placed in the dock, and their trial was adjourned until the next commission. In the meantime they were allowed out on bail.
MANCIIESTER SHIP CANAL SILL. PROMOTERS' CASE CONCLUDED.

The committee on this Bill sat again yesterday, Sir Joseph Bailey presiding.—Mr. William MacMillan, naval engineer, Glasgow, said he did not think Runcorn Bridge would be any obstruction to the traffic of the ship canal. Steamers up to 4,000 tons could be efficiently masted SOU logo under the bridge, which had a headway of 75 feet. The vessels would have to lower their topmast.—Mr. Leath, ship builder, of Rutherglen, Glasgow, gave evidence in favour of shortening the lasts of steamers. He believed that in time steamers crossing the Atlantic would cease to have masts.— Aspinall : What would happen to steamers without ,masts if her machinery broke dowu ? Unless she drifted ashore, she would wait until some one nicked her up. (Laughter.)—Does not the shortening of masts lessen the governing power of a steamer? Ido not think so.—Mr. Alexander Neil, shipwright, also gave evidence in favour of shortening masta.—Captain Pearson, marine surveyor and nautical assessor at Liverpool, said he had given consider- able attention to the proposed construction of the Manches- ter Ship Canal. Ho did not think the Runcorn Bridge and other bridges weuld offer any substantial impediments for steam to supercede sailing vessels —Captain King Scot, R.N., who said he was commander of the Sultan (luring the Egyptian campaign,gave evidence in favour of short masts. He believed in the future that all steamers would be con- structed with twin screws, aid without masts. That was the opinion of naval officers, who looked ripen masts as a hindrance. The cost of altering masts in order to allow large vessels to pars up to Manchester would be very trifling. Th.-re was a tendency all over the world to get water up to large towns. Water was Manchester's only hope. Mr. Frederick Edwards, shipowner, Cardiff, said he could not see any reason why freights cr ships from foreign Ports to Manchester should exceed the rate of freights to Liverpool. He did not think that vessels would have to Day additional insurance for using the Ship Canal. He thought that the chances of getting a return cargo from Manchester was very. good. Mr. Peter Hutchinson, shipowner, Glasgow, considered the ship canal a practicable undertaking, and one which would be of vast importance to traders of Lancashire. Mr. Briggs, steamship owner, Hull, expressed the opinion that the ship canal would in the end be very advantageous to shipowners. He would certainly make use of it if Manchester were made a port. They would be able to ship the South Yorkshire coals there at a lees price than at Hull or Grimsby. This concluded the case for the promoters.—Mr. Graham Hill, formerly marine surveyor to the Mersey Decks and Harbour Board, was the first witness called on behalf of the opponents. He said he had had 27 years experience of the Mersey, and he had noticed that any change in the position of the banks of the estuary always affected the depth of the bar at the mouth of the river ihe committee then adjourned until Monday.

DEPRFESED STATE OF AGRICULTURE. The Duke Of RUTLAND called attention to the depressed condition, of agriculture and trade. He understood that in 10 years a million acres had gone out of cultivation, and bad en- tailed a loss of 80 millions. Trade was also as depressed as agriculture.—The Marquis of BRISTOL said be was in favour, of taxation upon imports. Earl KIMBERLEY be- lieved that the main cause of depression of the agricul- tural interest was the succiissiwi bid seasons; but it could not be said trade was in a bad condition.—The Marquis of SALISBURY, whilst not:advecatiug reciprocity, said that a strong feeling was grosing up that our present system was not satisfactory.—Earl GRANYtuat denied the asser- tion, and said that pm erty was increasing in this country. —The subject then dropped.— Adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. ORDER OF BUSINESS —Mr. GLADSTONE said it was in- tended to proceed with the committee on 'the Corrupt Prac- tices Bill bef,re proceeding with the committee on the Tenants' Compensation Bill.

I SULEIMAN SAML—Lord R. CHURCHILL asked the Premier if he had seen a telegram published that day from Egypt stating the trial and condemnation to death of Sulei- man Semi, and whether he would ascertain before the man : was executed whether he had had a fair trial.—Mr. GLAD- / 1 STONE said the Government. had some information on the subject, and if grounds existed for interference, it would take place. Mr. Glads'one couldn't say more at that moment. —Sir S. NORTIMOTE said he would put a question on the subject before the House adjourned. TIIE EGYPTIAN HEROES.—Mr. Ge.epsraem explained that the change in the rewarde to Lords Alcester and Wol- seley had been made in deference to the wishes of the House. —On the motion for going into Lord Alcester's grant, Sir W. Lawsote opposed, and moved as an athendment that the House go into committee that day three months. He objected to giving Lord Alcester any money for his bom- bardment of Alexandria, on the ground that he had simply performed his duty; and further, because be had been tha occasion of drawing us into war by commencing that bom- bardment.—Mr. ILLINGWORTII seconded the amendment. Lord R. CHURCHILL said he had changed his views on this Bill, in consequence of the statements that had been made by Lord Alcester, ani he was strengthened in the course he proposed to take, as he deliberately charged the Khedive as being the' author of the massacre at Alexandria. Pending the clearing up of the mystery wh;ch e still surrounded the subject, he thought no sten in the direction proposed ought to be taken—Colonel Nonru con- sidered the reward to the two commanders ought to have been equal.—Mr. COWEN, while still considering the war unjustifiable, condemned any attempt to withhold rewards from men who had acted with valour and bravery. Mr. O'CONNOR POWER supported the arnendmentAir S. YORTE• COTE regretted-the course taken by Sir ,W Lawson and Lord R. Churchill, as it would place the House in a fa' s pos:tion. In voting for the grant to Lord A Ic9ster, h, thought it ought not be taken as approving the policy he had already condemned. He declined to fellow the lead of the noble lord, and he trusted the House would also decline to follow the noble lord into a position that would be degrang to its honour, (Loud cheers.)—Mr. GLADSTONE condethned the observations of Lord R. Churchill, and said the statement he had made that day was like that made before Whitsuntide, per- fectly valueless. He gave a direct and unqualiOed denial to the statements he had made with which the name of Lord Dufferin had appeared. With regard to the charge that Lord Churchill had made against the Khedive, it was opposed to all knawledge the Government could get and the opinion they entertained. He challenged the noble [cid to prove his assertion, and said the Oovernment were redder and willing to examine any charge the noble lord placed in their hands. Messrs. Rylaods, Hicks, and Ming- worth, condemned the bombardment of Alexandria. —Mr. O'DONNELL contended tbat if Lord Aicester's language did not mean tbet Alexandria was bombarded out of revenge for the massacre it means nothing ; and afi re- garded the splendiour of that bombaedment, it must be remembered that there was no substantial opposition to the guns of the noble fleet. He therefore objected to give reward for a promenade victory.—Mr. O'BRIEN also censured the bombardment, and said that conducted as it was, it was might against right, steel shot against wasted apples. Mr. J. Mc CARTY, amidst great inter- ruption, spoke in support of Mr. Lawson's amtndment.— Mr. LEAMY expressed similar views amid the same interr ruptions.—Mr. O'KELLY condemned the grant as political pocket-picking.—Mr. T. D. SULLIVAN was supporting the amendment when the debate ceased, and the House ad. journrd until the evening sitting. SULIMAN SAML—Lord E. FITZMAURICE, replying to Sir S. Northcote, said Major McDonald had watched the trial of Suliman Sam, who was sentenced to ,death for burning Alexandria, and without he made a request the Government did not propose to interfere.—The sitting was suspended..

div.head: WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE UNION.
div.p: WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE UNION.

A crowded meeting under the auspices of the Warrington Temperance Union was held on Tuesday evening in the Wor- kmen's Ciub, Market Nice. It had been announced that Mrs. Youmane, of Canada, would deliver an address, and that the Rev. John Bennett Anderson, of Liverpool, would occupy the chair; but the rev, gentlemen on putting in an appearance, said he was sorry to inform the audience that Mrs. Youmans had had a severe attack of ague, probably owing to charge of clumtte. She could not therefore attend the meeting, and although he never liked to stand in other persons, shoes, he must that night stand as a sub- stitute for his friend Mrs. Youmans. Councillor Dixon then toot: the chair, and he was supported on the platform by Mr. J. W. Hall and Mr. W. Roberts. The Blue Ribbon Army choir were again present, and rendered musical assist- ance. After some remarks by the Chairman,-Mr. ANDERSON delivered a characteristic address. He took for his theme "Drink's appetite, its power, and its cure," and he related in- stances which had come under his own observation as home missionary at Westminster, showing the power which tiriuk gained over its devotees, how it increased their desire for it until it became their all-devouring appetite, ending too often in results as deplorable as they were appalling. The question of temperance to him was an important one, because it was a question of life or death, of heaven er hell, to his brethren. He was glad that the temperance cause did not partake of politics. There were parties who trimmed their sails to catch the passing breeze, but he loved the temperance cause because it was neither political nor sectarian. They did not ask a man whether he was a Tory or a Radical, a Churchman or a Dissenter; they asked him if he was ready to take their hand and help them to drive intemperance from the land. He referred to the children who are being gatheted from our great towns and cities and taken over the Atlantic to Canada, where they are adopted by the Canadians, and said that prevention was better than cure. He announced that during a shcrt absence from the platform while the choir were singing, he had' given the ribbon to a parson at the door, and had been enjoined to give counsel to the women. He believed that every man should be the " Prime Minister" of, his own house, and that every wife should be "Chancellor of the Exchequer" and "Secre- tary of State for the Home Department." (Laughter. What did some men do? They said, "With this ring Ido I thee wed," and then they said, "With this fist I'll break thy I head." (Laughter.) They sang "Britons never shall be slaves," then why be slaves to drink? They sang "Rule Britannia" when they could not rule their own limbs. (Laughter.) If Warrington would give no her drink. she would be more celebrated for her workshops than for her ales and public-houses. Did they know that for every 20s spent in drink, not 2s of it went into the I thour market? But of every 205 spent upon clothes boots, shoes, drapery and things that were necessary for the body, 103 12s, and 14s want back into the labour market. If that bad been the f:.ase with the millions, trillions, that had been spent in drink in years gone ty, they would net have men emigrating, they wonlr not have suet, a large 1 number of men tryiqor orie job, 'but there Would be work enough for every man. He was glad to tell them that there were 30 public-houses within half a- mile of the sailora' Home, and not a single tenant could be got for them. (Ap- plause.) Might that go on; down with intemperance and up with sobriety, and God's blessing should be theirs; and in the end, when they came to look back; they would think with pleasure of the encouragement they gave to the tem- perance movermpt. (Applause )—A vote of thanks was ac- corded the speaker on the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. J. Hart, and sapported by Mr. W. RosEnTs. A similar compliment having been paid the chairman, the meeting separated, a good number staying behind to take the pledge and put on the blue ribbon.

THE BURGLARY AT WHISTON WORKHOUSE. - Th.e charge against James Richardson of breaking into, and robbin4 the Union Worknouse,Whiston, was partly heard on Tuesday, and concluded on Wednesday, before Mr. W. L. Evans at i'resoot. The prisoner, an old man, was chargtd. with breaking and entering the Union Worklum.e, Whiston, between six o'clock on the evening of the 26th and half- past six o'clock on the morning of the 27th May, tied ing therefrom 461 be. ef bread, four table knives, a spoon, three tin canisters, a fork and a coat, the property of the Guardians, and also with stealing from the boiler-house of the workhouse two pocket knives, a razor, feur towels, a tobacco-box; a small Inking•glass, and other small articles, the property of Humphrey Leather, an inmate of the work- house. Leather, ate old man, whose duty it was to attend to the fires in the boiler-house, stated. that on .the night of the 26th ult, he locked up the boiler house, but neglected to fasten the grid through which coals-- were taken int On the following morning he found the boiler house upset, and missed a number of articles, which he valued at 2a Ga.—Richard Robinson, cook and baker at the workhouse, stated that he locked the door of the bake— house at six o'clock on the night of the 26th ult., and next morning he found the door ajar. The spring lock seemed to have been opened with a key. He missed 124 six ounce col) lotaves.-I\ll.N. H. Bicknell, governor of the workhouse, valued the bread at ss. He also identified the otht r articles mentioned in the charge se belonging to.. the Guaidians. The, value of the whole of the articles, including the bread, was 73 6d.—P.o.Palmer deposed that he apprehended the pri- soner about 7 o'clock on Sunday evening, the 27th , ira a lane at Raiuhill leading from Blundell's-lane to Crouton. The prisoner was sltting on a vat produced, and many of the articles were in his pockets nr tied up in his clothes. He had kindled a fire, and was boiling water in the largeof the canisters. He took the prisoner to Prescet police station.- In reply to the charge, prisoner said another man broke into the house while he steed in the pigsties, and the man gave him some of the things he brought from the house, and took the rsst away with him. —P.C. Horn stated that he assisted Palmer to apprehend, the prisoner. He found a sack costaining 106 loaves in a dry ditch about 200 yards from where tho prisoner wee sitting.—The prisoner was committed for trial at the Sessions.

div.head: Tatters to the fditor.
div.p: Tatters to the fditor.
THE IM AGE OF TRUTH.

Sir,—The search for truth in the political, as in the reli- gimp, world is an arduous undertakine, not to be lightly entered upon. To take our re:igious or political ideas with- out question, somewhat as we take our re oiler's milk, would be an infallible sign of weakness. The robust mind, like the robust body, fears no hardship, courts no favour, asks only for fair play; and this, granted or not, seldom acts as a factor in the silent, though pereistent, search for truth, In spite of the wailings we hear around us, not a doubt can exist as to the benefits we to-day are receiving through the strivings of our forefathers for "more light." When Goethe I uttered those famous last words, he only reduced the "spirit of the age" to its more tangible form. To question everything that comes before us may betray a restless and an uneasy mind; bat it acts as a safeguard against imposi- tier], and for this reason, if for no other, is descrying of our sympathy. Truth, mirage like, is always seeming to be within reach, never attained. We are constantly about to tear off the disguise that surrounds her, so that she may be worthily worshipped. When the Pilgrim Fathers fled from persecution they were firmly convinced that they alone had truth on their side; yet we sea that thee in their turn persecuted each other when they arrived at their home across the sea. When Luther answered his friends, "Were there as many devils in worms as there are roof tiles I would go on," he also was a soldier on the side of truth. So we find truth always the companion of the robust and enquiring mind. When It. Carina suffered long imprisonment and the loss of a fortune, G. J. Helyoake in Gloster gaol, Mr. Foote to-day in Holloway prison, I say when we see these examples in more modern times, it is only further -proof that men can to- day, as in the past, suffer for what they think is the truth. This line of thought has been brought about in consequence of several visits to the Salvation Army. No one could watch the features and note the earnest language of these two pioneer lasses without being firmly convinced that tley also have truth on their side. The hard laborious life they are leading could not be sustained were they imposters; good pay could hardly be sufficient incentive; nothing but a firm conviction could lead them to wear so eccentric and Quaker-like dress. And vet, does the rest of the Christian world give them credit for being sole pursebearer of the jewel truth? Take the anewer of the Bishops in Convoca- tion. Some months since the Co-operative Hall was applied for, se that Mr. Bredlaugh might give a lecture, peliticil or otherwise. It was refused. and this by men who are nearly dissenters and Liberals, and the most influential of whom are looked upon by the out- side world as infidels. Now, these men also had truth on their side. So much so that one, a Liberal town councillor, said that Mr. Brailangh wanted license not liberty. Of course his knowledge on this subject being limited he was not to blame; we could but pity him for taking up arms in favour of blind prejadice. Some time after this event the hall was let to the Mormons. I attended, and a more dis- gusting sight I am sure no one ever saw at a Christian (?) meeting. A stout, sensual looking man, claiming to be an elder, preached a doctrine clothed in ambiguous language, but still sufficiently clear for all to understand that the great inducement was pelygamy, and this man after teach- ing immoral doctrines, after trying to undermine one of the most beautiful features in domestic life, held up his hands, and after asking the people to bow their heads in prayer, prayed for the blessing of God to rest upon them! This also is truth, and of a kind that found favour in the eyes of the Co-operative committee. More recent than this I at- tended a Christadelphian's meeting, and found that they also were worshippers of truth. In fact, if familiarity and knowledge of the scriptures count for anything, the credit of having found truth must rest with these people. They themselves are so satisfied of this that they feel justified in hurting at all other sects the Bth verse of the first chapter of Galatians. Now those who are confident of having truth on their side as a handmaiden through life, might for mere pity's sake withhold a few of the curses. Too much of the Athanasian, creed is apt to cause reaction. Were we to visit all the , churches, chapels, and little bethels in the land, we should find truth claimed by all alike, and yet how various in her forms. Nay, we should probably find ourselves insisting upon it, that each one in their turn worshipped but the image of truth, and the sincere enqnirer must fall back upon his own resources, must take no man's word, for as there is no vicarious punishment in this world so there will be none in any other possible world. lam quite aware that any attempt on my part to prove the necessity of at once staying the persecuting Writ that is unfortunately abroad just now would be mere waste of time; still the attention of the people cannot be too often drawn to the fact that the martyr of to-day is the hero of the future. Lord Salisbury and Bishop Vaughan each in his own way deplores the spread of Radicalism. One is deter- mined that the various classes of people are being set against each other by Reds, and his party alone must resist it, that is .that the poor must be made poorer and the rich richer, and yet live happily together ; the other, the Bishop, thinks that what the State cannot do by "life and imprisonment" it is now going to do by law, viz., to drive out religion, and in its place give a secular education. So we go on striving against each other, and truth constantly giving place toprejudice seems as far off as ever. le the meantime we reap some benefit.—l am, Zec., H. W. Warrington, June, 1853.

THE LANCASHIRE COAL AND IRON TRADE3.—There i 3 a continued absence of animation in the iron market. Nominally prices remain unchanged. Judging from the few inquiries for renewals coming into the market, contracts appear to be running out very slowly. For Lancashire pig iron quotations remain on the -basis of 453 to 465, less 2i delivered equial to Manchester. No business is being done at these figures; fair offers have, however, been made at a little less, but local makers, although not absolutely firm at their full list rates, do not appear prepared to give away to the extent expected by buyers, and offers have not resulted in actual transactions. District brands are also without alteration from the quetel basis of 44s 4d for forge and 45s 10d for foundry Lincolnshire, less 2i delivered here, but no sales of importance are reported. The business doing in the finished iron continues very limited, and shipping inquiries are still very dull. For good brands of bar iron delivered into the Manchester district makers are firm at £6 53 per ton. —The coal trade of this district is naturally beginning to quieten down. Stocks of house-fire coal are accumulating at some of the collieries, and many of the pits are getting on to short time, averaging four to five days a week. The de- mand, however, generally keeps fairly good considering the time of the year. The better classes of round coal still move off moderately well for house-fire purp3ses, and it is chiefly in th 3 commoner sorts, which are plentiful in the market, that there is any real pushing on the part of sellers. One cause of the unsatisfactory condition of the common coal trade is the continued very limited irquiry for shipment. The market is also in a somewhat exceptional position as regards engine fuel. With the close of the winter it was an- ticipated that slack would be scarce, and comp 1-zitively high prices were being obtained for contracts. There has, how- ever, since been an absence of any real pressure or demand, and supplier generally are quite equal to requirements. As regards prices generally, there is no material change beyond a little giving way here and there to secure orders, and col- liery proprietors are not at all keen at quoting for forward delivery. At the pit mouth prices average as under: Best coal 98, seconds 78 to 78 63, common round coal 5s 6d to 6s 31, burg's' 43 9d to ss, best slack 4s up to 4s 61, com Mon 3s to 3a gd: EPPs's COCOA.—GRATEFUL AND COMFORTING. ASHTON.
The Wigan and District (Support of Sewers) Bill was read a third time in the House of Commons, on Monday.

SCHOOL EXAMINATIONS AT ASIITON.—OH Monday and Tuesday last, the scholars attending the St. Thomas's day schools, Heath-lane, Ashton, were examined in the usual elementary subjects by Mr. E. L. Fillips, Government In- spector, and Mr. J. S. Foister, assistant Inspector. The master is Mr. Thomas Hollbrook, and there is good reason to believe that the scholars are well and efficiently taught. On Tuesday and Wednesday Mr. Phelps and Mr. Foister also examined the scholars attending St. Luke's School, at Stubshaw Cross, a school which is well looked after and the scholars well taught by Mr. Parkington.

ASHTON WESLEYAN METHODIST MISSION-BOOM: OPEN- ING OF A IlmtmoNium.—Special sermons were preached in the Wesleyan Methodist Meeting-room, Town Green, Ashton, on Sunday last, in connection with the opening of a harmonium for use in that building. The sermons were preached by Mr. John Fairhurst, of Haydock, and Master William Heyes presided at the harmonium. The choir was augmented by friends from other Methodist churches in the district, and the services in every respect were successful. Including subscriptions collected by Miss Johnson and Mrs. Cowell, the sum of £ll was realised, leaving a small balance yet to be raised. ACCIDENT AT PEWFALL COLLIERY, ASHTON.-011 Satur- day evening last a man named Patrick Sallanger, -employed as a top hand at Pewfall Colliery, Ashton, met with a seri- ous accident, though the circumstances attendinc, it are a little shrouded in mystery. It seems that for about 20 years past he has not been living with his wife, but lodged in Heath-lane. On Saturday last, it is stated, he was turned away for being drunk and creating a disturbance, and he then made his way to the colliery. It is supposed that he fell from on e of the brows, as he was afterwards found with his right thigh very badly injured. On the Monday morn- ing he was removed in a cart to the residence of his wife where he has since been confined to bed.

BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT ASHTON.—At the Wigan County Police Court, on Wednesday morning, Christmas Evans, a collier, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly at Orippin's-buildings, Askton, on the previous day, and also with violently assaulting his wife, Lydia Evans, on the same day.—The evidence of the prosecutrix showed that on Monday night her husband came home quite sober, but brought another man with him who was under the influ- ence of drink. The man was allowed to stop in the house all night, and on the following morning, after he had gone, defendant locked all the doors and went upstairs with a pick-shaft in his hand. With this he commenced to brutally beat his wife, who was lying in bed. Her skin was dis- coloured in a great number of places and it was afterwards found necessary to call in Dr. Hannah. The poor woman was found to have been very badly maltreated, and she was at first thought to be in a dangerous condition. The hus- band was afterwards seen drunk and disorderly in the street, and he was rock up.—He was remanded until to-day (Friday).

• _ REMARKABLE MATRIMONTAL COINCIDENCE AT ASITTON.—.- The death of Mrs. Sarah Heath, 66 years of age, wife of George Heath, of Liverpool-road, Ashton, which took place 'on Monday last, has brought to light a somewhat curious ciincidence. Prior to the year 1753 marriages were solemnised at St. Thomas's Church, Ashton, but after the 6th March in that year, when two couples were married, no similar ceremony took place in that church for a period of 92 years. On August 3rd, 1845, Sarah Green was united to George Heath, and in accordance with the usual custom, a handsome Bible was presented to the newly married Icouple because they were really looked upon as being the first couple married in the church within recent times, and of course their names were the first in the register. Marriages afterwards followed each other in rapid succession, and in the natural course of things the register was gradually filled. But it was not left to Mr. and Mrs. Heath alone to have the honour of being the first names in a new book, for, strange as it may seem, their son George, 24 years of age, was married to Alice Harrison on the 2nd October last, and this couple were the first to com- mence the next register. Thus net only does one man's name commence the book, bat after the lapse of 37 years it is found that his son heads the next volume, and what is more remarkable, both the father and eon bear the same Christian name.

were charged with wilfully damaging the property of the Huyton-with-Roby Local .Board.-31r. Swift, clerk to that Board, prosecuted.—lt appeared that the defendants I:ad diverted themselves by going on to the sewage farm and smashing the windows of a building erected thereon. Al- though the fact was not brought home to the defendants, it was stated generally that the Local Board suffered great inconvenience and loss from young people trespassing upon the farm, and not only damaging the buildings, but inter- fering with the tanks. One consequence of the latter tam- pering had been that sewage had been diverted into a neighbouring brook, the owners of which threatened the Board with a chancery suit in respect of the damage and nuisance thereby occasioned.—The defendants were each fined 10$ and costs.

THE ROBBERY FROM THE BLUE BELL, HUYTON —Last week we gave an account of a rabbery from the Blue Bell Inn, Huyton, and the courageous capture of the thief by Miss Brown, daughter of the landlord. On Tuesday, the prisoner, John Johnson, was brought before Mr. Evans, at Prescot, charged with stealing 9s. 61, the money of Mr. Brown.—The prisoner, it will be remembered, went into the bar of the hotel for a glass of ale, and while Margaret Brown was going upstairs in obedience to a call by her sister, took the opportunity of leaning over the bar and putting his hand in the till. Hearing the till open the girl returned; and found the priso- ner in the described position, whereupon she called to her sister, Mary Brown, who followed prisoner out of the house, and as he did not respond to her call to step seized him by the shoulder. Ther prisoner then offered her some silver which he had in his hand and asked her to let him go. She refused, and held him till Mr. Thomas Crosby, wheelwright, came up and took charge of him, and recovered from him 9s. 6d., which he held in his hand. Shortly afterwards pri- soner was handed over to P.C. Forster.—ln answer to the charge, prisoner said he had been guilty of a drunken freak, for which he was very sorry.—He was committed for trial at the sessions.

THE FOWL STEALING AT HIITTON.—Three young men named John Martin, Samuel Edward Taylor, and Thomas Toirney were charged at Prescot, on Tuesday, with stealing seven hens and a goose, the property of Mr. James Rigby, farmer, Huyton.—About half-past six o'clock on the morn- ing of the 26th May, while John Pennington, a carter in the employment of Messrs. Cannington and Shaw, glass manufacturers, St. Helens, was passing the Blue Bell Inn, Huyton, he saw the three prisoners sitting on a wall. Two of them came up with a hamper, and asked him to put it on his lurry.. He consented, and hoisted the hamper to the top of his load, and immediately afterwards the third prisoner came up with a bag, which he placal alongside the hamper remarking that Pennington was to put them down at the Legs of Man Inn, London- road. The three men walked behind the lorry at a distance of about three hundred yards. Noticing that blood was oozing from the bag, and some feathers protruding through the interstices of the hamper Pennington became suspicious and putting his hand into the bag, felt a fowl which was dead but warm. He thereupon determined to hand the men •over to the police on the first opportunity. On arriving at Horn: Smithies he noticed that the police office was closed, and fearing that the officer might be in bed, and that the prisoners would escape, he did not stop there but went on to Knotty Ash. Here he was deterred by similar circumstances from stopping, and continued his journey to Old Swan. He drew up opposite .the police office, and told the prisoners that before going any further they must give him an explanation of how, when, and where they had come by the fowls which he had discovered in the cart. They made no reply, but looked at one another and around, and catching sight of the sign of the police station took to their heels. Pennington then knocked at the door of the police office, and P.C. Robinson and another officer came out and gave chase to the pri- soners, whom they ultimately captured.—The prisoners were committed for trial at (lie Sessions. LEIGH.

EXCITING CHASE AFTER A THIEF.—An exciting chase after a thief has just been witnessed in Leigh. The prisoner, a young man, named John Lowe, of Liverpool, was observed to take money from the till of a shop in Bradshawgate, when the alarm was given and the "hue and cry" raised. Pelicemen and civilians joined in pursuit of the thief, who having gained a good start, made the best of it, and for some considerable time he baffled all the attempts of his pursuers. Across the fields and over hedges the chase was continued, the services of a horseman being brought into requisition. Lowe, finding himself hemmed in on all sides and com- pletely hunted down, was glad to give himself up. Prisoner was taken before a magistrate and remanded, in order that inquiries may be made as to his antecedents. RECKLESS STORAGE OF GUNPOWDER. At Leigh, On Monday, James Ashcroft and John Leonard were sum- moned for a breach of the Explosives Act of 1875. Super- intendent Jackson prosecuted. On the 30th ult. he sent Inspector Charnlev to the gunpowder store of Leonard at Plank Lane, Westleigh. Though Leonard had not held a licence to store for the last two years the inspector found that the place contained two barrels of powder, one of 1001 b and the other 751 b. Poultry are now kept in the store, and there were two holes in the door, through one of which a person could put his hand into a tub of powder which had been opened and left with a loose covering. Children play about, and adjacent to the store are about 20 houses. Ash- croft's explanation was that he got permission from Leonard's wife to store the powder; and on behalf of the other defend- ant Mr. Hoskins said Mrs. Leonard gave Ashcroft permis- sion to store it without her husband's permission or know- ledge. A second charge against Ashcroft was for storing 2501 b of powder in a store for which Frederick Ross was licensed to store only 200!b. The Bench considered the offence a serious one. Aahoroft and Leonard they fined is. for every pound of powder, amounting to £8 15s. each, and costs. in the second case Ashcroft was fined 20s. and costs, a summons against Ross being dismissed. RAINFORD.

RAINFORD DnumKEN CASES.—At the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, on Monday, the following persons were fined for having been drunk in the district of Rainford :—David Grimshaw, on the 19th ult., 55.; Abram Jones, on the 27th ult., 7s. 6d. and costs; William Glover, on the 27th ult., ss. THR RAINFORD POACHING CASR.—On Monday, at the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, before Mr. T. Pilkington and Mr. J. C. Gamble, an elderly man named Henry Marsh was charged with having unlawfully used a dog for the purpose of taking game at Rainford, on the 28th April.— Mr. J. 0. Swift prosecuted on behalf of Mr. Pennington, and Mr. R. W. H. Thomas defended.—Mr. Swift stated that this case had been adjourned from the 7th May owing to the absence of Mr. Thomas, the defendant's solicitor, on that occasion. The facts of 018 case were that on Saturday, the 28th April, between half-past five and six o'clock in the morning, a young man named Wm. Barnes, a gamekeeper in the employ of the Earl of Derby, saw a lercher dog cours- ing a hare across a field which forms part of a farm of Jos. Owen, over which the game is preserved by Mr. Penning- ton. The hare was closely pressed and ran on to the road, and then passed into the yard of the Rainford pottery, where it escaped the dog. Barnes watched the dog, and saw it go back to the defendant, who was standing on the road. He put a collar round its neck, but on seeing Barnes coming towards him he took the collar off again, and attempted to drive it away. On being questioned by Barnes defendant a: first denied that the dog was his, but afterwards said that it belonged to a gentleman for whom he. was training it.—ln defence, Mr. Thomas explained that the defendant was in the habit of receiving dogs from other people for the purpose of curing them of various diseases. On the day previous to that on which the offence was said to have been committed defendant received the dog in question from Manchester, and on the morning in question he was going to see Owen, who is his landlord, about putt- ing a chimney-pot on his chimney, taking the dog with him. On the way along the road a hare crossed before them, and the dog at once slipped from the leash and went after it. Mr. Thomas also pointed out that hares were at present out of season, and contended that it was altogether unlikely that defendant would attempt any poaching at a place where there were so many people about, and with a strange dogs—The magistrates, however, were of opinion that an offence had been committed, and fined defendant £1 and costs, £2 3s. in all.—Defendant had been once previously convicted of poaching, but that was about 15 years ag‹,. OVER.

The congregational sermons for the Marshall Memorial Sunday school were preached last Sunday by the Rev. G. J. Allen, 8.A., of Park Green, Macclesfield. Owing to the great attractions elsewhere the congregations were not what they might have been. As it was the collections amounted to nearly £lO, and as the school is free from debt, nO doubt it will be regarded as ample. CONFIRMATION AT ST. CHAD'S—On Tuesday afternoon Bishop Kelley held a confirmation at St. Chad's, when about 160 young people were admitted within the church's pale, and avowed their disconnection with the world. he day was fine and all passed off well.

after that Frank Pedford,nephew of complaioant,saw defend- ant discharge a gun which he had, and the two pigeons rolled off the house top. He went to defendant about the matter, and he at first denied having shot the pigeons, but subsequently turned round and admitted it, saying that he would not have done so but he " wanted something tasty for his wife." (Laughter) —Defendant said he made a com- promise with complainant's nephew that he would supply the place of the pigeons with two others. He came to War- rington the other day and bought two but they were too young to be removed just then, and he had to leave them. He was astonished when he received the summons.—Defend- ant was ordered to pay lOs and 78 ed costs for shooting the pigeons, and is each for the birds. WESTON POINT.

DEATH OF THE REY. A. FORD, OF WESTON POINT.— The funeral of the Rev. Adam Ford, incumbent of Christ Church, Weston Point, who died on Wednesday afternoon, took place at Liverpool Dn Saturday. For a long period the rev, gentleman had suffered from ill-health, and his decease was not unexpected. During the six years he had held the pastorate, Mr. Ford won the esteem and goodwill of his parishioners by his kind, genial disposition, and his death is deeply regretted. He had attained the age of 04. The living, which is of the value of £l5O, is in the gift of the Bishop of Chester. The funeral of the rev, gentleman took place, as we have intimated, on Saturday last, at St. James's Cemetery, Liverpool. The service was read by Archdeacon Bardsley, assisted by the curate of Runcorn Parish Church, and amongst those in attendance were Mr. T. Hughes, C.C., Captain Clarke, Harbour Master of Weston Point, the Revs. A. de L. James and George Ford (sons of the deceased), J. D.:Jones, J. K. Merrow, Eben, Smith, J. Davies, and about 20 other clergymen. An attendance of 200 of the working classes from the parish of St. Cleopas and from Weston Point testified the respect with which the deceased was held by his former parishioners. A very moving address was given at the grave side by Archdeacon Bardsley. At St. Gabriel's Church (the mission church of St. Cleopas), a minor service was given both on Sunday morning and even- ing in connection with the death of the late pastor. WHISTON.

A SPREE AND ITS CONSEQUENCES. James and John Bannister were sued at Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, under the Employers and Workmen's Act, for damages claimed by their employers, the Wigan'and Whiston Coal Company, in consequence of their neglect of work. Mr. J. 0. Swift prosecuted. The defendants were employed by the company at their Whiston and Prenot Collieries in the manufacture of gas, and it appeared that on the 26th May the defendants got on the spree, only attended their work at intervals, and when they did attend were so drunk as to be almost impotent. The consequence was that although the gas evolved itself well enough the by-products were spoiled, and the plaintiffs therefore claimed lOs and damages from each of the defendants.—There was no defence, and the de- fendants were ordered to pay the damages claimed and the costs, including those of the witnesses called to prove the case.

UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH BAND.—The brass band in connection with the United Methodist Free Church, Whiston, appeared in public for the first time on Saturday laet, and made a very successful debut. The band consists of twenty-five instrumentalists, mostly miners, who asso- ciated themselves together about four months ago. A pre- liminary difficulty in the formation of the band was the cost of instruments, but this impediment was speedily got rid of on its existence being made known to Mr. John Leatherbarrow, who immediately guaranteed the sum required, about £BO. The necessagy pur- chases were made without delay, and the services of Mr. Joseph Corns as instructor and leader having been secured, the band have since practised with much dili- gence and attained a very creditable degree of proficiency. This being the first time Whiston has rejoiced in a band of its own the appearance of the local musicians on Saturday was regarded with much interest, and large num- bers of people turned out to see and hear. The band paraded the village and made a circuit of the vicinity, and wherever they went their performances were rewarded with praise and encouragement. The instruments are all new and of excellent quality, and as has been said, cen- sidering the short time the performers have had for practice, their proficiency is highly commendable. The band intend having another march out next Satur- day.

div.head: CHILD WALL.
div.p: CHILD WALL.

CONFIRMATION SERVICE.—A confirmation service was held at Childwall Parish Church on Friday afternoon by the Bishop of Liverpool, when the rite was administered to 158 candidates, including 50 from All Saints', Childwall ; 27 from Woolton, 51 from Holy Trinity, Wavertree ; 29 from St. Mary's, Wavertree ; and 1 from St. Michael's-in- the-Hamlet. There was a large congregation, and Dr. Ryle impressively addressed the young people confirmed on their duties and responsibilities. CHURCH COPPENHALL.

Mr. Fox, the medical officer to the Nantwich Rural Sani- tary Authority, has reported the outbreak of a case of viru- lent smallpox at Church Coppenhall, near Crewe, and he adds that other. cases near Crewe are traceable to it. This is the first case reported to the authority for six years. The sanitary authority on Saturday gave instructions for strict isolation, and will attend to the defective sanitary arrange- ments of the district.

div.head: CRANK.
div.p: CRANK.

BEGGING AT CRAW.—Michael Farrell, an elderly man, who said he came from Wigan, was charged at the St. Helens Police Court, on Wednesday, with begging. An officer stated that on Tuesday afternoon he had occasion to be in the Crank Hotel, when the prisoner came in and begged from the landlord; and afterwards witness followed him and 83W him coming from Rainford Hall with a quan- tity of meat, (ke., in his possession, which he had begged.— He was sent to gaol for seven days. FARNWORTH.

MARRIAGE AT FARNWORTH CHTTRCII.—The marriage of I Miss Alice Eleanor Whalley, second daughter of Mr. Robert Whalley, farmer, of Bold, to Mr. Arthur Bunches Bourn- phrey. cotton broker, eldest son of Mr. Joseph Boumphrey, of the Elms, Wavertree, took place at Farnwerth Parish Church on Saturday morning. In consequence of the salons illness from which the bride's father is suffering, it was in- tendel that the marriage should be conducted in a quiet, unpretentious style. The popularity of Mr. Whalley, how- ever, rendered this next to impossible, and the village of Bold was gay with flags, while the Union Jack fluttered from the ancient church tower. At the entrance to Mill Green, the residence of Mr. Whalley, the employes had erected a handsome triumphal arch, which was bright with flowers, foliage, and flags. The church was thronged with spectators, who watched the ceremony with great interest. The bride, who was simply attired in travelling costume. wag accompanied by her brother, Mr. John R. Whalley, There were no bridesmaids, but Mr. E. J. Boumphrey, brother of the bridegroom, acted as best man. The wedding party included Mr. and Mrs. Boumphrey, Mr. and Mrs. R. A. Jackson, Mr. and Mrs. Walter Whalley, Misses Maggie and Emena Whalley (sisters of the bride), Mr. and Mrs Atkinson, Mr. and Mrs. H. E. , Williams, Miss Boumphrey, and Mr. .M Boumphrey (sister and brother of the bridegroom). The Rev. George Bond, M.A , I performed the ceremony, the bride being given away by Mr. J. R. Whalley. As the newly-married pair quitted the church, Mr. Glover played Mendelssohn's "Wedding March" on the organ. On the way back to Bold the car- riage was stopped by a millibar of Mr. Whalley's workmen, who unyoked the horses from the shafts, and, in the good old fashioned way, drew the vehicle to Mill Green, where the party sat down to breakfast. Subsequently the happy couple departed for the south. FLIXTON.

RATES IN FLIXTON AND UEMSTON. - The overseers of these townships have laid the following rates :—Poor-rates, is. Bd. in the £ ; main drainage, is. In the township of Urmston a further rate of 6d. in the £ has been laid to meet the cost of lighting and other special expenses.

div.p: FRODSRAM.

TYE Penni{ CHURCIL—Soom after the re-opening of the Parish Church the Restoraticm Committee found that their liabilities were greater than they anticipated, and that there would be a deficit of about £450. We are happy to state that through the munificence of three gentlemen, namely, Mr. William Hayes, sen., of Ashton Hayes, Mr. Charles Reynolds, and Mr. John Hayes, the whole of this amount will be discharged, and consequently there will be no debt connected with the restsration of the church. Such public- spirited liberality deserves more than a passing notice, for it constitutes a lasting claim on the gratitude of the parish- ioners, which we feel sure they fully recognise.—Parish Magazine. . .

eRODSIIAM NATIONAL Scrroors.—A statement of account of the Frodsham National Girls' and Infants' School for the year ende. April 30th has just been issued, from which we learn that the total receipts have been £403 193 14, while the expenditure has amounted to £458 193 7d, so that there is a balance on the wrong side of £53 Os 63. The receipts from subscriptions and donations, collections, and bank interest reached £64 14s 103; from the National Schools, £2Bl 19s 54: and from Five Crosses School, £57 4s 103. The payments for the National Schools were £363 33 o,ll,and for Five CrosOs School £B9 178 14, which, together with the balance of £5 193 sid owing on April 30th, 1882, mskes•the total of £458 193 74.

div.head: HUY TON.
div.p: HUY TON.

BAD NElGHDol7l29.—Hannah Halliday was charged at Pres- cot, on Tuesday, with assaulting Hannah Halyroyd, and defaming the defendant at Hnvton, on the 21st May,—Thc parties were neighbours, and having fallen out about the proprietorship of a clothes prop, complainant alleged that defendant struck her with her fist, and would also have laid about her ears with a saucepan had she not been restrained by her husband—On the other band, defendant alleged that complainant accused hero? stealing the prop.— Defendant was fined ss. and costs for the assault, and the cross-summons was dismissed.

DEATH OF MRS. FOUTHWAR.D.—Much regret is felt in Huyton at the death of Mrs. Southward, mother of the Rev. T. W. Southward, senior curate of the parish. Mrs. Southward resided with her son at Huyton Park. She had been ailing for some time, and had been attended by Dr. Gorst, but no apprehensions were entertained. However, on Friday night, Mrs. Southward's illness assumed a serious and painful cbarocter, and she died on Saturday morning. Mr. Southward was at the time absent in Wigan. The remains of the deceased lady were interred in St. James's Cemetery, Liverpool, on Monday. The funeral service•was read by the Rev. W. Cullen, a friend of the family, and the ohoristers of Huyton Parish 'Church attended and sang hymns in the course of the ceremony.- Mrs. Soutllward was 89 years of age.
TRESPASS AND DAMAGE OH THE SEWAGE FAWM.—At Prescot, on Tuesday, tour young men named Richard War- ing, Richard Woodward, and William and Richard Lyon

div.head: -RAINHILL.
div.p: -RAINHILL.

BREACH OF THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT.—At Prescot on -Tuesday, Thomas Lowe, of Rainhill, appeared in answer to a summons charging him under three informations with contravening the orders issued by the Privy Council, on Vie 22nd March last, under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act, 1889. The substance of the charges was that defendant hawked a number of pigs about Prescot and Knowsley when legally ho was only entitled to sell them on his own premises after having had them there for fourteen days. In this way he had sold. to Mrs. William Roughsedge, Knowsley, two pigs for £2 us; a similar number to Mrs. Ulendining' Derby-street, Prescot, for a like sum, and two others to Mr. Green, of the Court Houses Hotel, Prescot (next door to the Police Court), for .£2 18i.—The defendant, for whom Mr J. 0. Swift appeared, pleaded that he had received .the pigs from Ellesmere, and, having kept them for fourteen days, had endeavoured to sell them outside his farm, in ignorance of the fact that the sale could only legally take place there.—ln cross-examina- tion by-Mr Swift, Supt. Barber, who was one of the wit- nesses, stated that on the 18th of May there was a case of foot and month disease in his division, and the division had not been declared free. Nor was the district free from swine fever, for he.was sorry to say that disease was spreading all over the division as it had done last summer, through the very act of which f the defendant was accused—hawking pigs about the country.—Defendant was fined 20s and costa in each of the three cases, in all £B. RIXTON.

"GETTING SOMETHING TASTY" FOR HIS WlFE.—Josepb Shaw, landlord of the Eagle and Child, Rixton, was sum- moned at Warrington Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, for unlawfully shooting two pigeons, value ss, the property of Mrs. Pedford, landlady of the Red Lion.—Mr. Moore ap- peared for the complainant.—lt appeared that on the 14th ult defendant's boy was throwing stones at complainant's pigeons, and was told by Mrs. Pedford to desist, but he went on tkroalog and used bad languagn to her. div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

ANNIVERSARY SERMONS.—The annual Sunday school sermons were preached at the Free Methodist Chapel, High- street, Winsford, on Sunday afternoon and evening by the Rev. W. J. Hopper, of Ramsbottom, late of this place. Though the gentleman has left many months ago, his memory is sweet in the town, and was the occasion of large gatherings at both sorvices. The/school funds have benefit- ted to the amount of nearly .£3B ; and the town has a better appreciation of Mr. Hopper than it had when he left Wins- ford about ten months ago. The children sang very nicely, and the choir first-class. Miss Buckley (Academy) presided at the organ. ITEMS OF CHES LURE NEWS.

Cattle disease is almost extinct in Cheshire, Tuesday's official weekly returns showing that only two cases are now under treatment, Monday, July 2, has been fixed for the visit of the Prince of Wales to open the "abattoirs" at Crewe, but the date will be altered, if necessary, to suit tha convenience of His Royal Highness. At the Earl of Harrington's half-yearly audit. on Wednes- day afternoon, of the Bosley and Gawsworth estates, Cheshire, the steward announced that his Lordship, who only recently entered upon possession of the estates, would for the next three years remit 10 per cent, of the rents. The acme intimation applied to the Earl's Derbyshire estate. CHESFIIRE CHEESE FAIR.—At the monthly cheese fair, held under the auspices of the Cheshire Dairy Farmers' Association, at Nantwich, on Thursday morning, there was a fine picture of new season's cheese, and a large attendance of factors and dealers from Liverpool, Manchester, and Bir- mingham. Some of the dairies were hardly ripe for con- sumption. Cheese of this class realised 50s to 60a; medium quality, 633 to 68s; and fine, 703 to 75s per cwt. The crops in Cheshire are now looking most promising. Potatoes, of which immense quantities are grown for the Manchester and Liverpool markets,bave this year been spared by the late frosts. The rains have greatly strengthened the wheat plant, which was somewhat yellowed by drought. Grass is growing with great luxuriance, and Cheshire dairy farmers, under the stimulus of the enhanced prices prevail- ing, are now making very large quantities of fine cheese. SUNDAY SCHOOL CONFERENCE IN CHESHIRE,—A con- ference of ministers, teachers, and friends of Sunday schools in association with churches of the Congregational Union in Cheshire, was held at Middlewich, on Monday evening. Mr. Algernon Fletcher, of Northwich, presided. The Rev. T. Davies (Alsager) gave an address, in the course of which he pointed out that, considering the advanced elementary instruction given in the Board schools, their Sunday schools ought to keep pace with the intelligence and discipline of the day schools in giving religious instruction to the young. The Rev. D. R. Davies (Sandbach) also gave an address on the same subject. Mr. Francis Milne (Manchester) offered a few remarks on the importance of efficient teaching. Mr. T. J. Cox (from the Sunday School Union, London), gave the results of personal ohseryation and experience, and, dealing with the latter part of the subject, said that teachers of true religion had nothing to fear from the tendency of modern thought. The touch of truth would ever unmask error. The Rev. J. T. Maxwell (Over) and Rey. A. W. Potts (Crewe) gave addresses on the mode by which Sunday school work could be adapted to reach tho parents of Sunday scholar; who were not in attendance at any place of wor- ship. Mr. Potts advocated that Sunday schools should Lave pastors of their own who could devote their whole time, talents, and energies to making the schools successful. An interesting discussion foltowed.

div.head: SERIOUS TRAP ACCIDENT AT HUYTON.
div.p: SERIOUS TRAP ACCIDENT AT HUYTON.

A serious accident happened at Huyton, on Saturday last, to a party consisting of Mr.-B. Jones, coal agent, Huyton,, and Mr. and Mrs. Samuel Fraser and child, of Mount Pleasant, Liverpool. While the party were driving in a. wbitechapel down Blacklow-brow the horse becante restive, kicked violently, and set off at a gallop down the hill. Find- ing himself unable to control the animal, Mr. Jones, who was driving, jumped out, and in doing so was very severely injured, breaking his leg and ankle joint. Mr. Fraser also jumped down, with a view of stopping the horse, but in this he was unsuccessful, and injured his hand and wrist. Almost immediately afterwards Mrs. Fraser and her child, a little boy, were thrown out of the vehicle, and alighting on her head, the lady received a deep scalp wound. The boy hap- pily escaped unharmed. The injured persons were taken to Dr. Gorst's surgery, when it was found that Mr. Jones had sustained a very severe compound fracture of the leg; pieces of bone protruded through the akin, and when the stocking was removed several loose pieces of bone fell from it. How- ever, after careful attention from Dr. Gorst, the injured parties were able to return home before night.

DEATHS FROM STARVATION IN; Laistuote.-A parliamentary return, obtained on the motion of Mr. J. G. Talbot, was issued on Wednesday, showing the number of deaths in the metropolitan district in 1882, upon which a coroner's-jury returned a verdict of death from starvation or death accelera- ted by privation. From this it appears that the total was 58 deaths, of which 28 occurred in the eastern division of Middlesex, 23 in the centrai,. in the western, 3.in Green- wich, and 1 in Westminster; while there were none in East Surrey, the City and Southwark, the Duchy of Lancaster, the Tower of London, and, the verge of the Royal Palaces. HOLY TRINITY (WARBINGTON).—A pleasant match was p`ayed on Saturday last between the above clubs on the ground of the former, the lattei club securing an easy and decisive victory by an innings and 25 runs to spare. Talbot gave a chance at 30, but his score of 37, which included one of 5, three 3's, and six 2's was a very hard hit one.
