div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. In the 1, absence of Dr. Steele, Mr. Norman was voted to the chair. There were also present Dr. MacDougall, Messrs. P. Speak- man, J. W. Lightburn, .1. Williams, %V. Whittaker, E. Tim- mins, .1. Pritchard, F. Lake, R. Shaw, P. Briscoe, Taylor, J. Meadowcroft, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), W. Brookes (secretary), and %V. Barker (surveyor). THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN. The Medic' Officer of Health (Dr. hiouritz) reported that the number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 22. Of these, five were clue to diseases of the nervous system, four to abdominal disease, three to premature birth, two dropsy, and two bronchitis; cancer, childbirth, disease of the heart, scarlatina, measles, and whooping cough each accounted for one death; repre- aenting a death-rate of 17 per 1,000 per annum. Nine deaths occurred among children five years and undo. ‘nd five under one year. Five inquests were held. WAS IT PERSONAL? The minutes of lest meeting contained a reselution appoieting Mr. P. Speakman a member of the Ship Canal Committee.—Mr. LAKE observed that although lie was at that meeting each a resolution was not passed io his presence, and Dr. MACDOUGALL expressed hirroeil in similar terms, adding that he thought the resolution could not be legally passed until the motion appointing the committee was rescinded.—The CHAIRMAN explained that he left the chair on that occasion, but resumed his seat on oeing in- formed there was further business to transact. Several members, however, had left the room.—Mr. SPEAKMA.N said he was quite aware from what had come to his knowledge why these objections were taken.—Mr. LAKE and Dr. MacDotroaet. declared they had no personal motive in the matter. Al they wished for was that business should be condusted legally.—Mr. Speakman nevertheless gave in his resignation as a member of the Shir Canal Committee, and the minate; were passed. THE STREET CONTRACTOR AND HIS WORK: AN ULTIMATum. The Highway and Sanitary Committee having received Complaints of the manner in which Mr. Cliff carried out his contract, resolved that the consideration of the payment of Mr. Cliff's account amounting to £37 lOs for. street cleans- ing for the month ended May Ist be referred to the Board. —Dr. MAoDotteseao moved, and Mr. BRISCOE seconded the adoption of the minutes.—Dr. MACDOUGALL remarked that numeraus complaints had been received of the inadequate attention given to the streets for a considerable period. The contractor had been afforded an opportunity of discharging his duty, bat the complaints still continued, and hence the action of the committee. Whatever might be the cause of the non-fulfilment of the contract the Board had not to de- cide in a judicial capacity, but it was clearly their duty to take the matter into own hands, and to put an md to what many people considered a disgraceful state of things.— Mr. Seraw said the public seemed to be of opinion that Mr. Cliff was not earning the money which was being paid to him month after month ; and if the Board were satisfied that Mr. Cliff would not perform his work they had power under the agreement to re-let the contract, and charge Mr. Cliff the difference in the price.—ln answer to a question, the SURVEYOR said Mr. Cliff denied that he was not carry- ing out his contract. He stated he was doing his best, and could not do any better. The greatest complaints he (Mr. Barker) had were about the water, and if he had a water cart at hand he should set it to work. If there was any sweeping neglected, he did the work and charged Mr. Cliff with the cost. Mr. Cliff had only one water cart, and it was impossible to do the work with it.—Dr. MACDOUGALL said it was for the staff, who had got the power, to see that Mr. Cliff carried out his contract.—The CLERK , remarked that the difficulty was that Mr. Cliff tried to lay the blame on someone whose name be would not mention.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN observed that be understood that allusion. When the committee stopped payment of the bill, Mr. Cliff attacked him in the street. Be thought he would have struck him, because, as Mr. Cliff alleged, he had prevented the bill from passing.—Mr. *UAW: I would net enter into that.—Mr. SPEAKMAN: I want to know why Mr. Linaker mentioned it ?—The CLERK said Mr. Cliff did not mention Mr. Speakman's name. He heard him sly it was personal feeling on the part of some- one.—Mr. SPEAKMAN: What I have to object to is this, that because a member of this Beard happens to speak his mind, which be bad done frequently on Mr. Cliff's conduct, he should be attacked in this manner.—Mr. MEADOWCROFT moved that Mr. Cliff be called into the room and informed that it was the unanimous feeling of the Board that he was fulfilling his contract in a very inefficient manner, and un- less there was an improvement extreme measures would be adopted Mr. BRISCOE seconded. Dr. AfecDono.toa regarded the course suggested as an undignified 'one. It was for the Surveyor to see that Mr. Cliff fulfilled his contract, and the notices which he served, when Mr. Cliff failed to do so, would be valuable evidence in the court of law.—The resolution was then named, and Mr. Cliff called into the room. The CHAIR- MAN addressing him, said the Board were unanimous in their opinion that he was not doing his work as it ought to be done. There had been so many complaints of the work being improperly done, that the Board wished to know dis- tinctly if he intended in future to carry out the contract. If not the contract would be caecelled.—Mr. CLIFF said he could not help that. He referred to some grocer across the street whom it was impossible to satisfy, and said before be took the work only 27 to 29 loads of water were placed on the arrests per day. Now he was putting on 40 to 43.—The CHAIRMAN observed that the question was whether he Mould carry out the terms of his contract. Ho knew the consequences if he did not. He then ordered Mr. Cliff to retire.—On the motion of Dr. MacDonaeta., seconded by Mr. TIMMINS, it was decided that Mr. Cliff's account be ipaid.—The minutes were then passed. TUB CANAL BOATS' BILL, Mr. TAYLOR moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Canal Boats Committee, which contained a resolution driving the attentirol of the Board to clause 5 of the Canal 13 we' Act Amer d nent Bill, now before a Select Committee of the House of Commons, and suggesting that representa- Ceps should be made to the county members and to Mr. Burt, that the expenses of any inquiry instituted by the Local Government Board should not be wren out of the local funds, but should be borne by the Imperial Exchequer.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN Seconded the motion. He observed that Runcorn was the terminus of about 800 boats owned by persons in the town, and the Commissioners had the oversight of about 800 Others, and the committee thought it hard that besides look- leg after these craft they should have to bear the charge of any intoiry that night be instituted.—The SECRETARY said be had not a Bill at present in his possession, but it also taacte i that the salaries of inspectors appointed by the lo cal Government Board should be paid by Local duthorities.—Mr. PRITCHARD: Where does the revenue from these boats go to?—The SECRETARY re- pthd that, after the paynient of expenses, the surplus went the benefit of the ratepayers.—Mr PRITCHARD asked was it likely then that the Government would allow the costs of any inquiry into the remissness of locil authorities to be tame by the general funds of the country when the local authorities derived a revenue from the boats? He did not think such a thing ought to be asked for. If they did, the Government might very properly turn round and claim the whole of the fees —Mr. SPEAKMAN : We shall be glad to trUd ahem over.—The SECRETARY said the registration fee for each beet was ss. If this Bill was passed, the Local •Goyerement Board would have a right to a certain propor- tion of the registration fee far the general inquiries they might institute, and for the payment of the salaries of per- manent inspectors who might be appointed.—Mr MEADOW. ,i-sorr explained that by the Bill power was sought to fix the fee annually, so that if there w .s a deficiency in -e year, the Local Government Board could increase it in the 1: Ibiwing year. But the real point to be censidered in this clause was the fact that the local Authority might lose .fees of which they now had the benefit. There was no pro- v'.eion in the Bill for inquiries into the remissnessof authori- thee. It spoke only of general inquiries, and they did not ;mow hew often they might have them instituted. The Lecal (leverement Board might appoint an inspector at £7O or year, and althoueh they had a large number of isaats ie the district, the payment ef his salary might have to come from the rates.—The CLERK observed that no call could be made on the rate for such a purpose.—Mr. SPEAK- MAN said the beatholders in the town had taken the subject op and made a representation to the House of Commons. If the Bo ird passed this resolution it would considerably help those gentlemen.—The minutes were passed. THE LIBRARY COMMITTEE AND WATERLOO HOUSE. The following resolution was submitted :—The Library Committee having met the Commissioners' Special Com- mittee respecting the appropriation of certain rooms at Waterloo House for the purpose of the Library, and sug- gested the desirability of approariating other rooms on the rowth-east side of the house giving the required accommo- dation, they respectfully ask the Commissioners to grant the cee of the rooms suggested, and empower the Library Com- mittee, in conjunction with the Commissioners, to carry out ihe necessary alterations.— Mr. MEADOWCROFr was mov- iag time adoption of this regOution, when Mr. SHAW qaestioned whether the Board could legally act in accord- ance with the request of the committee.—The CLERK said time Commissioners could not delegate their powers to the committee. It was observed that the Waterloo House Com- mittee bad every desire to work in harmony with the Library Committee and would re cave any suggestions the letter %sighed to malie.—Ultimately, the reeolution was re- le. red to the former committee. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. THE BOARD TN A FIX: AMUSING DISCUSSION. Mr. SHAW said he had a few questions to ask of the chair- 'tan of the Ship Canal Committee, from whom they had Laird nothing fur some time. Seeing that a considerable time leed elapsed since the formation of the committee, he thought they ought to be able to put something before the IC)ard, so that they might now exactly how they stood and what they had to face. His first question was, "Is the Isle water channel to he constructed on the Runcorn side of the river, and through the first spin of the London arid rorth-Western Railway Bridge, as stated by the committee same time ago?" He thought they onght to know whether their position remained that day as it did some months a4o, '4:ben promises to that effect were made. Secondly: Is it now proposed to give a depth of -21 feet of water, as was then stated ? Acid th:rdly. Have satisfactory terms for securing trading ant other facilities for Runcorn been arranged with the Manchester Ship Canal Company, and will the chairman inform the Beard what such terms are. He did not iateni to offer any remarks now, but he thought ehose (rues - liens were really important, and ought to be answered before -they launched in any other extensive operations in connec- tion with the matter. He was sure the Board had given the

committee every facility for carrying out their views, 1 which were that, taking all the promises of the promoters into consideration, they would be able in a very efficient way, and almost without expense, to get concessions that could not be got by opposition, which some members of the Board considered ought to be taken at an earlier day. These were questions he thought the chairman of the committee would be able 0 answer.—The CHAIRSIA.N: Have you given him private notice ?—Mr. Slum eaid he raised the subject at the Highway Committee, and the chairman was quite aware that he would be asked again at the Board for the information in his power to give at that meeting.—Mr. LIGHTBURN replied that he was sure the Ship Canal Committee was most anxious to keep the ' Board well supplied with information. In the first place, he had had no notice of the exact position where the channel ' was going to run. Nobody could promise, at the time Mr. Shaw referred to, where the deep channel would be. As to the general procedure of the committee, he might inform them that the petition was lodged a few days after they I were empowered to do so so that there was no time lest. j They could not appose the bill in the House of Commons because the Ship Canal Committee was not in existence in j time for them to do so. After lodging the petition, the com- mittee received a communication from the promoters of the scheme asking what they required. The committee sub- mitted in writing the terms they should like for them, and subsequently a conference was held in Manchester on the 124th April. At that conference certain promises were made to the committee by the promoters, who were requested to forward them in writing. These had not been sent down to them up to that day, but inasmuch as there could be no advantage gained by forcing on the matter and putting the ratepayers to the expense of going to London, and as they had plenty of time to do so, they had waited. The committee had no desire to put the town to the ex- pense of sending a deputation to London, if they could effect the same end by more friendly and leas expensive means. The committee had held a meeting that day, ad- journed it until the following day (Thursday), when they would take into serious consideration whether they would give them any longer time to send the concessions down and consider any other action they might think proper to take. It was not the fault of the committee that opposition was not made on an earlier day, because they had no locus st xndi until the Bill got into the House of Lords.—The CLERK said several matters were submitted in writing to the promoters of the scheme at the meeting in Manchester. The first was with reference to the sewerage of Runcorn to the east of Mersey-street. Provision, it was pointed out, should be made in the Bill for the reception and carriage into the deep of the river Merser of the whole of the pre- leant and all the future sewerage on the south of the me of demarcation shown on the deposited plans. The promoters said they would give the Board a clause embody- ing this. is they were giving a similar clause to a trading firm in Runcorn; but they would not interfere at all with the Old Quay docks and the property they would purchase there, except so far as cutting off a portion of the canal. They would not at all interfere with these basins, which they would leave as they now were, and therefore the sewer- age could not be interfered with. The second point sub- mitted was " Whenever any public road is by the Bill pro- posed to be interfered with or stopped, provision should be made for connecting such roads with the other streets of the town in a manner satisfactory to the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners." The pro- moters promised to give a clause, that they would not in- terfere with any of the roads on the line of demarcation. They would leave those intact. "3. Depth of water in the Mersey. Provision should be inserted in the Bill making it incumbent on the canal company to leave to the docks and the foreshore of the district of Runcorn a depth of water equal at least to the depth which exists at the present time." The promoters promised to give the Board a clause which they thought would meet their requirements in that respect. "4. The port of Runcorn. Runcorn is at the present time a port and harbour authority, having defined limits and possessing certain rights and privileges, and a clause must be inserted in the Bill maintaining the port and harbour of Runcorn, and reserving to such port and harbour all rights and privileges now appertaining to them." The answer of the promoters was that they would give a clause in the terms asked for. "5. The Runcorn Improvement Commissioners strongly object to the clauses in the Bill enabling the Ship Canal Company to acquire the Duke of Bridgewater Canals and the dock and property of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, Limited, without some provision being made for keeping open at fixed rates the water carriage by means of the existing canals between Runcorn and Manchester. The Commissioners are advised that if the canal company acquire the right to close the Bridgewater canal communication between Runcorn and Manchester the company will have a monopoly ef the water carriage, and thereby the trade of Runcorn might be greatly injured, and obstacles placed in the way of the development of the trade which has so long been identified with the town." The promoters said they would give a clause to keep the canal open at the existing rateftif they did acquire it, but added that they had no present intention of buying, and the Bridgewater Navigation Company had no intention of selling it. The deputation was not satisfied with such a clause, because it came out that there were fresh rates, and they wished it to be stipulated that the canal should be kept open at the lowest rates. With reference to the next ques- tion, the promoters said they could not put in a clause giving the Commissioners the privilege of carrying material free, because if they did so every authority would ask for a like privilege. They would, however, give a clause for the free carriage of night soil and town refuse.—Mr. SHAW: And that is all you have done! You are just now where you were.—Mr. LIGHTBuRN : It is not our fault, certainly.—The CHAIRMAN said they had no locus standi before the House of Commons. There was no doubt that the Bill would be before the Committee of the House of Lords for at least three weeks. The committee thought they must wait with some amount of patience before they tried to force the hand of the Canal Company.—Mr. SHAW said the position was something like this: that the promises which the committee bad received were very much like the promises which were given by a representative of the promoters who came down to Runcorn some months ago and assured them on the highest authority that they would have 26 feet of water at the Runcorn side in this deep cut- ting. At the meeting in Bethesda schoolroom, Mr. Riley, the gentleman referred to, said "I have Mr. E. Leader Williams's authority to tell the meeting that the deep channel will come alongside the present quays of Runcorn so that the largest vessels may come up the canal and load and unload there." The Ship Canal Company had, how- ever, already decided that the deep should not be at the Runcorn side at all. They now told them that the deep should be in the middle, and go through the middle arch of the Runcorn Bridge. So much for the promises of the pro- moters of the Ship Canal. They also told the people of Runcorn that they were to have 26 feet of water but in the House of Lords they said they would give Runcorn 12 feet of water, There was not a single promise that had led the Commissioners ta the conclusion they arrived at some time ago, that had been carried out; and the inference was that the promises the committee had now got were simply to delay them, to put them in the background, and they would acconrelish ncthing. It seemed to him that they had got to this point: that the friendly op- position which they had carried out to their utmost ability had brought them no nearer than they were before. Op- position of a different character in nearly every other case had led to complete and satisfactory results. Individuals in Runcorn had got all they asked for, local "authorities on the other side of the river had got most complete and ac- ceptable terms arranged with the Ship Canal Committee, but they (the Runcorn Committee), who were going to do the thing so much better, in a different way, had got nothing, and they were no nearer a settlement that they were a while ago. [Mr. LIGHTBURN : Whose fault is.it P] Some gentlemen at that Board did not believe that that policy would lead to any- thing else, and the gentleman who took the thing in hand would not allow a number of members to do anything. Resolutions were brought there that would have accom- plished the same results for Runcorn as had been obtained elsewhere without a large expenditure of money, but they were upset. Of course, if the committee sat where it was now sitting, and the Board allowed it to remain, they would be landed in a very extensive undertaking. The question was whether seeing that they had completely failed [Mr. Lightburn, satiric- ally: We have not disputed that.] Oh, you dispute it, only it is too late. The question was whether they had to go to the Lords, and then they would find what it would cost the ratepayers to get what other Boards had been able to obtain without this shiffle-shuifie policy. He was not going to move any resolution. He was not disappointed by the re- port they had got that day. The Board was no nearer, and nobody else expected they would but this committee, but he thought it was time for the Board to consider its position and to take some decided action in the m Ater, not in this friendly fiddle-faddle sort of way, but in a proper business• like manner; and if they could not get, not promises, but actual clauses, inserted in the Bill which would he of benefit to the town, they should be prep ired to bring such opposi- tion to bear that would secure favourable clauses. He did not blame anybody, because these men had carried out what they said they would, and the Board hid heard the result.—Dr. MACDOUGALL said he thought the committee ought to be grateful that Mr. Shaw had vouch- safed this kind friendliness towards them Ifs was invited to be a member of the committee, but he could not find tthie. He could find time, however, to find fault with what the committee bad done. Perhaps it would tie as well to refresh Mr. Shaw's memory. On April 6th the Commissioners unanimously agreed to the following resolution :—" That the Commissioners present a petition in Parliament against the Ship Canal Bill through the Law Clerk, and that a committee consisting of Messrs. Fisher, Lightburn. Nor- man and MacDougall confer with him during the progress of the petition, and that the costs subsequent upon such petition be charged upon the general district rate." It was competent for Mr. Shaw if he anticipated pusillanimity or incapacity on the part of the committee to take exception to its appointment, but he did not do so. At that time it was not possible to present a hostile petition b3fore the House against this Bill.—The CLERK pointed out that on the 7th March he drew the attention of the Board to the fact that if they intended to take any steps with regard to the Ship Canal Bill it was time to do PO, but no action was taken. So far as time having elapsed, his shoulders were .',2ar.—Mr. Slum said he wae not blaming the clerk in auv way.—Dr. MacDounate thought the clerk's step just- liable; and he read an extract from the report of the meet- ing referred to by the clerk. At that meeting Mr. Shaw said there was nothing before Parliament affecting the interests of Runcorn. Here the doctor laughed heartily, and said : Pardon me; really this is 80 very goed I cannot help

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 9, 1883
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 9, 1883

smiling over it.—Mr. SHAW: Go on, doctor.—Mr. LAKE : Let the law clerk read it, doctor, if it is too much for you. —Dr. McDoricierx then read that Mr. Shaw said the plans relating to the Mersey below Runcorn would not ig lodged for another 12 months, and that the drainage of -Runcorn was not then affected in the least. Dr. MacDougall, resuming his remarks, said whatever his views were then, certainly he had no reason to doubt either the sincerity 9r integrity of the promoters of the Bill. The Board were given to understand that they would get concessions, and that a friendly spirit would perhaps bring them more than a hostile spirit and an expenditure of money. Mr. Shaw, whatever he might think about the feebleness of the committee, might fairly be charged with insincerity. It was through Mr. Shaw's observations at the meeting, on March 7th, that the Board did not take any action on that day. He was actually responsible for the Board being too late to lodge a petition in the House of Commons; and it was impossible on the 6th April to do anything except in a friendly way. At the conference in Manchester the committee were led to b.lieve that they would get almost all they wanted, and cLuses were to be forwarded for the consideralon ,of the oard ; but he believed these had not yet arrived. Theis:Lee the members of the committee could not be charged with not doing their duty, but whether other people had kolzeu faith with the committee or net, was a matter he would not attempt to say one word upon. Clause 25 of the bill relating to the deep channel was not now before the committee of the House of Commons. It was simply alluded to to get information, before they took evidence of the feasibility of the scheme from the Mersey to Manchester, as to whether it was feasible from Runcorn to Liverpool. He considered twelve feet at low water would be a good depth.—The CLERIC: This is not before us.—Dr. McDonG- ALL : Mr. Shaw has digressed to discuss it.—Mr. Slum: I didn't discuss it. I asked a question.—Dr. McDouckau, said he did not wish to discuss the question, but he asserted that the Commititee had done what they could. There was plenty of time to oppose the bill, and if Mr. Shaw wished the Committee to spend money, they were perfectly willing to do so if they could get anything better than they could by acting in a friendly way; but he took it that the proper mstitutional way would be to exhaust every possible means before they commenced to spend money. If they could not get what they wanted, then fight. Mr. LIGHT- BURN asked what was done by the Ship Canal Committee of which Mr. Shaw was appointed Chairman on December 28th 1882. Mr. Shaw was about to reply, when Mr. MEADOWCROFT rose and said it would be discovered that Dr. McDougall had only found a mare's nest in the extracts he had read. In a matter of this description it was important to have a good memory. When Mr. Shaw made the statements alluded to, he (Mr. Meadowcroft) and others entertained the same views to a certain extent—that the examiner of standing orders had decided that that part of the Bill relating to the Mersey was cut off—and therefere Mr. Shaw said that so far as the Mersey was concerned the interests of Runcorn were not affected. The promoters of the scheme now said they had power, under certain Acts, under which the Mersey Conser- vancy were constitued to do certain things which the exa- miner stated they had not ; a change came over the spirit of the dream. It was asked why Mr. Shaw did not object to the Committee. It would have been unwise to object to such an array of talent and experience as was there to be found amongst them. (Laughter.) He asked what were the powers of the Committee with regard to expenditure.—The CLERK said be should advise the Committee not to incur the least expense without asking the sanction of the Board. —Dr. MacDouchaLL said the Board did not fully trust the committee, which was therefore terribly crippled. Mr. Thrums : I think we are wasting a good deal of our time. —Mr. MEADOWCROFT blamed the committee not for what they had done, but what they had rot done, especially for not pressing for the clauses they ha a asked for.—The CLERK said he had been to Manchester once since the committee, and had written to threpromoters several times. He had a letter from the promoters on the previous morning, saying they would let him have the clauses by the following morn- ing's post.—Mr. MEADOWCROFT said he simuld have been more satisfied if the committee had come with some resolu- tion asking the Board to take a definite course.—The CHAIR- mew : Would you suggest that the committee have further powers, and that a leputation go to London to try what they .c en do ?—Mr. Mnapowcaorr : No. I think the committee ought to formulate resolutions and bring them before the Board for approval. The CHAIRMAN: There is no time, you know. We have been waiting five weeks, and cannot get an answer. If we got to London, and get the promoters in a corner, perhaps they would grant us something.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN : Empower me, and I will settle it all to-morrow.—Dr. MacDonoeu, said it was a great mistake that the resolution appointing the committee was not of a wider character. They had already been to Manchester, and incurred expense, and each individual would have to pay his own costs. That was exactly how it , was.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN expressed his sorrow that this dis- cussion did not take place in committee. These proceedings were going to the public, and they would be looked upon as gentlemen who did not know how to conduct their business. He urged that some energetic action should be taken or else the Board would be too late to obtain anything. He did not despair of something being done, if the committee would tackle the thing in a proper manner.— Mr. LIGHTBURN said the committee had been charged with apathy, and with not doing the work they were delegated to do.—Mr. Snaw : Who charged you with apathy ?—Mr. Liairraunte : In general terms you have, and your whole remarks tended to that idea. But it is the Board that has been apathetic. We have done a greet deal. We have at once approached the Ship Canal people.—Dr. MacDouGALL : At our own expense ?—Mr. Ltuirrnuner : No, not exactly. , We have approached the Ship Canal.—Mr. Sitew : That you have told us. (Laughter.)—Mr. Ltarrrnumr: I will tell you again if you will not interrupt me. We have tried suaviter in mod° —(hear, hear)—with them, and we have put the town to no expense. One of the first gentlemen in the room charged us with wasting public money. Mr. SHAW : I was not aware that I had charged anything. Mr. LIGHTBURN : You have insinuated.—Mr. Slaw : Mr. Chairman, this is only soft talk. (Loud laughter.)—The CHAIRMAN: Come, come, now.—Dr. MacDoerGau, : I rise to a point of order. Surely Mr. Sbaw will withdraw that expression.—Mr. SHAW: No- body has charged you with spending a cent.—Mr. LIGHT- BURN: I say you would have done if we had spent a cent. What! do say, and still say, is that if we had spent money without first asking permission we should have been charged with a want of regard for the ratepayers' pockets.—Mr. SHAW: That's only supposing.—Mr. LIOHTBURN : Never you miss The CHAIRMAN : I must appeal to you, gentlemen.—Mr. SHAw : This is all supposition.— Mr. LIOHTBURN : I am only judging by the tenor of the remarks. Mr. SHAW: He has no right to judge n that way. Mr Chairman.—The CHAIRMAN: Quite enough has been said about it.—Mr LIGHTBURN: I must insist I upon being allowed to sky what 1 have got to say. What ! I have got to say is this, that no member of this Board has I been able to point to any neglect of duty, and, under these , circumstances, I do think that when we do our best we ought to get more sympathy and consideration than some 'gentlemen are disposed to vouchsafe to us. Ido think we ' ought to have powers, if we are to do anything, to form a deputation to go to London [laughter. Mr. P. Speakman: We must have no going to London], if you think it neces- saiy.—Mr. P. Spuenaux : If we can meet at Manchester, let's all go down.—Mr. LIGHT/31MR : If we can meet at Man- chester, it will meet our best wishes. We have no wish to spend money.—The CLERK: As this matter is before you, have you any instructions for me ?—Mr. LAKE: Meet the committee.—The CLERIC: I shall have nothing to do .with the committee any further.—The CHAIR- MAN: The committee's hands are fast.—Dr. MacDovaALL asked if it would simplify matters if the committee were to I resign. If the committee were not to be entrusted with the conduct of this affair, then the best thing for them to do is to tender their resignation. He would no more come there to be bullied and badgered by certain parties any more than he would kiss their toes. He came there to give disinterested service to the public—After some further talk, Mr. LIGHT- BURN proposed "That the committee have power to wait lupon the promoters of the Ship Canal Committee in London or elsewhere if thought necessary."—Dr. MecDouciam, , ! seconded the motion to test the meeting. A great deal had been said there that day. They knew that Mr. Shaw was very capable of instructing the committee, and he thought if Mr. Shaw would consent to act upon the committee he might be of some advantage in rescinding the present reso- lution.—Mr. MEADOWCROFT objected to this motion being passed, because the Board would be placed in a ridiculous position. The committee might obtain clauses, but would they be acceptable to the Board P—Fcr the motion tbere voted—Messrs. Taylor, Lake, MacDougall, Lightburn, Whittaker, Pritchard, and the Chairman-7. Against : Messrs. Timmins, Shaw, Meadowcroft, Briscoe, Speakman, and Williams.—The Board then separated at half-past five, after sitting for three hours.

Miss Braddon is going to bring an action for breach of promise against Mr. Caine, M.P. He put down his mea- sure for Wednesday, which was to have abolished such actions as led Biggar the other day into difficulties. Miss Braddon came down to the House to hear the very in- teresting question threshed out. It would have made a good chapter in a novel, but a droary debate on a stand- ing order occupied the whole time of the House, and Miss Braddon is so disappointed at her loss of time that she rationally thinks she has a claim for compensation; and Mr. Biggar now complains bitterly of the obstruction in the 'louse of Commons which stands in the way of a measure so good as Mr. Caine's.

Mr. Parnell as a "patriot" is a familiar figure, but Mr. Parnell as a pavement contractor is a spectacle of absolute novelty. Nevertheless, that gentleman, eager to do busi- ness, has announced his readiness to supply the Dublin Cor- poration with paving-stones at twenty-four shillings a ton, and the Corporation, with that Cautious prudence which prevails amongst commercial men, have agreed to take some "on trial." If Mr. Parnell's paving-stones are equal to the quality of his "patriotic" intentions wa may expect to see Oa streets of the Irish capital as well paved as those of a certain region, which shall be nameless.

There appears to be a strong opinion in official quarters that there will be no War between France and China. The difficulties of military operations at any distance remote from the seaboard would be extremely great, and if France is not desirous of fighting her way through the belt of inde- pendent territory wieich extends between Tonquin and the Chinese frontier, the Pekin Government will, it is believed, be prepared for peace. The Chinese authorities will not consent to have France adjoining their border, and for France to get there would be a most hazardous enterprise. It is thuoght that the French operations will carefully be confined to limits such as will not occasion a conflict with the Imperial Government.

Sir George Bowyer is dead, and with him disappears one of the most familiar of London figures. He knew life from every point of view—as a politician, as a theologian, as a man of the world, as a Protestant, as a Romanist, as a trainbearer of a cardinal, as a Liberal, as a Tory, as a Home- Ruler, as a seceder from Parnellism, and as an authority upon archmalogy; but to one idea he was always constant. He was, and he loved to be thought, a constitutional lawyer. His delight in the technicality and difficulty of this study knew no bounds, and he craved for no greater pleasure than to see his authority quoted in Parliament, at least when I knew him. He was long-winded and tedious, but he was very much liked, and his little vanities only made him more interesting to his contemporaries. He had been somewhat enfeebled for some months past. I met him a very little while ago when he was visiting some archm)logical curiosity, and he was even then complaining; but his death has come very suddenly, and it caused genuine sorrow among his old friends in St. Stephen's. At all events, he died where he wished to die—in the shadow of the Temple, whose gardens he loved so well. A story is told of Sir George which is, I,believe, true—a virtue which cannot be claimed for all Parliamen- tary stories. He sat in the House during the last Parlia- ment. He had a bushy grey beard, and plenty of hair on his head. On one occasion he dyed both beard and hair, and he dyed them with such effect that the doorkeeper would not let him pass. Sit George Bowyer was compelled to seek the intervention of an irish friend, who was able to vouch ter his individuality notwithstanding the disguise. After this he allowed tbe dye to fade away, without any attempt to renew it. Another "Moderate Home Ruler" who was some years ago as grey as a badger is now as dark as was Sir George on this noteworthy occasion.

In his speech at Chatham, on Tuesday night, Lord Ran- dolph Churchill challenged his opponents to prove the charge of veiled obstruction against the Conservative party in the House of Commons. One piece of evidence sup- porting the indictment may be found in the fact that at the first ten meetings of the Grand Committee on Law his Lorship showed extraordinary activity, and only ten clauses of the Court of Criminal Appeal Bill were disposed of. Being indisposed, he failed to attend the two remaining sittings, the result being that 18 clauses were agreed to. The noble Lord seemito reverse his opinion very easily. At the tenth meeting of the Grand Committee he emphatically explained that the bill was a sham, and that was the reason of his opposition. At Chatham, however, he remarked that it "will make a wise and useful change."

Another Irish duel is on the carpet—or at least the materials have been found, and an ultimatum will shortly be sent to an hon. member who of late hasmot distinguished himself by a loyal following of Mr. Parnell. That member is Mr. Macfarlane, one of the representatives of Carlow County, a Pervert to the Roman Catholic Church like his colleague Mr. Gray, but altogether out of sympathy with the half-dozen irreconcilables who now constitute the Irish national party. Because Mr. Macfarlane ventured to put a question in the House reflecting upon the editor of an Indian paper, whose imprisonment for contempt of court has lately attracted some attention, Mr. O'Donnell, at the next meeting of the Irish party on Mond ty, has resolved to move a vote of censure on Mr. Macfarlane. The upshot, I imagine, will be that that gentleman will follow Mr. Coon's example and remove to the other side of the House. That, I under- stand, is what is desired by Mr. Parnell, who is anxious to weed his party of all doubtful followers. It is no less desired by Mr. Macfarlane, vf hose relationship to his Church as brother-in-law of the Roman Catholic Bishop of Notting- ham, places him out of harmony with the Parnellites in their present condition.

Sir William Harcourt made a statement on Thursdny night which ought to modify the judgment which has been universally passed upon the Resebery incident. It seems that Sir William Harcourt has a personal affection for Lord Rosebery, and Lord Rosebery a personal affection for Sir William Harcourt. The Home Secretary made this announcement on Thursday night in his most unctuous manner, and with an expression of surprise that any other idea should have entered anybody's bead which was mani- festly genuine. What we are entitled to say, therefore, is that he gave Lord Rosebery an opportunity of bringing clearly before the Premier the unsatisfactory nature of his appointment as Minister for Scotland without either ad- ministrative power or legislative initiative. In s.o doing. it is now obvious that Sir William Harcourt acted as frienA to Lord Rosebery.

The" women of England "do not seem to be very much in earnest in deprecating the marrime of their husbands with their sisters-in-law. The machTfiery of the Conserva- tive patty and the machinery of the Church has been used to get a big national petition up against this alteration of our family relations. The result is that the total number of signatures to the petition reaches only 37,000. It is not good enough to be a great demonstration, and will hardly influence a single vote.

Astonishment fell upon visitors to the House of Commons on Tnurtelay who happened to enter the House at a certain hour. They found the Prime Minister's favourite place oc- cupied by a fine-looking, bald-headed gentleman, whom many even inveterate politicians failed to recognise, but who spoke with a decision, assurance, and authority which would not have been strange in the Prime Minister himself. One's first impulse was to believe that there had been a change of Government in the night ; the second grim suggestion was that this was the Elisha whose coming Lord Randolph Churchill is always predicting. "Elisha !" cried the at- tendant when he heard the idea. " Who's Elisha This is Smith." Of further detail everybody was greedy. Then it came out. This is the Colonel Smith, returned a few weeks ago for High Wycombe, who became a member of Her Majesty's Government before he had set foot in the House of Com- mons,aud is drawing £3OO a year in that postof Parliamentary Groom, for his ambition to fill which Mr. Grenfell lost his seat at Salisbury. Colonel Smith had none of the air of the novice about him. No stranger would have suspected that he was makings maiden effort. If he had been a Minister for a quarter of a century, and this had been his 252nd speech. he could not have been less nervous or more busi- nesslike. He quoted Acts of Parliament like a lawyer, and showed a knowledge of commercial life which proved that his financial experience had not been thrown away upon him ; and he did not a little to establish the doctrine in the House of Commons that it was right for a railway company to pay dividend oat of capital before it has begun to make any profi's.

Mr. G. W. Rus?ell is the new man of the Ministry. To- day he is Secretary to the Local Board. Some ten days ago he solemnly abjured Whiggery and threw in his lot with the Liberals. His reward has not been long in coming. The Russells never did have long to wait for their rewards. His rapidly-arising recognition comes with an offer of office. I do not think that a voice will be raised against the appoint- . ;neut. Though Mr. Russell is only 30 years of age. his ability has enabled him to take a distinct place in politics. Of a Whig family, grandson of a Duke of Bedford, his whole training was Whig. To have been strong before 30 to cast off purely Whig traditions and to have disclaimed them ia the very week when, the Whigs about him were trying to organise a faction for the recovery of power, and who. were turning upon him for disloyalty to his order, is to show signs of great strength. He is still viewy, but what would a man of thirty be worth if he were not " viewy." At that age "viewiness" is a sign of thoughtfulness. Mr Russell has academical distinction. He was scholar and prizeman at University College, oxford He is a lawyer, anl has studied his subject; and hie opinions about land reform have been taken up in opposition to both family tradition and legal training. Personally, he exercises that peculiar charm which has always been associated with the. best men of the Russell family; and he should soon rise hig'eter in the rinks of the Ministry. His appointment comes after very little parliamentary experience, for he has been ia the House only since IMO; but it says not a little that hz has won a front rank among independent members wtithout exciting ,07,- of that hostility which mere intrusiom, 'an,variably pro- duccs.

On Tuesday, in the House of Commons, Mr. McMinnies presented a petition from the master builders of Warrington against the Employers' Liability Act Amendment Bill and the Steam Boilers' Explosions Bill. The meeting held in Golborne-street schoolroom last week was that of the "Warrington Workingmen's Per- manent Benefit Building Society," and not that of the "Warrington Permanent Benefit Building Society," as stated In our last issue.

WidtamaroN Scgoor, OF SCIENCE.—The session has just been brought to a close by the holding of the annual May examinations. The following are the numbers of can- didates who have sat for examination in the various subjects :—lron and steel 16, steam 13, applied mechanics 11, mathematics 7, chemistry (theoretical) 10, chemistry (practical) 12, brewing 2, carriage building 1, mechanical engineering 1, making a total of 73. The successes of the students will be announced in due course. A LOCAL CRICKETTER IN THE COUNTY ELEVEN.—Mr. S. M. Crosfield, a member of the Warrington Cricket Club, last week played in the match Lancashire v. Oxford Univer- sity, and distinguished himself by making the highest score of his eleven in the first innings, and the second highest in the second innings. Mr. Crosfield scored 43 runs in the first innings, and the second time Lancashire defended the wickets he played a most promising innings of 49, in which were six 4's, three 3's, and three 2's.

AN IMPUDENT ROBBERY AT WARRINGTON.-011 Mon- day, at Warrington Police Court, Thomas Leatherbarrovr, labourer, 64, St. James'-street, was charged with having stolen a boy's suit, value 5s 61, from Mr. Morton's shop. near Warrington Bridge. In consequence of articles having been stolen from the shop, a boy was set to watch on Satur- day, by the manager, Mr. Kerr. During the evening prisoner went to the iad and persuaded him to fetch some sweets from a shop a short distance away, and during his absence prisoner took the suit of olothee produced. A young woman, however, saw him walking off with his booty, and gave in- formation to Mr. Kerr, who pursued the man and brought him back to the shop, where he was given into custody.— The Chief Constable said prisoner had been several times convicted, and at his request prisoner was committed to the Sessions for trial.

ANOTHER ROBBERY FROH WARRINGTON MARKET HALL. —John Nolan, a labourer at Bewsey Wire Ropery, and re- siding at Ashton-street, was charged at Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with having stolen two pocket knives, value Scl., the property of Thomas William Podmore, of Corporation-street, Manchester.—Prisoner pleaded guilty.— The Chief Constable said the prosecutor kept a stall in the Market Hail, and on Saturday night prisoner was seen to go to it and examine a number of articles thereon, after which be took up the two pocket knives and put them up the sleeve of his coat, and then put his hands in his pockets. Information of what had taken place was given to P.C. Chantler, who was only a short distance away, and be took the prisoner into custody.—Prisoner. who said he had been looking at the knives and put them into his pocket without thinking, was sentenced to one month's imprisonment.

THE BIRTH AND, DEATH" RATE OF WARRINGTON.—For week ending June 2nd. The mean temperature was 51.1 Fahrenheit, and therefore about the same as the pr ceiling week. The maximum temperature 65 F. was recorded on the Ist inst., and the minimum temperature 31 F. on the 27th ult. The rainfall measured .23 inches. The general direction of the wind was south-west. During the week, which was the 22nd of the current year, 33 births and 20 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 234 per 1,000; against 196 the average of the previous four weeks, and against 346 the corresponding week of last year. The deaths included 1 from croup, 1 from whooping cough, 1 from burning, 1 from drowning, and 5 from lung disease.—Two cases of infectious disease were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.—Jomq H. GORNALL, medical officer of health. SAVAGE ASSAULT BY A WARRINGTON WOMAN.-013 Wednesday, at Warrington Police Court, Annie Crayton or Gordon, a potter, living in Winwick Road, was charged on a warrant with having assaulted Mrs. Brooks, also a pot- ter. Prosecutrix, who appeared with her head bandaged and large blood stains on her dress, said that on Monday night, she was going up the street when prisoner called to her to stop. When she turned round prisoner came up and asked her "why she had told those tales about her" to which she replied that she had said nothing about her and had nothing to say to her now. Prisoner then hit her on the head with a quart can which she took from her (prose- cutrix) and knocked her to the ground twice. She had lost two or three gills of blood from the wound on the head, and was under the care of a doctor.—A witness was called who corroborated the foregoing s'atement, and prislner was ordered to pay 20s. and costs or go to prison for a month.

ASSAULT ON A WIFE: JUDICIAL SEPARATION GRANT E D —A tailor,. named John Wm. Dickenson, of 5, Greenall- street, was charged on Wednesday, at the Warrington Police Court, with having assaulted his wife on Saturday. Prisoner, it seemed, had been in the habit of ill-using his wife, and had been before the magistrates on other occa- sions for similar offences. Frequent quarrels had taken place between them lately, and on Saturday prisoner went to his wife's aunts, at 3, School-street, Latchford, dragged his wife about by the hair, and gave her a violent blow on the eye —Prosecutrix now said she desired a separation. Her husband when not under the influence of drink was very good, 'hut she compla.iced that he was guilty of im- morality, and that when drunk he ill-used her.—The Chief Constafite gave the woman a very good character for being a hard-working woman, and said he believed there was not 'a better wife in Warrington..—The Bench sentenced defen- 'dant to one month's hard labour, granted a judicial separa- tion, and made as order for the prisoner to contribute 12s per week towards his wife's maintenance.

The parties are both stallholdars in War- rington Market, the complainant being a dealer in second- hand clothes, and the defendant a vendor ois oil cloths. The case was disinissA on na.yment of costs by defendant, which he dirt with great readiness, remarking that he never had no intention sto.ksurniver, assaulting tht oraplainaut.

ASSAULTING A SOLDIER WITH A WHIP STOCK AT WAH- ItlNGTON.—Thomas hall, farm labourer, Penketh, was charged at Warrington Police Court on Monday with hav- ing assaulted James Nevin, a soldier, in the White Bear beerhouse, Buttermarket-street, on Saturday night.—P.S. Spinks said that when passing the White Bear about half- past nine on Saturday night he noticed that the lobby was crowded with soldiers, and they were making a great noise, lie went in, and while there saw prisoner, who was seated on a table, get up and go to prosecutor, who was a short distance away, and strike him across the head with the whip stock produced. Witness Chen went for the assist- ance of two constables to quell the disturbance that was going on, and when they returned they found prisoner hail rreptitiously left the hoe, but he was found concealed in shippon.—Prosecutor gave his evidence leluctantly, and /AM be did not wish to press the the charge.—Prisoner ws fined 10s and costs, or 16 days' imprisonment in de- fault of payment. _

ASS-kill; Ply A BROTHER AT WA,RRINOTON.—On Thurs- day, at Warrington. Police Court, Patrick Farrel, a yonnE; man living in Bank-street, was char.7'ed with having as- saulted his sister, Annie Farrel, who lives close by her brother.—Complainant eaid that on Tueaday defendant came into his mother's house and waalted money, and because there was none for him lie began to kick an drag her (com- plainant) about. He threatened her with a knife. It was not the first time he had assaulted her, and she wanted pro- tection against him.—Defendant said that when he came home from his work on Tuesday he went to his mother's and asked for a pint of ale, which she gave him, and then he asked for money with which to buy tobacco, and his sister thereupon took up a basin and threw it at him, butltimissed biin, and coming in contact with a door, was broken. lie followed her out into the street and pulled her hair for what she had done.—Complainant denied this statement. lit answer to the Bench, defendant said he was married'anti earned his own living, and the provocation given to-liis sister was his going to his mother's begging. Defendant was ordered to find two sureties in £5 each. KICKING CASE AT WARRINGTON. A sentence of six months' hard labour was passed upon John M'Carmick at Warrington Borough Court, on Tuesday, for an assault upon his wife, Julia. M'Cormick is a labourer at Messrs. Evans and Co.'s coal yard, and resides in Foundry-street. On Sunday night he went to his father-in-law's house and asked for his wife. He was told she was there sitting on a stool, and although she had a child in her arms, he gave her a sa- vage kick, which knocked her off the stool. He then caught his wife by the hair of the head, and would undoubtedly have severely ill-treated her had not his father-in-law thrown him to the ground, whereon he was held until P.C. Corcoran arrived. The prisoner had previously served two terms of two and three months' imprisonment respectively for similar offences, and the Chief-Constable stated "John believed in thumping the women, and would fight very hard and fast when there was a lot of his pals with him, and a policeman, was in view."—Major Cartwright said the ptisoncr was a great coward, and richly deserved the full penalty.—A judi cial separation was granted to the wife, and prisoner was or- dered to pay 12s a week towards the maintenance of his wife and three children.

A STRANGE SATURDAY NIGHT ADVENTURE AT WAR- RINGTON.—At Warrington Police Court, on Monday, a carter named Edward Murphy, residing at 41, School-brow, was charged with having entered the housa occupied by George Ryder, Hopwood-street, with intent to commit a felony. On Saturday night Mrs. Ryder was taken home in a state of helpless drunkenness by her sister, Ellen Gallop, who locked her in the house alone, and took her (Ryder's) children back with her to her own house, until their father came home. As their father had not returned at a quarter past eleven Ellen Gallop took the children back home, and when they were approaching the house one of the children drew her attention to the house window being broken, and said that someone was in the house. She unlocked the door, and saw prisoner run upstairs. Having a frying-pan in her hand she called to prisoner and told him if he came down she would hit him with. it; but rather than face the frying pan he risked a fall from the bedroom window and so escaped. Mrs. Ryder, who was lying asleep on the sofa in the house, was awakened by the noise that was going on, but she had no recollection of what had passed. Prisoner wc.s afterw.rds apprehended at his lodgings by P.C. Smith. The assumption was, the Chief Constable said, that prisoner was aware of the helpless condition of Mrs. Ryder, and that he entered the house for an immoral or some other unlaw- ful purpose.—Prisoner, who said he was knocked through the window by a man, was sent to gaol f.*r one mcnth's hard labour.

A DRUNKEN. FEAM—At the Manchester City Police Court, on Tuesday morning, Patrick O'Hara, described as a general dealer, living in Ashley's-lane, Rochdale-road, was charged before Mr. Headlam with being drunk and disor- derly on the premises of the Cheshire Lines Railway Com- pany, and doing damage to the company's property to the extent of £3.—lt appeared from the evidence given that on Monday evening the prisoner was a passenger by an ex- press train from Liverpool to Manchester, and when the train stopped gt Warrington the guard was told that the prisoner had been very quarrels3me on the way up from Liverpool. The other persons who were in the compart- ment changed carriages at Warrington, and the prisoner was looked in. When the train was passing through Urin- ston the guard heard the sound of glass being broken, and on the arrival of the train at the Central Station in Man- chester, it was seen that the prisoner had broken the win- dows in- both the doors, and had also broken one of the side lights. In doing so he had cut his right hand very severely, and the cushions and fhior of the compartment were covered , with blood. He was taken to the Infirmary, where his hand I was dressed.—ln reply to the usual question from the Veneta the prisoner said he had been drinking heavily since Whit- suntide, and was-drunk on Monday. He did not know how he came to treak the windows.—A fine of 403 and costs was-imposed, and-the prisoner was also ordered to pay £3, the amount of the damage. In default he would have to gh to-prison for one month with hard labour. THE FIERCE ASSAULT ON COUNTY POLICEMEN.—At War- rington Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, William Stokes, a puddler, whose residence is at Warburton-street, Orford, was charged on a warrant with having assaulted P.S. Pattieon and P.C. Whittingham, on the 7th ult.—The officers went to serve a commitment order on prisoner's brother on the day named, and they found him and prisoner in the Star beerhouse, Longford-street. The brother said he could not pay, and he was invited by the officer to go to Mr.Buckton's office. He went a short distance with them, and then attempted to escape, and became so violent that they found it necessary to put an the handcuffs. While this was being done prisoner came up the street and gave P.S. Petition a "run kick," in the side, smashing his watch to pieces. The officers struggled- some time with prisoner's brother and prisoner during that time threw two bricks at there, one of which came in contact with a door, and did considerable damage to it. He then procured an iron stool, and was just about to dash it OR the officers' heads when it was snatched from his hands by some women who were h the crowd which had assembled. The brother was then overpowered and taken to the police station, and dealt wieh at the last Petty Sessions, but prisoner escaped, and bad since been apprehended at Wellington, in Shropshire.—The Bench said the police muet be protected in the executiotual their duty, and prisoner, who had previously served a'ex months' im- prisonment for highway robbery with violeoce, was sent to gaol for- six.months with hard labour. AB$tl7LT ON A YOUNG GIRL AN W.L.RINOTON.—Lewiso Williams, about 30 years of age, who iaemploved by the London and- North- Western Railway Corapany as an engirat- tirem in, and resides at 43, Hovle-streaa, was charged at Warrington Pa/ice Court, on Mondays with having cam- tnitted an indecent assault on a girl rained Eliza WOotten, 11 years of age, at the Vulcan beer:louse, Dallam-lane, on Saturday.—From the statement of the Chief Constable, which sass corroborated by, the witneeaes, it seemed that the girl, whose parents live at Dewsbura, Yorkshire, was-.en a visit to her uncle at the Vulcan hae.thense, Dallain-laae. Prisoner after a while went out' of the snug, where le had been, into the tap-room, where he called for anot'aar glass of beer, which was also eerved by the girl, but 0)13,1W) did not pay for, saying he would see the landlord (her luz,/.e) at the beginning of the week. kbe then carried the bey r into the snug, and a short time alter the girl had occaaliVa to go into the room to replenish the- box on the trasteitepiece with matches. Prisoner was afterwards apprehended.—The priroj plea-led in extenua- tion of the offence, which lee adtr.eitted, that he was under the Mum:l3 al beer.—The Mayor said this was about as I,a-I a care as could be brourpt before them, atld it was a 7eat Me,4y for the poor 'girl that she had escaped the ,ifisonar's clutches. TO CONSUMERS OF GAS.—The Warrington CorporE• tion Gas Committee, being desirous of further encourag- ing amongst their consumers the use of gas for cooking and other purposes, are now prepared to sell, let on hire, or pur- chase lease, GAS COOKING STOVES, at a small half-yearly rest charge. country.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE endorsed the Premier's observatiens.—On a division the numbers were For Mr. Broadhurst's motion, 80; against, 247. Mr. PARNELL then moved that in the opinion of the House the question of corrupt and illegal practices at Pariiatnentary elections in Ireland should be reserved for separate con- sideration. He said there was no more reason for including Ireland in this bill than there was for including England in the Crimes Bill of last year.—Mr. G-- d th motion, and Mr. GT - LBSOX Oppose e -..Vv01/2 said it c)uld not be accepted. levoral Irish members, in supporting the motion, accused the Irish judges of being unfitted to deal with election matters.—ln reply to this objection, the ATTORNEY- GENERAL for Ireland said that of the last four appointments to the Irish bench three of the judges had never sat in the House of Commons.—After considerable discussion, Mr. Parnell's amendment was rejected by 243 votes against 31. M. ERRINGTON'S MISSION.—The House then went into Committee proforma, and the House resuming, Report of Supply was brought up, and Loreßandolph Churchill again returned to Mr. Errington's alleged mission to Rome. The noble lord (speaking at half-past twelve) introduced some novelty into the subject by referring to the Premier's speech at Stafford House on Saturday in eulogy, as he said, of Garibaldi, and marvelled at such a return for the rope's ser- vices in Ireland. Mr. Gladstone, rising with apparent in- tention to reply to this tirade, was met with loud cries of •' No ! "from the Liberal benches. He explained that his re- ferences to Garibaldi had been purely personal, and dis- claimed the intention attributed to his speech by Lord Randolph Churchill. As to Mr. Errington the right hon. gentleman repeated what has been frequendy asserted —that Mr. Errington went to Rome "for his own personal occasions," but that his opportunities of communicating to the Head of the Roman Catholic Church a true and impert- ant statement of tke state of affairs in Ireland had been 'gladly recognised by Earl Granville. Mr. Errington's visit had been so prolonged, and such importance had been attached to it, that a record of the correspondence would be left at the Foreign Office for the information of the succes- sor of Lord Grauville.—After an animated speech from Mr. Cowen, tho report of Supply was agreed to.—The remaining orders were disposed of, and the House adjourned.

13RESCOT UNION.--CONTRACTS FOR PROVISIONS, &c.—Persons desirous of CONTRACTING with the Guar- dians of this Union, for the next six months, for supplying at the Workhouse the several articles hereinafter named, viz. : Flour, catmeal, salt butter, bacon, lard, cheese, peas, beef, mutton, suet, groceries, wine and spirits, eggs, potatces, hay, wheat straw, coal, burgy, linen drapery, woollen drapery, smallwares, tinware, hardware, ironmongery, earthenware, leather, boots and shoes, brushes, timber, coffins, and other articles, are requested to deliver sealed Tenders, upon forms to be obtained at my office, at the Board-room of the said Union, in Whiston, on or before Thursday, the 14th June, before 10 a.m. Such tenders will be opened at the meeting of the Guar- dians on the last-named day. The Guardians will also take tenders for new milk and fresh butter for twelve mosths. The daily consumption of milk is about BO gallons. Samples to be seen at the Workkouse. Security will be required for the per- formance of the contrac's, It is competent for any person within the Linton to tender for any of the articles separately. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any tender,—By order of tke Board. B. H. HARTLEY, Union Clerk. Union Offices, Whiston, Prescot, 31st May, 1883.
